Part 0  ·  Lesson 1 of 13

Why this part exists

The syllabus lists pre-algebra and pre-calculus as prerequisites. This part is that prerequisite, written out.

Quantitative Methods does not teach arithmetic, fractions, powers or how to solve an equation. It assumes them, from the first slide. Week 1 opens with "Levelling Up" and moves through first-order equations, systems and quadratics in nine slides, at a speed that only works if none of it is new.

So this part comes first. It assumes nothing. If you can already do all of it, you will lose twenty minutes confirming that, and the rest of the document will be easier. If you cannot, this is the part that decides your semester, because every later topic is built on it: a derivative is a limit of a fraction, an elasticity is a ratio of percentages, a present value is a power of (1 + r), and a regression line is y = mx + b with data attached.

On Cyberlearn. Week 1 of the course points to a Levelling Up module: videos, a quiz, and a blank HES-SO entry exam. The syllabus calls it an optional online levelling-up course. It is the official version of this part, it is free, and it is the fastest way to find out which of the sections below you actually need.
How to use Part 0
  • Read the rule, then cover the worked example and try it yourself.
  • Do the exercise at the end of the section. It gives you one question at a time, tells you at once whether you are right, and shows the working afterwards. Hints are there if you want them.
  • Work each question on paper before you answer. Answering in your head is how a topic feels learned without being learned.
  • If a section is easy, skip to the next. If a section is hard, that is the one to repeat tomorrow.

Part 0  ·  Lesson 2 of 13

Numbers, notation and the order of operations

The alphabet the course is written in, and the one rule that decides what every calculation means.

Before this lesson you need
  • Arithmetic with whole numbers and decimals
  • Nothing else. This lesson assumes no mathematics
  • If a symbol below is new to you, that is expected
In this lesson you will learn
  • The four sets of numbers, and which numbers live in which
  • What the course means by no solution in ℝ
  • Every symbol the slides use, read aloud in plain words
  • Interval notation, and open ends against closed ones
  • The order of operations, used on several expressions
  • Why −32 and (−3)2 are different numbers
  • Rounding, and when to round at all
The same topic on Khan Academy
  • Pre-algebra, unit 5: Exponents and order of operations
  • Algebra 1, unit 15: Irrational numbers
  • Algebra 1, unit 1: Algebra foundations

Free, no account needed to watch. Their exercises need one.

A sentence you are expected to read

Slide 4 of week 1 opens with Let a, b ∈ ℝ, a ≠ 0, with no explanation underneath, because the lecturer assumes you can read it. It says: let a and b be real numbers, and let a not be zero.

Nothing there is hard. It is written in symbols you may have last met in a French classroom years ago, or never. A sentence you cannot read is a sentence you cannot use, so this lesson is a vocabulary lesson first. Every symbol here appears on the quiz, silently, inside a question about something else.

The four sets of numbers

Numbers are sorted into sets, and the four that matter fit inside one another like nested boxes. Each box holds everything in the box before it, plus something new. That matters because saying which box you are in changes what counts as an answer.

Each set contains the one before it, and adds something new
SymbolNameWhat is in itSomething in it that was not in the set before
ℕNatural numbers0, 1, 2, 3, ···Nothing. Counting starts here.
ℤIntegers··· −2, −1, 0, 1, 2 ···−4, because you cannot count minus four beans.
ℚRationalsone integer over another12, a ratio of integers but not an integer.
ℝRealsevery point on the number line2 ≈ 1.414, which no fraction equals exactly.
Nested, not separate

ℕ ⊆ ℤ ⊆ ℚ ⊆ ℝ: every natural number is an integer, every integer is rational, every rational is real. The number 3 is all four at once. To tell a rational apart from a real that is not rational, write it as a decimal: if the decimal stops or repeats a block for ever, it is rational. If it runs on with no pattern, as 2 and π do, it is real only.

What “no solution in ℝ” is saying

Later you will meet a quadratic with a negative discriminant, and the slide will say it has no solution in ℝ. That phrase looks like padding. It is not.

Take x2 + x + 1 = 0, whose discriminant is 1 − 4(1)(1) = −3. The honest statement is not that the equation has no solution, but that it has none among the real numbers. Solutions do exist in a larger set, the complex numbers. This course stays in ℝ all year, so the qualifier is a boundary marker: it says where the search was carried out.

It usually has a plain business reading too. If you set profit to zero and find no solution in ℝ, the profit curve never touches the axis: XY Coffee Co never breaks even at those prices and costs. That is an answer. Write it in words as well.

The symbols, read aloud

The right-hand column is the one to learn. Reading a symbol as a sentence is what makes an exam question parse.

The notation, and how to say it
SymbolSay it asWhat it means
∈belongs tox ∈ ℝ says x is a real number.
∉does not belong to2 ∉ ℚ says it is not rational.
≠is not equal toa ≠ 0 allows anything except zero.
≤less than or equal toq ≤ 40 allows 40 itself. The line under the sign includes the endpoint.
≥greater than or equal tox ≥ 0 is what a square root demands of its input.
ℝ\{3}the reals without 3The backslash means take these out. Domain answers are written this way.
ℝ\{−2 ; 3}without minus two and threeTwo values removed. The semicolon separates them, Swiss and French style.
[0 ; 100]the closed intervalBoth ends included. Square brackets turn inwards to include.
]0 ; 100[the open intervalBoth ends excluded. Reversed brackets turn outwards. Some books write (0 ; 100).
[0 ; 100[half open0 is in, 100 is out. Mixed ends are allowed and common.
∞infinityA direction, not a number. You cannot add to it or divide by it.
∑the sum ofAdd up many terms. It arrives with the statistics half of the year.
∀for all∀x ∈ A means every x in A, with no exceptions.
∪union, orEverything in A or in B. This is how a domain in two pieces is written.
∩intersection, andEverything in both. This is the domain of a sum of two functions.
Infinity never gets a square bracket

You will see ]−∞ ; 5] and [2 ; +∞[, never [2 ; +∞]. A square bracket means the endpoint is included, and there is no endpoint to include: infinity is not a number the interval reaches.

Write “every real number except 0 and 5” in both accepted forms
  1. ℝ\{0 ; 5}
    The short form. Start from all the reals, then remove the two values. Use this when the exclusions come from denominators.
  2. ]−∞ ; 0[ ∪ ]0 ; 5[ ∪ ]5 ; +∞[
    The interval form. Removing two points leaves three pieces, so three intervals joined by unions. Every bracket touching 0 or 5 is reversed, because those are the excluded values.
  3. Both mean the same set.
    Use whichever the question used. For a domain the short form is faster and safer.

The order of operations

2 + 3 × 42 has no meaning until everybody agrees what comes first. Different orders give different numbers, and only one is what the writer intended. The agreement is universal, your calculator obeys it, and it is one rule with four levels.

The rule, in four levels

Work down the levels. Inside one level, work left to right.1. Brackets  ›  2. Powers and roots  ›  3. × and ÷  ›  4. + and −Left to right matters more than students expect. 12 ÷ 2 × 3 is 18, not 2, because × and ÷ share level 3 and the division came first on the page.

Evaluate 2 + 3 × 42
  1. 2 + 3 × 42 = 2 + 3 × 16
    Level 2 first. The power applies to the 4 alone, not to 3 × 4.
  2. = 2 + 48
    Level 3 next, then level 4.
  3. = 50
    Blind left to right would give (2 + 3) × 4 = 20 and then 400, eight times too big.
Evaluate 10 − 2 × 32, then (10 − 2) × 32
  1. 10 − 2 × 32 = 10 − 2 × 9 = 10 − 18
    Power, then multiplication, then subtraction.
  2. = −8
    The answer is negative.
  3. (10 − 2) × 32 = 8 × 9 = 72
    One pair of brackets turns −8 into 72. Brackets carry meaning when you copy a formula off a slide.

The next one is a cost function of the kind XY Coffee Co uses all year. C(q) = 10 000 + 200q + 5q2 gives the daily cost in CHF of roasting q tons of beans, and Jane wants it at 20 tons.

Evaluate C(20) for C(q) = 10 000 + 200q + 5q²
  1. C(20) = 10 000 + 200(20) + 5(20)2
    Put 20 in place of every q, inside a bracket each time. That habit will save you in Part 1.
  2. = 10 000 + 4 000 + 5(400)
    5(20)2 squares the 20 and then multiplies by 5. It does not square 5 × 20.
  3. C(20) = 16 000
    Sixteen thousand francs a day. Square 5 × 20 instead and the last term reads 10 000 rather than 2 000, and the day costs 24 000 CHF on paper.
A fraction bar is a bracket you cannot see

The whole of the top is worked out first, the whole of the bottom second, and only then are they divided. So 12 + 82 + 3 is 205 = 4. Typed as 12 + 8 ÷ 2 + 3 a calculator gives 19, because it sees no brackets. Put brackets round the top and the bottom every time you transfer a fraction.

Why −32 is not (−3)2

A power is an instruction about a base: 32 means 3 × 3. The only question is whether the minus sign is part of the base.

In −32 there is no bracket, so the base is 3. The power is level 2 and the minus is level 4, so the squaring happens first. Read it as 0 − 32 and you get −9.

In (−3)2 the bracket is level 1, so the base is the whole number −3, and (−3)(−3) = 9. This is not a convention to memorise. It follows from the four levels you already have.

The bracket decides, and only the bracket
ExpressionThe baseValueWhy
−323−9Square the 3, then apply the minus.
(−3)2−39The bracket makes the minus part of the base.
−242−1624 = 16, then the minus.
(−2)4−216Four negatives multiplied, an even count, so positive.
−232−8Odd powers hide the trap: these last two agree.
(−2)3−2−8Three negatives, an odd count, so negative.
Where this bites

It bites when you substitute a negative number. With f(x) = −x2 + 4, the value at x = −3 is not 9 + 4. Substitute inside a bracket: f(−3) = −(−3)2 + 4 = −9 + 4 = −5. The bracket came from the substitution and the minus in front came from the formula. Two separate things.

Rounding, and when not to

Two instructions get confused constantly. Decimal places counts positions after the point. Significant figures counts digits from the first one that is not a zero, wherever it sits. For a number near 1 they agree. For a small or a large number they do not.

The same number under both instructions
NumberTo 3 decimal placesTo 3 significant figures
0.0384615···0.0380.0385
14.062514.06314.1
12 34512 345.00012 300
0.6666···0.6670.667

In 0.0384615··· the leading zeros are placeholders, so the first significant digit is the 3 and three of them give 0.0385, while three decimal places give 0.038. Row three surprises people: three significant figures of 12 345 keeps 1, 2 and 3, and the rest become zeros to hold the size of the number.

Carry exact values, round once, at the end

Round only the number you are about to write down as a final answer. A rounding error made early does not stay small: the later steps multiply it, raise it to powers, or add it up many times.

Cost per box: 9 000 CHF of fixed costs over 640 boxes
  1. 9 000640 = 14.0625
    The exact cost per box in CHF. Keep this number.
  2. 14.06(640) = 8 998.40
    Round first and the total comes back 1.60 CHF short of the 9 000 you started with.
  3. 14.1(640) = 9 024
    Three significant figures instead, and now you are 24 CHF out. The error grew because you multiplied it by 640.
  4. 14.0625(640) = 9 000
    Carry the exact value and round only the figure in the report. Finance will notice if the totals do not reconcile.

Powers make it worse, because they multiply the error by itself. The app subscription grows 5 per cent a year, and Jane needs the monthly rate.

A monthly growth rate, rounded early against rounded late
  1. the monthly rate r satisfies (1 + r)¹² = 1.05
    Twelve months of growth must compound to one year of growth.
  2. r = 0.0040741···
    About 0.407 per cent a month.
  3. (1.004)¹² = 1.04907
    Round r to three decimal places and the year comes out at 4.907 per cent, not 5 per cent.
  4. on 2 000 000 CHF that is about 1 860 CHF
    The exact figure forecasts 2 100 000 CHF, the rounded one about 2 098 140 CHF. One rounding decision, three lines too early.
What to write in an exam

Give the exact value when it is short: 23 beats 0.67. If a decimal is asked for, follow the instruction exactly. With no instruction, two decimal places for money and three significant figures for a rate are safe. Use ≈, not =, for a rounded value: 126 ≈ 0.0385.

Where marks are lost in this topic
  • Dropping the qualifier. Writing no solution where the truth is no solution in ℝ.
  • The wrong bracket. [2 ; 5] includes 5, [2 ; 5[ does not, and a domain turns on that.
  • A square bracket next to infinity. Always reversed at the infinity end.
  • Squaring the wrong thing. 5(20)2 is 5 × 400.
  • Losing the minus. −32 is −9. Substitute negatives inside a bracket.
  • A fraction typed without brackets. The bar brackets the top and the bottom.
  • Rounding at every step. Round once, at the end, and mark it with ≈.
What to remember
  • ℕ ⊆ ℤ ⊆ ℚ ⊆ ℝ, and this course lives in ℝ.
  • ∈ is belongs to, ℝ\{a} is every real except a, ∪ is or, ∩ is and.
  • Square brackets include the endpoint, reversed brackets exclude it, and infinity is always excluded.
  • Brackets, then powers and roots, then × and ÷, then + and −, left to right inside a level.
  • A minus in front of a power is not part of the base unless a bracket puts it there.
  • Decimal places count after the point, significant figures from the first non-zero digit.
  • Carry exact values through the working and round only the answer you hand in.

Part 0  ·  Lesson 3 of 13

Fractions and signs

Half of the algebra errors in this course are fraction errors, and they never announce themselves: the answer comes out wrong three lines after the mistake, with nothing on the page to point at.

Before this lesson you need
  • The order of operations, and that a fraction bar brackets the top and the bottom
  • Multiplying and dividing whole numbers, including negative ones
  • Nothing else. Every rule here is derived, not assumed
In this lesson you will learn
  • What a fraction means, in the two ways it has to be read
  • The four operations, each worked, each with a reason
  • Why dividing by a fraction means multiplying by its reciprocal
  • Common denominators, and why only two operations need one
  • Cancelling a factor against cancelling a term, the costliest error here
  • How to untangle a fraction inside a fraction, as week 2 will need
  • When a fraction may be split, and when it may not
  • Where a minus sign goes, and what it does to a numerator
The same topic on Khan Academy
  • Arithmetic, unit 4: Understand fractions
  • Arithmetic, unit 13: Adding and subtracting fractions
  • Arithmetic, unit 15: Dividing fractions
  • Arithmetic, unit 19: Multiplying and dividing negatives

Free, no account needed to watch. Their exercises need one.

One number, two meanings

XY Coffee Co sells a subscription box at 25 CHF, and the beans inside cost 7.50 CHF. Jane writes that as 7.5025 and asks what the number is.

Two answers are both honest. It is a division: 7.50 ÷ 25 = 0.30. It is also a part of a whole: beans are 310 of the box, which is what you say in a meeting.

The division reading computes. The part-of-a-whole reading tells you what you found. Learn only the first and you get the arithmetic right without knowing what it means.

A division

ab means a ÷ b. This reading puts a fraction into a calculator, and explains why a0 has no value.

A part of a whole

34 means: cut the whole into 4 equal pieces and take 3. This makes 34 of 25 CHF an obvious 18.75 CHF.

A rate

7.5025 is also 30 centimes in the franc. Margins and growth rates are read this way.

The words for the two parts

In ab the top is the numerator and the bottom the denominator. The denominator says how many equal pieces the whole was cut into, which is why it is never zero: cutting something into zero pieces is not an instruction anybody can follow.

Multiplying, the operation that needs no preparation

Multiply the tops, multiply the bottoms. The reason is the part-of-a-whole reading: 23 × 57 asks for two thirds of five sevenths. In a square of side 1, take a strip five sevenths tall, then two thirds of its width. The piece left is 2 out of 3 wide and 5 out of 7 tall, so 10 tiles out of 21. Area does the multiplying for you.

Multiplication

(ab)(cd) = acbd

Compute 23 × 57
  1. 23 × 57 = 2 × 53 × 7
    Tops together, bottoms together. No common denominator is needed.
  2. = 1021 ≈ 0.476
    Nothing cancels, so it is finished. Size check: two thirds of a little over a half lands a little under a half.

Dividing, and why you turn it upside down

The rule is famous and the reason is usually not taught, which is why it goes missing under pressure. Here it is, twice.

As fitting. 6 ÷ 2 asks how many 2s fit into 6. So 1 ÷ 14 asks how many quarters fit into a whole: four. So dividing by a quarter multiplies by four, because many small pieces fit in.

As undoing. Dividing by cd must undo multiplying by it, and multiplying by dc does, because (cd)(dc) = 1. That is what reciprocal means.

Division

(ab) ÷ (cd) = (ab)(dc) = adbcOnly the second is flipped. Flipping both gives the reciprocal of the right answer.

Compute 23 ÷ 57
  1. 23 ÷ 57 = 23 × 75
    Flip the divisor and change the sign to a multiplication. The first does not move.
  2. = 1415 ≈ 0.933
    A check: 23 ≈ 0.667 divided by 57 ≈ 0.714 gives 0.933. The two readings agree, as they must.

Adding and subtracting, and why only these two need a common denominator

You can add 3 apples and 2 apples because they are the same kind of thing. A denominator is the name of the pieces: thirds and quarters are different kinds of thing, so rename both in a unit they share and the pieces match.

Multiplication needs none of this, which people find odd. Multiplying does not put pieces side by side, it takes a part of a part, so the denominators never have to agree.

Addition and subtraction

ab + cd = ad + bcbdNot a fourth rule to memorise. It is what renaming gives you: ab becomes adbd, cd becomes bcbd, and the tops can now be added.

Method: finding a common denominator
  1. Multiplying the two denominators always works.
  2. The smallest number both divide into is tidier: for 6 and 8 use 24, not 48.
  3. Rescale each fraction: whatever multiplied the bottom must multiply the top. That is multiplying by 1 in disguise, so nothing changes.
  4. Add or subtract the numerators only. The denominator stays.
Compute 23 + 14
  1. 23 + 14 = 812 + 312
    Rename both in twelfths: 23 scaled by 4 top and bottom, 14 by 3.
  2. = 1112 ≈ 0.917
    The denominator is not added: you are counting pieces of one size. A little under 1, which is right.
Compute 34 − 25
  1. 34 − 25 = 1520 − 820
    Twentieths, from multiplying the two denominators.
  2. = 720 = 0.35
    Subtract the numerators only. Subtraction is addition with one sign changed, so there is no extra rule.
The denominators are not added

12 + 13 is not 25. A half plus a third is more than a half, and 25 is 0.4, which is less. The answer is 56 ≈ 0.833. When a fraction answer looks odd, turn it into a decimal and test the size.

Simplifying, and the error that costs the most marks

Simplifying means dividing top and bottom by the same thing, which is allowed because it is dividing by 1 in disguise: 1218 = 23, both divided by 6.

Everything hangs on what that thing may be. It has to be a factor of the whole top and the whole bottom. A factor multiplies. A term is added on. Cancelling a term is not allowed.

Factor against term

In 3x the 3 and the x are factors: it is a product, so cancelling one is legal. In 3 + x they are terms: it is a sum, so cancelling one is not. Before crossing anything out, ask whether it multiplies the rest or is added to it.

A worked wrong example, and the test that catches it
  1. a + bb = a
    The error: the b underneath was crossed off against the b on top.
  2. with a = 2 and b = 5: 75 = 1.4, but a = 2
    Put numbers in. One counterexample kills a rule.
  3. a + bb = ab + 1
    What is actually true. Same numbers: 0.4 + 1 = 1.4. It agrees.
  4. the b on top is a term, not a factor
    It is added to a, not multiplying it, so there is nothing to cancel against. This costs more marks in Part 0 than anything else.
A correct cancellation: simplify x2 − 9x − 3 for x ≠ 3
  1. x2 − 9 = (x − 3)(x + 3)
    Factorise the top. Now it is a product, so it has factors to cancel with.
  2. (x − 3)(x + 3)x − 3 = x + 3
    A factor was cancelled, not a term. Test at x = 7: 404 = 10, and 7 + 3 = 10.
  3. valid for x ≠ 3
    x + 3 looks harmless at 3, but the original had a zero denominator there, so 3 stays excluded.
Factorise first, then cancel, never the other way round

If you cannot see a factor, you do not yet have permission to cancel. Factorising creates the factors. And note any excluded value before you cancel: the simplified expression will not remember it for you.

A fraction inside a fraction

These look alarming and are not, because you have every rule they need. A bar is a division, so a stacked fraction is one division on another, and dividing by a fraction means multiplying by its reciprocal.

Week 2 produces them constantly: finding an inverse means solving y = f(x) for x, and when f is a fraction the x lands underneath one.

Method: three lines, every time
  1. Write the top as a single fraction, and the bottom as a single fraction.
  2. Read the big bar as a division sign between those two.
  3. Flip the second, multiply, then cancel.
Simplify 1234
  1. 1234 = 12 ÷ 34 = 12 × 43
    The big bar is a division. Flip the bottom and multiply.
  2. = 46 = 23
    Cancel the factor 2. Check: 0.5 ÷ 0.75 ≈ 0.667.

Now the shape from the week 2 inverse-function slide, worked in full.

Simplify 50005000p + 1
  1. 50005000p + 1 = 5000 ÷ 5000p + 1
    Read the big bar as a division. Top and bottom are each already single.
  2. = 5000 × p + 15000 = 5000(p + 1)5000
    Flip the divisor. All of p + 1 moves up, bracket and all.
  3. = p + 1
    5000 is a factor of the whole top and bottom, so it goes. Check at p = 4: the inner fraction is 1000, and 5000 ÷ 1000 = 5.
Simplify 1 + 1x1 − 1x
  1. top: 1 + 1x = x + 1x
    The 1 becomes xx so the two can be added.
  2. bottom: 1 − 1x = x − 1x
    Same treatment underneath.
  3. = x + 1x × xx − 1
    One fraction over another. Flip the second and multiply.
  4. = x + 1x − 1
    The x is a factor top and bottom, so it cancels. Test at x = 3: 43 divided by 23 is 2, and so is 42.

Splitting a fraction, and when you must not

You may break a fraction up when the sum is on the top, never when it is underneath.

Splitting the top is legal because sharing a + b francs between c people is the same as sharing the a and then the b. Splitting the bottom is illegal because sharing a francs among b + c people is not the same as sharing them among b and then again among c, which hands the money out twice.

One is true and one is false

a + bc = ac + bc    trueab + c = ab + ac    falseIf you remember one thing: a sum on the bottom is untouchable.

Test both claims with numbers
  1. 6 + 42 = 5 and 62 + 42 = 5
    The true one. Split the top and nothing changes.
  2. 122 + 4 = 126 = 2
    The false one, worked properly: the bottom is added first, because the bar is a bracket.
  3. 122 + 124 = 9
    Split the bottom and you get 9. Nine is not two.
  4. top yes, bottom no
    When unsure: put small numbers in and compare. Ten seconds, and never wrong.

Where the minus sign goes

A single minus can sit in three places and all three mean the same number, because a negative over a positive and a positive over a negative are both negative.

The three positions

−ab = −ab = a−bAnd two cancel: −a−b = ab. Put the sign in front of the fraction or on the numerator; left on a denominator it is not wrong, but it hides the next step.

The danger is that a minus in front of the whole fraction applies to every term on the top, not only the first. The bracket rule again, with the bracket invisible.

Simplify −x − 32
  1. = −(x − 3)2
    Move the sign on to the numerator and write the bracket in. It was always there, held by the bar.
  2. = −x + 32 = 3 − x2
    Distribute over both terms: x becomes −x and −3 becomes +3. Both forms are accepted.
  3. check at x = 5: −22 = −1 and 3 − 52 = −1
    They agree. The wrong version −x − 32 gives −4 there, a different expression.
Subtract a whole fraction: 102 − 3 + 12
  1. = 10 − (3 + 1)2
    The subtraction applies to the whole second numerator, so it goes in a bracket. The line students skip.
  2. = 10 − 3 − 12 = 3
    Both terms change sign. Without the bracket you get 10 − 3 + 12, which is 4.
  3. bracket what you subtract, then distribute
    Two pen strokes, and the commonest sign error cannot happen.
A minus in front of a fraction is a bracket in disguise

−x + 25 is −x − 25, not −x + 25. At x = 3 the left side is −1 and the wrong one gives −0.2. When a sign question is close, substitute a number rather than arguing with yourself.

Where marks are lost in this topic
  • Adding the denominators. 12 + 13 is 56, not 25.
  • Cancelling a term. a + bb is not a. Only a factor may go.
  • Splitting the bottom. ab + c is not ab + ac.
  • Flipping both fractions when dividing. Only the divisor turns over.
  • Dropping the bracket after a minus. It reaches every term on top.
  • Forgetting the excluded value. Ask what makes the denominator zero before you cancel.
  • Not checking the size. Turn the answer into a decimal and test it.
What to remember
  • A fraction is a division and a part of a whole. One computes, one explains.
  • Multiply: tops together, bottoms together. No common denominator needed.
  • Divide: flip the divisor and multiply, because a fraction times its reciprocal is 1.
  • Add or subtract: rename both in a shared denominator. Only pieces of one size count together.
  • Cancel factors, never terms. Factorise first.
  • A stacked fraction is one division on another. Flip and multiply.
  • A sum on top may be split. A sum on the bottom may not, ever.
  • A minus in front of a fraction applies to every term in the numerator.
  • When in doubt, put small numbers in and compare.

Part 0  ·  Lesson 4 of 13

Powers and roots

A power is a counting shorthand, and every rule about powers is a statement about counting. Week 2 puts eight of them on one slide and assumes they are known.

Before this lesson you need
  • Multiplying and dividing signed numbers, and what a reciprocal is
  • Adding fractions, because exponents become fractions here
  • The order of operations
In this lesson you will learn
  • What a power means, and why the rules follow from counting rather than memory
  • The product, quotient and power-of-a-power rules, each derived in front of you
  • How a power spreads over a product and a quotient, and why never over a sum
  • Why x0 = 1 and x−m = 1xm need x ≠ 0
  • How to convert between roots and fractional powers, both ways
  • Why x2 = |x|, and where powers stop being defined
The same topic on Khan Academy
  • Algebra 1, unit 11: Exponents and radicals
  • Algebra 2, unit 6: Rational exponents and radicals

Free, no account needed to watch. Their exercises need one.

A growth question that looks like a trick

The XY Coffee Co app subscription grew by 6 per cent a month for three months, then by 6 per cent for two more. Jane asks whether that is the same as 6 per cent a month for five months.

Growing by 6 per cent means multiplying by 1.06. Three months of it is 1.063, two more is 1.062, and one after the other multiplies by 1.06 five times. So yes: 1.063 · 1.062 = 1.065.

Nothing was remembered there. Three copies and two copies make five copies. Every rule here is that sentence in a different costume, so do not memorise the eight. Memory fails under pressure. Counting does not.

What a power means

Definition

For a whole number n ≥ 1:xn = x · x · … · x   (n factors)The x is the base, the thing being copied. The small n is the exponent: how many copies sit in the product.

Read the exponent as a count and nothing here will surprise you. One copy means x1 = x, and 23 is 2 · 2 · 2 = 8, never 2 · 3 = 6. Say the word copies and those two cannot be confused.

Why does multiplying add the exponents?

Derive xm · xn = xm + n
  1. x3 · x2 = (x · x · x)(x · x)
    Replace each power by what it stands for.
  2. = x · x · x · x · x
    Multiplication ignores brackets, so all the copies join one row.
  3. = x5
    Count them. Five.
  4. xm · xn = xm + n
    The bases must match, because only then are the copies copies of the same thing. x3 · y2 does not simplify at all.

Why does dividing subtract them?

Derive xmxn = xm − n
  1. x5x2 = x · x · x · x · xx · x
    Five copies over two copies.
  2. = x · x · x
    Each x below cancels one above. Two pairs go, three survive.
  3. = x3
    And 5 − 2 = 3, the count of the survivors.
  4. xmxn = xm − n
    Valid only for x ≠ 0. Cancelling a factor means dividing by it.
The condition that runs through the whole lesson

Every rule that divides, and every negative exponent, needs x ≠ 0. The cancelling above is the reason: at x = 0 the bottom is zero.

Why does a power of a power multiply them?

Derive (xm)n = xm · n
  1. (x3)2 = (x3)(x3)
    The outer exponent counts copies of the whole inner power.
  2. = (x · x · x)(x · x · x)
    Expand each copy.
  3. = x6
    Two rows of three. And 3 · 2 = 6.
  4. (xm)n = xm · n
    Against numbers: (23)2 = 82 = 64, and 26 = 64.
Look for the bracket

(x3)2 = x6 multiplies the exponents, while x3 · x2 = x5 adds them. At x = 2 that is 64 against 32. The bracket tells you which exponent is counting what.

What a power does to a product and to a quotient

Now let the thing being copied be a product. (xy)3 is six factors in a row, and a product reorders freely, so gather them: (x · x · x)(y · y · y). Three copies of a product is three copies of each factor.

The two spreading rules

(xy)m = xmym     (xy)m = xmymThe second is the same argument with fractions, and it needs y ≠ 0. Numbers for both: (3 · 5)2 = 225 = 32 · 52, and (62)3 = 27 = 6323.

A power spreads over multiplication. Never over addition.

(x + y)2 is not x2 + y2. Test it: (3 + 4)2 = 49, while 32 + 42 = 25. The gap of 24 is the 2xy term, 2 · 3 · 4, and the next lesson shows where it comes from.

Two disguises of the same mistake: x + y ≠ x + y and ln(x + y) ≠ ln x + ln y.

Why is anything to the power zero equal to one?

Zero copies ought to be nothing at all, so suspicion is the right first reaction. The counting definition does not reach this case, so the value is not discovered. It is forced, by insisting the quotient rule keeps working when the exponents are equal.

Force the value of x0
  1. x3x3 = 1
    Top and bottom are the same number, and a non-zero number divided by itself is 1.
  2. x3x3 = x3 − 3 = x0
    The quotient rule, applied to the very same expression.
  3. x0 = 1
    One expression, two values, so they are equal. Nothing else would keep the quotient rule true.
The argument breaks at x = 0

That first line divided x3 by itself, which is only allowed when x ≠ 0. At x = 0 it reads 00 and says nothing at all, so the derivation is silent about 00, and 00 is undefined. The rule is x0 = 1 for every x ≠ 0, and writing that condition down earns the mark.

Why is a negative exponent a reciprocal?

Force the value of x−2
  1. x3x5 = 1x2
    Cancel three pairs. Every copy on top finds a partner, and two are stranded below. Here x ≠ 0 throughout.
  2. x3x5 = x3 − 5 = x−2
    The quotient rule on the same fraction.
  3. x−2 = 1x2
    Against a number: 2−3 = 18 = 0.125.
Both directions, and what they buy you

For x ≠ 0:x−m = 1xm     1x−m = xmA factor may cross the fraction bar in either direction so long as the sign of its exponent changes as it crosses. That is often the quickest way to tidy an expression, and it is how week 5 differentiates 1x2 with no rule for fractions.

A negative exponent does not give a negative answer

2−3 = 0.125, which is positive and small. The minus in the exponent turns the number over; it does not move it past zero. Only a negative base does that, as in (−2)3 = −8.

Roots are powers with a fraction in the exponent

A square root asks: what number, multiplied by itself, gives this? Write that question with an exponent and the answer falls out. Suppose x = xp for an exponent p we do not yet know.

Derive x = x12
  1. x · x = x
    The definition, for x ≥ 0. Two copies give back x.
  2. xp · xp = x2p
    The same statement, with the root written as an unknown power.
  3. x2p = x1
    Both lines describe the same number, and x is x1.
  4. x = x12
    Same base, same value, so 2p = 1. A root is a power whose exponent is not a whole number.
Roots and fractional powers

For x ≥ 0 and whole m, n ≥ 1:x = x12    3x = x13    nxm = xmnBottom is the root, top is the power. The order does not matter, but taking the root first keeps the numbers small: 1634 = 23 = 8.

The same reading, both ways
Root formPower formValue
388132
4163163423 = 8
312521252352 = 25
132727−1313

Going the other way is the same reading: x25 is 5x2, and x−12 is 1x. Converting is not tidying. It is the move that lets the three counting rules reach an expression they could not otherwise touch, and it is how week 5 differentiates q.

Mixing roots and powers: three moves, in this order
  1. Turn every root into a fractional power and every reciprocal into a negative power.
  2. Collect one base at a time, adding exponents where you multiply and subtracting where you divide.
  3. Convert back only if the question asked for a root, and state the condition on the base.
Simplify x · x3 ÷ x3, for x > 0
  1. = x12 · x3 ÷ x32
    Every root becomes a power: x3 is x32, root 2 below and cube 3 above.
  2. = x12 + 3 − 32
    Add for the product, subtract for the division. No roots are in the way now.
  3. = x2
    Because 12 − 32 = −1. Check at x = 4: 2 · 64 ÷ 8 = 16 = 42.

Squaring and un-squaring are not quite opposites

It is tempting to say a root undoes a square, so x2 must be x. One number settles it.

Test x2 = x at x = −4
  1. (−4)2 = 16
    Squaring destroys the minus sign, because a negative times a negative is positive.
  2. 16 = 4
    The root symbol returns the non-negative answer. That is part of what it means.
  3. (−4)2 = 4, not −4
    The square threw away which sign you started with, and the root cannot give it back.
  4. x2 = |x|
    Absolute value is “the size, sign discarded”: x when x ≥ 0, and −x when x < 0.
What this costs you in practice

Undoing a square means deciding the sign separately, so x2 = 16 has two solutions and the honest step is x = ±16. Context usually settles it, because a price or a quantity of beans cannot be negative. Write that sentence down when you use it.

Odd roots are different: 3(−8) = −2, because cubing keeps the sign and so cube rooting can return it.

A root will not split across a sum either

A root is a power, and a power does not spread over addition. Two numbers settle it.

Test a + b = a + b at a = 9, b = 16
  1. 9 + 16 = 25 = 5
    What is under a root is grouped, so it is worked out first.
  2. 9 + 16 = 3 + 4 = 7
    The wrong version, for comparison.
  3. 5 ≠ 7
    One counterexample is a complete disproof. Over a product it would have worked: 9 · 16 = 12 and 3 · 4 = 12.

Where a fractional exponent turns up in the business

XY Coffee Co expects its subscriber base to double over a year. Jane asks what that means per six months, and the tempting answer is 50 per cent. Test it: growing 50 per cent twice multiplies by 1.52 = 2.25, a rise of 125 per cent. Growth compounds, so halving the rate overshoots.

Find the six-month growth factor behind a yearly doubling
  1. r2 = 2
    Let r be the six-month factor. Two of them make a year, and the year doubles the base.
  2. r = 212 = 2 ≈ 1.4142
    Undo the square with a root, the positive one, since a growth factor cannot be negative.
  3. about 41.42 per cent per six months
    Check: 1.41422 ≈ 2.000. The quarterly figure is 214 ≈ 1.1892, 18.9 per cent.
What that means for Jane

Rates over different periods are not scaled by multiplying and dividing. They are raised to powers, and the exponent is the fraction of the period. This is what connects a quarterly figure to a yearly target.

Where powers stop being defined

The cases that carry marks

00 is undefined: the argument for x0 = 1 divides x3 by itself, which is illegal at zero. So is 0−m for m > 0, since 0−2 = 10. But 0m is fine for m > 0: it is zero.

x needs x ≥ 0, as does every even root, because no real number squared is negative. Odd roots have no such restriction, and an even number below a fractional exponent carries the condition with it: x34 needs x ≥ 0, x35 does not.

The question behind every undefined case

Only two exist. Is something divided by zero? Is an even root taken of a negative number?

Where marks are lost in this topic
  • Multiplying base by exponent. 23 = 8, not 6.
  • Adding when the rule multiplies. Look for the bracket.
  • Combining unlike bases. x3 · y2 stays as it is.
  • Spreading over a sum. Test with 9 and 16 whenever you doubt it.
  • Making a negative exponent negative. 2−3 = 0.125.
  • Writing x2 = x. It is |x|.
  • Dropping the condition. Name the base your answer forbids.
What to remember
  • An exponent counts copies. Every rule is that sentence rearranged.
  • xm · xn = xm + n, xmxn = xm − n, (xm)n = xmn.
  • A power reaches every factor of a product or a quotient, never a term of a sum.
  • x0 = 1 and x−m = 1xm, only for x ≠ 0.
  • nxm = xmn. Bottom is the root, top is the power.
  • x2 = |x|, and 00 and 0−2 are undefined.

Part 0  ·  Lesson 5 of 13

Expanding and factoring

Two directions of one skill. Expanding is mechanical and factoring needs practice, and a business analyst needs both, because the two forms of the same expression answer two different questions.

Before this lesson you need
  • How to multiply signed numbers, since most factoring errors are sign errors
  • What a power is, in particular that (a + b)2 is not a2 + b2
  • What a bracket groups, and that a minus in front of one applies to everything inside
In this lesson you will learn
  • Why a business student needs both directions, not only one
  • The distributive law, and why it is a statement about area
  • How to multiply two brackets in an order that misses nothing
  • The three identities, each derived rather than asserted
  • Why a2 + b2 does not factor over the reals
  • The factoring procedure in order, with the sign discipline that makes it reliable
  • How to factor a quadratic whose leading coefficient is not 1, and read break-even points off the result
The same topic on Khan Academy
  • Algebra 1, unit 13: Quadratics, multiplying and factoring
  • Algebra 2, unit 3: Polynomial factorisation

Free, no account needed to watch. Their exercises need one.

Why Jane wants the same expression written two ways

XY Coffee Co opens a roasting line. Each week it sells q crates at 90 CHF, and the cost of roasting q crates is C(q) = q2 + 1400 CHF, the square because beans roasted in a rush cost more per crate. So weekly profit isP(q) = 90q − (q2 + 1400) = −q2 + 90q − 1400

Jane asks two questions about that one line. How much does an extra crate add to profit at low volume? And at what volumes does the line break even?

The expanded form above answers the first: the coefficient of q is 90, so the first crates add about 90 CHF each. It answers the second badly, because you cannot see where it hits zero.

The factored form answers the second on sight: P(q) = −(q − 20)(q − 70) is zero at q = 20 and q = 70. It hides the 90. Neither form is better. You need the ability to move between them, and that is this lesson.

Expanding

Brackets out, terms added. Shows the coefficients: what each unit contributes, what the fixed cost is.

Factoring

Brackets in, a product of pieces. Shows the roots: the inputs that make the whole thing zero.

Why both

Break-even is a root question. Marginal contribution is a coefficient question. One expression, two readings.

The distributive law, and why it is true

Everything in this lesson is one rule applied repeatedly. Think of a(b + c) as the area of a rectangle a tall and b + c wide. Cut it vertically at b and you have two rectangles, of areas ab and ac. The area did not change when you drew the line.

Distributive law

a(b + c) = ab + acThe factor outside reaches every term inside, not only the first. With numbers: 7(20 + 3) = 7 · 23 = 161, and 7 · 20 + 7 · 3 = 140 + 21 = 161.

A minus outside the bracket reaches every term as well

−(x − 5) is −x + 5, not −x − 5. The minus is a factor of −1, and it distributes like any other factor. That is the step that lost the profit line above its sign: 90q − (q2 + 1400) is 90q − q2 − 1400, with both signs flipped.

Multiplying two brackets without missing a term

Apply the same law twice. Treat the whole of (c + d) as one object, distribute the first bracket over it, then distribute again. Four products come out, and the reliable way to get all four is always to work left to right through the first bracket.

Derive (a + b)(c + d) = ac + ad + bc + bd
  1. (a + b)(c + d) = a(c + d) + b(c + d)
    Distribute (c + d) over the two terms of the first bracket.
  2. = ac + ad + bc + bd
    Distribute again, twice. Each term of the left bracket has met each term of the right bracket exactly once.
  3. four products, always
    Two terms times two terms gives four. Count them before you simplify: a missing term is the commonest error here. Numbers: (3 + 4)(2 + 5) = 7 · 7 = 49, and 6 + 15 + 8 + 20 = 49.
Expand (2x + 5)(3x − 4)
  1. = 2x(3x − 4) + 5(3x − 4)
    Left to right through the first bracket. Carry the signs with the terms they belong to.
  2. = 6x2 − 8x + 15x − 20
    Four products. Note 2x · −4 = −8x: the sign travels with the number.
  3. = 6x2 + 7x − 20
    Collect the two x terms only. Check at x = 1: (7)(−1) = −7, and 6 + 7 − 20 = −7.

The three identities, derived and not asserted

These three are worth recognising instantly, but recognising is not the same as memorising. Each is one line of the work you did above.

Derive the three identities
  1. (a + b)2 = (a + b)(a + b) = a2 + ab + ba + b2
    A square is a product with itself, so the four-product rule applies. Two of the four are the same.
  2. (a + b)2 = a2 + 2ab + b2
    The middle term is there because ab appears twice. Numbers: (10 + 2)2 = 144, while 102 + 22 = 104, and the missing 40 is 2 · 10 · 2.
  3. (a − b)2 = a2 − 2ab + b2
    The same derivation with −b in place of b. Only the middle term changes sign, because (−b)2 = b2.
  4. (a + b)(a − b) = a2 − ab + ba − b2
    Now two different brackets. Four products again.
  5. (a + b)(a − b) = a2 − b2
    The middle terms cancel, because one is +ab and the other −ab. This is the one that saves time: 103 · 97 = 1002 − 32 = 9991, with no long multiplication.
a2 + b2 does not factor over the real numbers

The difference of two squares factors. The sum of two squares does not, and the reason is worth understanding rather than remembering.

If x2 + 9 had real factors (x − r)(x − s), then putting x = r would make it zero. But x2 is never negative, so x2 + 9 is at least 9 for every real x. It never reaches zero, so no such r exists.

So the minus sign in a2 − b2 is not decoration. x2 − 9 = (x − 3)(x + 3), and x2 + 9 stays as it is.

Factoring: the same steps, in the same order

Factoring is expanding run backwards, and backwards is harder because you are searching rather than following. A fixed order removes most of the searching.

In this order, every time
  1. Common factor first. 3x2 + 3x − 18 = 3(x2 + x − 6). This costs one line and makes every later step smaller. Skipping it is why students end up with numbers they cannot split.
  2. Then look for a pattern. Two terms, both squares, a minus between them means a difference of squares. A perfect square trinomial has first and last terms square and the middle term twice the product of their roots.
  3. Then two numbers with a given product and sum. For x2 + bx + c, find two numbers multiplying to c and adding to b.
  4. If none of that works, use the quadratic formula from the next lesson. Factoring is a shortcut, not an obligation.
Factor 3x2 + 3x − 18 completely
  1. 3x2 + 3x − 18
    Every coefficient is divisible by 3, so step one applies.
  2. = 3(x2 + x − 6)
    Take the 3 out. The bracket now has a leading coefficient of 1, which is the easy case.
  3. product −6, sum +1
    Two numbers multiplying to −6 and adding to +1. The pair is +3 and −2.
  4. = 3(x + 3)(x − 2)
    Check by expanding: 3(x2 + x − 6) returns the original. The roots are −3 and 2.
Why two numbers with that product and that sum

Expand (x + p)(x + q) and you get x2 + (p + q)x + pq. So the coefficient of x is the sum of the two numbers and the constant is their product. You are not guessing. You are reading the expansion backwards.

Sign discipline: read the product first, then the sum

The product tells you whether the two numbers share a sign, and the sum then tells you which sign.

Product positive, sum negative means both negative. For x2 − 13x + 40: the product 40 is positive so the signs match, the sum −13 is negative so both are negative, and the pair is −5 and −8, giving (x − 5)(x − 8).

Students who write (x + 5)(x + 8) there have found the right two numbers and lost the marks on the signs.

Product negative means one of each sign, and the number further from zero carries the sign of the sum.

When the leading coefficient is not 1

For ax2 + bx + c with a ≠ 1, the product-and-sum trick needs one adjustment. Look for two numbers multiplying to a · c rather than to c, still adding to b, then use them to split the middle term.

Factor 6x2 + 11x + 3
  1. a · c = 6 · 3 = 18
    Multiply the outer two coefficients. Look for two numbers with product 18 and sum 11.
  2. 9 and 2
    9 · 2 = 18 and 9 + 2 = 11. Both are positive, because the product and the sum are both positive.
  3. = 6x2 + 9x + 2x + 3
    Split the middle term into those two pieces. The expression has not changed, only its appearance.
  4. = 3x(2x + 3) + 1(2x + 3)
    Take a common factor out of each pair. The bracket that appears must be the same both times, or the split was wrong.
  5. = (3x + 1)(2x + 3)
    The repeated bracket is one factor and what multiplies it is the other. Check: 6x2 + 9x + 2x + 3 is the original.
Why splitting the middle term works

Expand (3x + 1)(2x + 3) and the middle term arrives as 9x + 2x, two separate products that get added at the last moment. Splitting puts them back where they came from, and the grouping then reads the factors off directly. Write the 1 in + 1(2x + 3) explicitly: dropping it is how the second bracket goes missing.

Factoring answers Jane’s break-even question

Back to the roasting line. Profit is P(q) = −q2 + 90q − 1400, and breaking even means P(q) = 0. A sum of three terms tells you nothing about where it is zero. A product does, because a product is zero exactly when one of its factors is.

Find both break-even volumes for the roasting line
  1. −q2 + 90q − 1400 = 0
    Set profit to zero. That is what breaking even means: revenue exactly covers cost.
  2. = −(q2 − 90q + 1400)
    Take out the common factor −1 so the leading coefficient is +1. Every sign inside the bracket flips.
  3. product 1400, sum −90
    Product positive, so the two numbers share a sign. Sum negative, so both are negative.
  4. −20 and −70
    (−20)(−70) = 1400 and −20 − 70 = −90. Both conditions hold.
  5. P(q) = −(q − 20)(q − 70)
    The factored form. A product is zero when a factor is zero, so this is zero at q = 20 and q = 70.
  6. break even at 20 and 70 crates a week
    Check both against the original: P(20) = −400 + 1800 − 1400 = 0 and P(70) = −4900 + 6300 − 1400 = 0.
Read the answer back to Jane

Below 20 crates the fixed roasting cost is not covered, and above 70 the rising cost per crate has eaten the margin. Profit is positive only between them, and the factored form makes the interval visible: (q − 20) and (q − 70) have opposite signs exactly when q is between 20 and 70, and the minus in front turns that into a positive profit. At the midpoint, P(45) = −(25)(−25) = 625 CHF a week.

That last line is the whole argument for learning to factor. Two numbers and an interval, read off a product, with no formula used.

Where marks are lost in this topic
  • Distributing over only the first term. 2(x2 − 3) = 2x2 − 6, not 2x2 − 3.
  • Losing a sign after a minus. −(x − 5) = −x + 5.
  • Dropping the middle term. (a + b)2 = a2 + 2ab + b2. Test with 10 and 2.
  • Forgetting the common factor. Take it out first or the numbers stay large.
  • Right numbers, wrong signs. Read the product first, then the sum.
  • Trying to factor a sum of squares. x2 + 9 does not factor over the reals.
  • Not checking. Expanding your answer takes ten seconds and catches almost everything above.
What to remember
  • Expanded form shows the coefficients. Factored form shows the roots. You need both directions.
  • a(b + c) = ab + ac, and the factor outside reaches every term inside, minus signs included.
  • Two brackets give four products. Count them before collecting.
  • (a ± b)2 = a2 ± 2ab + b2 and (a + b)(a − b) = a2 − b2. A sum of two squares does not factor.
  • Common factor, then pattern, then two numbers with product c and sum b.
  • When a ≠ 1, use product a · c and sum b, then split the middle term and group.
  • A product is zero when a factor is zero. That is why break-even questions want the factored form.

Part 0  ·  Lesson 6 of 13

Linear equations

One unknown, raised to the power one. Almost every business question you meet this year either is one of these or becomes one after a line of work.

Before this lesson you need
  • How signs behave, from the order of operations
  • How to add fractions, and what a common denominator is
  • How to expand a bracket, from expanding and factoring
In this lesson you will learn
  • What solving means, and why an answer can be tested
  • Why doing the same thing to both sides is allowed
  • The five steps, including how to clear fractions in one move
  • What happens when the coefficient of the unknown is zero
  • How to make a named variable the subject of a formula
  • How to turn a sentence of business English into an equation
The same topic on Khan Academy
  • Algebra 1, unit 2: Solving equations and inequalities
  • Algebra basics, unit 3: Linear equations and inequalities

Free, no account needed to watch. Their exercises need one.

A question the roastery asks every month

The Nyon shop pays 4800 CHF a month in rent, wages and electricity, whatever happens. A bag of beans costs 6.20 CHF to roast and deliver, and sells for 14.50 CHF. Jane asks: how many bags must the shop sell before it stops losing money?

You cannot read that off the numbers. Name the unknown instead. Let q be the bags sold in the month: money in is 14.50q, money out is 6.20q + 4800, and the month breaks even when they agree.14.50q = 6.20q + 4800That is a linear equation. This lesson gets you from a line like that to a number, and back to a sentence.

What does it mean to solve an equation?

An equation is not a calculation. It is a claim with a gap in it: 3x + 1 = 5x + 7 says there is a number which, placed in both gaps, makes the two sides come out the same.

For most numbers the claim is false: at x = 1 the sides are 4 and 12, at x = 0 they are 1 and 7. Solving means finding every number that makes it true. A linear equation usually has one, but you will see below that it can have none, or every number there is.

Definition

For a, b ∈ ℝ with a ≠ 0, the equationax + b = 0has exactly one solution, x = −ba. Every equation here becomes that shape once tidied. The condition a ≠ 0 is not decoration; a section below shows what goes wrong without it.

Why are we allowed to change both sides?

Every method below does the same thing to both sides, and knowing why that is legal stops you doing it to one side by accident.

If two quantities are the same size and you add 7 to each, they are still the same size. Take 3 from each, still the same size. Double each, still the same size. Nothing you did could separate two things that were already equal, so the new equation is true for exactly the numbers the old one was. The claim changed its appearance, not its content, and that is why a chain of steps ending in x = 4 proves 4 was the answer from the start.

Always safe

Adding the same number to both sides, or taking it away. The reverse move undoes it exactly.

Safe when not zero

Multiplying or dividing both sides by k ≠ 0. You can get back, so nothing is lost.

Not safe

Multiplying by zero. 3 = 5 is false, yet 0 · 3 = 0 · 5 is true: a solution was invented.

The move you must not make without thinking

Dividing both sides by something containing the unknown is dangerous, because that something might be zero. From x2 = 5x you might divide by x and get x = 5, losing x = 0, which also works. Here you divide only by plain numbers, so you are safe, but remember the reason.

The procedure, and why it is in this order

Every step has one goal: get the unknown alone. They are ordered so each removes an obstacle the next would trip over.

Method: five steps
  1. Clear the brackets. A term trapped inside one cannot be moved, so brackets go first.
  2. Clear the fractions. Multiply every term on both sides by a common denominator.
  3. Collect. Every x term to one side, every pure number to the other. A term crossing the equals sign changes sign, because crossing is subtracting it from both sides.
  4. Divide. You now have (a number) · x = (a number). Divide by the coefficient of x. Last step, never the first.
  5. Check. Substitute into the original equation and confirm both sides agree.
Solve 3x + 1 = 5x + 7
  1. 3x + 1 = 5x + 7
    Both sides contain x, so neither is ready.
  2. 3x − 5x = 7 − 1
    Take 5x from both sides and 1 from both sides, in one written move. Each term that crossed changed sign.
  3. −2x = 6
    Collect. The coefficient is −2, minus included.
  4. x = −3
    Divide by −2. A positive divided by a negative is negative.
  5. 3(−3) + 1 = −8 and 5(−3) + 7 = −8
    The check. Both sides of the original agree.

When there are brackets on both sides

A bracket is a parcel: everything inside is multiplied by what stands outside, and until it is opened those terms cannot move.

Solve 5(2x − 3) = 3(x + 4) + 2x
  1. 10x − 15 = 3x + 12 + 2x
    Expand both. On the left the 5 multiplies the 2x and the −3.
  2. 10x − 15 = 5x + 12
    Tidy the right side on its own. Tidying one side changes nothing, because it does not change what that side is worth.
  3. 10x − 5x = 12 + 15
    Move 5x left and −15 right. Both change sign on the way across.
  4. 5x = 27 so x = 275 = 5.4
    A non-integer answer is normal. Keep 275 when an exact value is wanted.
  5. 5(7.8) = 39 and 3(9.4) + 10.8 = 39
    The check, on the original line with its brackets in place.
The minus in front of a bracket

8 − 2(x − 5) is not 8 − 2x − 10. The multiplier is −2, so −2 times −5 is +10 and the expression is 18 − 2x. Attach the sign to the multiplier before distributing; that habit removes most sign errors here.

How do we get rid of fractions?

Multiply every term on both sides by a number every denominator divides into, and all the fractions go at once. The smallest such number is the most comfortable, but any common denominator works, so multiply the denominators together if you cannot see it.

The move is legal because it multiplies both sides by a non-zero number. The word that matters is every: a term you forget becomes wrong.

Solve x3 − x − 24 = 56
  1. common denominator = 12
    The smallest number 3, 4 and 6 all divide into.
  2. 12 · x3 − 12 · x − 24 = 12 · 56
    Multiply all three terms, the one on the right included. Writing this line out is what stops a term being missed.
  3. 4x − 3(x − 2) = 10
    Each denominator cancels. The bracket appears because the whole numerator x − 2 was multiplied by 3.
  4. 4x − 3x + 6 = 10
    Expand: −3 times −2 is +6.
  5. x = 4
    Collect. The coefficient is already 1, so there is nothing to divide by.
  6. 43 − 24 = 86 − 36 = 56
    The check, back in the original fractions.
The bracket that appears from nowhere

Multiplying x − 24 by 12 gives 3(x − 2), not 3x − 2. The fraction bar was already a bracket holding the numerator together, so when the bar goes a written bracket takes over its job. Forgetting it is the commonest way a fraction question goes wrong.

What if the coefficient of x turns out to be zero?

Step 4 divides by the coefficient of x. If it has collapsed to zero there is nothing to divide by, and the equation is telling you something else. This happens whenever the two sides change at the same rate, and an exam will set one to see whether you panic.

Solve 2(x + 3) = 2x + 5, and then 2(x + 3) = 2x + 6
  1. 2x + 6 = 2x + 5
    Expand the first.
  2. 0 = −1
    The unknown vanishes and what remains is false, so there is no solution.
  3. 2x + 6 = 2x + 6
    Now the second, with a 6 instead of a 5. The sides are identical.
  4. 0 = 0 so every real number is a solution
    The unknown vanishes again, but what remains is true. The two sides were never two quantities; they were one quantity written two ways.
The three outcomes

Tidy any linear equation and it becomes ax = b. Then exactly one of three things holds.a ≠ 0: one solution, x = baa = 0 and b ≠ 0: no solutiona = 0 and b = 0: every real numberEach side is a straight line and solving asks where they cross. Different slopes cross once; parallel lines never cross; two copies of one line cross everywhere. Nothing else can happen to two straight lines, so nothing else can happen here.

Checking is free marks, so lay it out properly

Verifying takes ten seconds and catches sign slips. For x = 5.4 in 5(2x − 3) = 3(x + 4) + 2x: left side = 5(7.8) = 39; right side = 28.2 + 10.8 = 39; they agree. Left, right, conclusion. It cannot catch an equation set up wrongly, because it tests your equation, not the sentence.

Making a different letter the subject

A business formula is an equation whose unknown has not been chosen yet. Rearranging one uses the same five steps, and the other letters behave like numbers you do not need the value of. Here p is the price per unit, v the variable cost per unit, q the quantity sold and F the fixed cost for the period.

The profit formula

P = (p − v)q − FThe quantity p − v has a name: the contribution margin per unit, what one extra sale contributes towards the fixed costs once its own variable cost is paid. Read it as one thing rather than three.

Make q the subject of P = (p − v)q − F
  1. P + F = (p − v)q
    Add F to both sides. It crossed the equals sign, so it changed sign.
  2. P + Fp − v = q
    Divide by p − v, the coefficient of q. The whole of P + F goes over the bar, because the whole of it was multiplied.
  3. q = P + Fp − v, valid when p ≠ v
    State the condition. If p = v each unit contributes nothing and no quantity reaches the target.

Set the target profit to zero and you have the break-even formula:qBE = Fp − vRead it before using it: how many units it takes to pay off the fixed costs, one contribution at a time. The formula is the sentence.

The Nyon shop: F = 4800, p = 14.50, v = 6.20
  1. p − v = 8.30
    Each bag contributes 8.30 CHF towards the fixed costs.
  2. qBE = 48008.30 ≈ 578.31
    Fixed cost divided by contribution. A bag is not divisible, so this is not the answer yet.
  3. 579 bags
    Round up for a break-even quantity. At 578 bags the shop is 2.60 CHF short; at 579 it is 5.70 CHF ahead.
Say what the number means

The answer to Jane is not "579". It is: the shop must sell about 579 bags a month, roughly 19 a day, before it earns anything at all. That sentence is what lets her decide whether the shop is viable.

Turning a sentence into an equation

This is the part exams test. Nobody hands you 5(2x − 3) = 3(x + 4) + 2x at work; they hand you a paragraph.

Decide what the unknown is, build each side separately, and only then write the equals sign. Students who write the equals sign first put the wrong things either side of it.

Method: from words to algebra
  1. Name the unknown, with its unit. An answer in francs cannot be a number of people, and an unlabelled letter is the most expensive thing on the page.
  2. Build each side separately from the given numbers and the letter you named.
  3. Find the word that means equals. It is rarely "equals". It is "comes to", "breaks even", "totals", "is left".
  4. Solve, then answer in a sentence using the words of the question and the unit from step 1.
The phrases that keep coming back
In the sentenceIn algebraThe usual error
15 per cent off the price p0.85p0.15p, the discount, not the amount paid
the shop breaks evenrevenue = total costsetting profit equal to revenue instead of to zero
A wholesale invoice
  1. the words
    A wholesale customer gets 15 per cent off the list price of a bag and pays a flat 40 CHF for delivery. The invoice for 120 bags came to 1 519 CHF. What is the list price?
  2. let p = the list price of one bag, in CHF
    Name the unknown and its unit first.
  3. price paid per bag = 0.85p
    Fifteen per cent off means 85 per cent is paid.
  4. 120(0.85p) + 40 = 1519
    Each side built on its own. "Came to" is the word that means equals.
  5. 102p + 40 = 1519
    120 · 0.85 = 102. Tidy the coefficient before moving anything.
  6. p = 14.50
    Take 40 from both sides to get 102p = 1479, then divide by 102.
  7. in words
    The list price is 14.50 CHF, the shelf price we already charge, so this customer pays the standard rate less the agreed discount.
Where marks are lost in this topic
  • Losing the sign when a term crosses. 3x + 1 = 5x + 7 becomes 3x − 5x = 7 − 1.
  • A minus in front of a bracket. −2(x − 5) = −2x + 10.
  • Forgetting a term when clearing fractions. Every term, whole numbers included.
  • Losing the numerator bracket. 12 · x − 24 = 3(x − 2).
  • Rounding a break-even quantity down. Round up, or the costs are not covered.
What to remember
  • Solving means finding every number that makes the statement true, and an answer can be tested.
  • The same operation on both sides preserves truth, unless it is by zero.
  • Brackets, fractions, collect, divide, check.
  • Clearing fractions multiplies every term, and each numerator keeps a bracket.
  • If the coefficient collapses to zero, the answer is no solution or every real number. Say which, and why.
  • To make a letter the subject, use the same steps and state that the coefficient is not zero.
  • qBE = Fp − v: fixed cost divided by contribution per unit, rounded up.
  • Name the unknown with its unit, then answer in a sentence.

Part 0  ·  Lesson 7 of 13

Quadratic equations

One unknown, raised to the power two. The moment a business quantity depends on a price that also changes the quantity sold, the algebra stops being linear and becomes this.

Before this lesson you need
  • How to solve a linear equation, and why both sides move together
  • How to expand and factor, from expanding and factoring
  • What a square root is and when it exists, from powers and roots
In this lesson you will learn
  • What a quadratic is, and where one comes from in business
  • Why everything must be moved to one side before anything else
  • What the discriminant measures, and what each of its three cases looks like
  • How to use the formula without losing a sign
  • How to spot a factorisation quickly, and when not to look for one
  • How to decide which root a business question actually wants
The same topic on Khan Academy
  • Algebra 1, unit 14: Quadratic functions and equations

Free, no account needed to watch. Their exercises need one.

Where a squared term comes from

The app subscription costs 9 CHF a month and has 4000 subscribers. Marketing has tested the price, and Jane has the result: every 1 CHF added to the price loses about 250 subscribers.

So the number of subscribers at price p is 4000 − 250(p − 9), which tidies to 6250 − 250p. Revenue is price times subscribers:R(p) = p(6250 − 250p) = 6250p − 250p2The p2 did not come from nowhere. It appeared because p is in the formula twice: once as the price each subscriber pays, and once inside the number of subscribers. Whenever a quantity multiplies something that depends on the same quantity, you get a square.

Jane wants to know at what price the app brings in 39 000 CHF. That question is 6250p − 250p2 = 39000, and you cannot collect your way out of it. You need a different method, and it is the one this lesson is about.

What counts as a quadratic

Definition

A quadratic equation in x is one that can be writtenax2 + bx + c = 0, with a ≠ 0That is called standard form. The numbers a, b and c are the coefficients, and each carries its own sign. The condition a ≠ 0 is what makes it quadratic: with a = 0 the squared term is gone and you are back in the previous lesson.

The graph of y = ax2 + bx + c is a parabola, a symmetric curve that opens upwards when a > 0 and downwards when a < 0. Solving the equation asks where that curve meets the horizontal axis. Keeping that picture in mind will make the discriminant obvious rather than arbitrary.

Why everything has to be moved to one side first

Two separate reasons, and both matter.

First, a, b and c only mean anything relative to a zero on the other side. 2x2 + 5x = 3 has no c; you cannot read one off until the 3 has moved across and become −3.

Second, the whole of the method rests on a fact about zero, which is stated below in the section on factoring. Zero is the only number that fact works for, which is why the right-hand side has to be zero and not 3.

Put 3x2 + 2x = 4x2 − x + 6 into standard form
  1. 3x2 + 2x = 4x2 − x + 6
    Squared terms on both sides, so nothing can be read off yet.
  2. 3x2 − 4x2 + 2x + x − 6 = 0
    Move every term to the left. Each one that crosses changes sign, exactly as in a linear equation.
  3. −x2 + 3x − 6 = 0
    Collect the like terms.
  4. x2 − 3x + 6 = 0
    Multiply both sides by −1 so that a is positive. This is optional, but it removes a whole family of sign errors.
  5. a = 1, b = −3, c = 6
    Only now read the coefficients, each with its sign attached.
The sign belongs to the coefficient

In 3x2 + 3x − 18 = 0 the value of c is −18, not 18. That matters immediately, because −4ac = −4(3)(−18) = +216. Dropping that minus is the commonest single error in this topic. Write a =, b = and c = on their own line, signs included, before you use them for anything.

The discriminant, and what it measures

Before finding the solutions you can find out how many there are. The quantity that tells you is called the discriminant, written Δ.

It is the quantity that ends up under the square root, so its sign decides whether the root exists at all. A parabola has one lowest or highest point, and Δ measures which side of the horizontal axis that point falls on. That is the whole of its meaning.

The discriminant

For ax2 + bx + c = 0 in standard form,Δ = b2 − 4acIts sign decides how many real solutions exist, before any of them is computed.

The three cases, and what each one looks like
CaseSolutions in ℝThe parabola
Δ > 0two distinct solutionscuts the horizontal axis at two separate points
Δ = 0one solution, a double roottouches the axis at exactly one point, its lowest or highest
Δ < 0nonemisses the axis completely, staying entirely above it or entirely below

The two roots sit symmetrically either side of x = −b2a, which is where the parabola turns. When Δ shrinks to zero the two roots have slid together onto that turning point, which is why the case is called a double root rather than "only one".

The formula, used carefully

The quadratic formula

When Δ ≥ 0,x = −b ± Δ2aThe ± is what produces the two answers. The whole numerator sits over 2a, not over a, and not only the root.

Solve 3x2 + 3x − 18 = 0
  1. a = 3, b = 3, c = −18
    Standard form already. Read the coefficients with their signs.
  2. Δ = 32 − 4(3)(−18) = 9 + 216 = 225
    Two negatives multiplied give a positive, so the 216 is added. Δ > 0, so expect two solutions.
  3. 225 = 15
    A perfect square, which is a sign the exercise was designed to come out exactly.
  4. x = −3 ± 156
    Apply the formula: −b = −3 and 2a = 6.
  5. x = 2 or x = −3
    126 = 2 and −186 = −3. Check the first: 3(4) + 6 − 18 = 0.
Solve 2x2 − 7x − 15 = 0
  1. a = 2, b = −7, c = −15
    Two negative coefficients, which is where signs go wrong.
  2. Δ = (−7)2 − 4(2)(−15) = 49 + 120 = 169
    (−7)2 = +49: a square is never negative. And −4(2)(−15) = +120.
  3. 169 = 13
    Another perfect square.
  4. x = 7 ± 134
    −b means minus the value of b, and b is −7, so −b = +7. This is the step students lose.
  5. x = 5 or x = −1.5
    204 = 5 and −64 = −1.5. Check: 2(25) − 35 − 15 = 0.
Three places the formula goes wrong

The first is −b when b is already negative: it becomes positive. The second is b2 when b is negative: it also becomes positive, so (−7)2 = 49 and never −49. The third is the division: everything above the bar is divided by 2a, so write the bar long enough to cover the whole numerator.

When the numbers are kind: factoring

The formula always works. Factoring is faster when it works, and it rests on a fact about zero that is worth stating on its own.

The zero product rule

If two numbers multiply to give zero, at least one of them is zero.MN = 0 ⇔ M = 0 or N = 0No other number has this property. MN = 6 tells you nothing about M. That is why standard form insists on a zero, and not on any other convenient number, on the right.

So if you can write the left side as a product of two brackets, each bracket gives you a linear equation, and you already know how to solve those.

Two quick tests tell you whether to look. If a = 1, search for two numbers whose product is c and whose sum is b. More generally, compute Δ first: if it is a perfect square the roots are rational and a factorisation exists, and if it is not, go straight to the formula.

Solve x2 − 3x − 40 = 0 by factoring
  1. product −40, sum −3
    Here a = 1, so look for two numbers multiplying to c and adding to b.
  2. −8 and +5
    (−8)(5) = −40 and −8 + 5 = −3. The product is negative, so the two numbers have opposite signs.
  3. (x − 8)(x + 5) = 0
    Each number appears in a bracket with its sign reversed, because the bracket is zero when x equals that number.
  4. x = 8 or x = −5
    By the zero product rule, one bracket or the other must vanish. Check with the discriminant: Δ = 9 + 160 = 169 = 132, a perfect square, as predicted.
Never divide an equation by the unknown

x2 = 5x looks like it wants dividing by x, giving x = 5. That loses a solution. Move everything to one side instead: x2 − 5x = 0, then factor to x(x − 5) = 0, which gives x = 0 or x = 5. Dividing by x silently assumed x ≠ 0, and in a business setting the lost root is often the interesting one, because zero output is a real possibility.

When there is no solution, stop

Jane asks a second question: what price would bring in 40 000 CHF? Set the revenue equal to that and see.

Solve 6250p − 250p2 = 40 000
  1. 250p2 − 6250p + 40000 = 0
    Standard form, written with a positive leading coefficient.
  2. p2 − 25p + 160 = 0
    Divide every term by 250. Dividing by a non-zero number is safe and keeps the same solutions.
  3. Δ = (−25)2 − 4(1)(160) = 625 − 640 = −15
    Δ < 0.
  4. no real solution
    Stop here. Do not take the root of −15 and do not write a number down. Writing Δ < 0 and "no real solution" is the complete answer.
What the empty answer is telling the business

It is not a dead end, it is information. The parabola R(p) = 6250p − 250p2 turns at p = −b2a = 12.5, where revenue is 39 062.50 CHF. That is the most the app can earn at any price. 40 000 is above the peak, so no price reaches it. The honest answer to Jane is that the target is unreachable by pricing alone, and that she needs more subscribers rather than a better price.

The business quadratic, and choosing the root

Back to the reachable target. At what price does the app bring in 39 000 CHF?

Solve 6250p − 250p2 = 39 000
  1. 250p2 − 6250p + 39000 = 0
    Everything to one side, leading coefficient positive.
  2. p2 − 25p + 156 = 0
    Divide through by 250 to keep the arithmetic small.
  3. Δ = 625 − 624 = 1
    Δ > 0, so two prices reach the target. A discriminant of 1 is a warning that the two roots will be close together.
  4. p = 25 ± 12
    1 = 1, and 2a = 2.
  5. p = 13 or p = 12
    Two prices, both positive, both plausible for a monthly subscription.
  6. at 12: 3250 subscribers; at 13: 3000 subscribers
    Substitute back into 6250 − 250p. Both give 39 000 CHF: 12(3250) and 13(3000).

Now the mathematics has finished and the judgement begins. Both roots are genuine solutions of the equation, and the algebra has no opinion about which to choose.

The business does. Same revenue, but 12 CHF keeps 250 more subscribers, which means more people inside the product, more usage data and more to sell to later. 13 CHF serves fewer customers for the same money, which costs less to support. Jane would choose 12 if she is growing and 13 if she is short of support staff. Your job is to present both roots with their consequences, not to hide one of them.

When a root must be thrown away

Sometimes the context rules a root out completely, and saying so is part of the answer. A roasting floor is to be 6 m longer than it is wide with an area of 216 m2: w(w + 6) = 216, so w2 + 6w − 216 = 0. Then Δ = 36 + 864 = 900 and 900 = 30, giving w = −6 ± 302, so w = 12 or w = −18. A width cannot be negative, so the floor is 12 m by 18 m. Reject the other root in writing, with the reason. A rejected root that is never mentioned looks like a root that was never found.

Where marks are lost in this topic
  • Reading a, b, c before standard form. Everything on one side, zero on the other, then read.
  • Dropping the sign of c. In 3x2 + 3x − 18, c = −18, so −4ac = +216.
  • Squaring a negative b wrongly. (−7)2 = 49.
  • Dividing by a instead of 2a, or dividing only the root and not the whole numerator.
  • Taking the root of a negative discriminant. When Δ < 0, the answer is that there is none.
  • Dividing through by the unknown, which deletes the root x = 0.
  • Giving both roots when the context allows one, or giving one when it allows both, without saying why.
What to remember
  • Standard form first: ax2 + bx + c = 0 with a ≠ 0, then read the coefficients with their signs.
  • Δ = b2 − 4ac gives the number of real solutions before you find any: two, one, or none.
  • Geometrically those three cases are a parabola cutting the axis, touching it, or missing it.
  • x = −b ± Δ2a, with the whole numerator over 2a.
  • Factoring works because a product is zero only when a factor is zero. A perfect-square Δ tells you a factorisation exists.
  • A squared term appears in business whenever a price also changes the quantity sold.
  • Finish by asking what each root means. Keep the ones the context allows, and reject the others in writing.

Part 0  ·  Lesson 8 of 13

Equations with the unknown in a denominator

The one kind of equation where you must write down what the unknown cannot be, before you solve. Average cost and price per unit both have a variable underneath, so this is a business method as much as an algebraic one.

Before this lesson you need
  • How to add fractions, and what a common denominator is
  • How to expand a bracket and collect terms, from expanding and factoring
  • How to solve a linear and a quadratic equation, because clearing denominators produces both
In this lesson you will learn
  • Why an unknown in a denominator changes the rules, and what exactly goes wrong
  • How to list the excluded values before you touch the equation
  • How to clear denominators, including two different ones, and when cross-multiplication is allowed
  • What an extraneous solution is, where it comes from, and how to catch it
  • Why the honest answer is sometimes no solution, and how to say so
  • How to answer a question about average cost per unit reaching a target
The same topic on Khan Academy
  • Algebra 2, unit 10: Equations, including rational ones
  • Precalculus, unit 4: Rational functions

Free, no account needed to watch. Their exercises need one.

A question with the unknown underneath

XY Coffee Co roasts beans in Geneva. The roasting line costs 2 400 CHF a week to keep running whether it produces anything or not, and every kilogram of beans that goes through it adds 4 CHF of gas, labour and packaging. The total weekly cost of roasting q kilograms is therefore C(q) = 4q + 2400.

Jane, the Head of Insights, wants the cost of one kilogram, which is the total shared over everything produced: A(q) = 4q + 2400q. At what weekly output does a kilogram cost 10 CHF to roast?

That question is an equation: 4q + 2400q = 10. It looks like every other equation in this part, with one difference that changes everything. The unknown is underneath, and that takes away the freedom to multiply and divide without asking whether the step was allowed.

Why these equations need different care

A fraction is an instruction to divide, and division by zero has no answer. This is not a rule somebody invented. 123 = 4 because 4 · 3 = 12, so 120 would have to be the number giving 12 when multiplied by zero, and no such number exists.

So 1x − 5 is not a number when x = 5. It is not zero and it is not infinity. The value 5 sits outside the world this expression lives in.

The excluded values

For an equation containing somethingx − 5, the value x = 5 is excluded. It cannot be a solution, it cannot be tested, it cannot appear in the answer.set each denominator equal to zero, solve, and forbid those valuesYou do this first, before any algebra, because the algebra itself will destroy the evidence.

One denominator

x + 4x forbids x = 0.

A linear denominator

32x − 7 needs 2x − 7 = 0 solving, giving x = 3.5.

A factorised denominator

5(x − 1)(x + 6) forbids 1 and −6, since a product is zero when either factor is.

If a denominator is not factorised, factorise it first. x2 − 9 is (x − 3)(x + 3), so both 3 and −3 are excluded. Reading only the first is the commonest way of losing this mark.

The method, in the order that keeps you safe

Method: exclude, clear, solve, check
  1. State the excluded values. Set every denominator to zero and solve. Write the results as a line of your answer, not in your head.
  2. Clear the denominators. Multiply both sides by the common denominator, so that no fraction is left.
  3. Solve the polynomial equation you now have, by the ordinary methods.
  4. Check every candidate against the exclusion list. Any candidate on it is thrown away. If all of them are, there is no solution.
Why step one cannot wait until the end

By the end of the solving, the denominators have gone. Once xx − 2 = 2x − 2 has become x = 2, nothing on the page remembers that 2 was forbidden. Writing the exclusions first keeps the evidence.

Solve x + 4x = 15
  1. x ≠ 0
