Fixed for this problem, but a different number elsewhere. Rent of 18 600 CHF a month, a cost of 2.40 CHF a cup. Handed to you.

An assumption

Something you decided to believe in order to write anything at all. "Demand falls as price rises, by this much." Not given, and not checkable inside the model.

How to tell them apart in a described situation

Does it change inside this problem? A variable. Is it a number somebody handed me? A parameter. Did I decide it, and could a reasonable person decide otherwise? An assumption. A parameter can become a variable later, and saying so earns a mark.

One situation, sorted
From the situationWhich is itWhy
Cups sold in a monthVariableWhat we solve for, and it changes.
Rent of 18 600 CHF a monthParameterFixed for this cafe; another cafe differs.
The price of 5.50 CHFParameter here, variable laterFixed while we ask about volume; the variable once we ask about pricing.
Every cup costs the same to makeAssumptionWe decided it. Bulk buying would lower it.
Rent does not change with volumeAssumptionBelievable until more space is needed.

Units, and why they are not decoration

Carry the unit with every number. It catches a class of error that checking the arithmetic never finds, because the arithmetic is correct and the meaning is not.

The two sides must match, and only quantities with the same unit can be added. Multiplication combines units instead, so CHF per cup times cups gives CHF, and the "cup" cancels.

CHF per cup × cups = CHF
CHF per month ÷ CHF per cup = cups per month
CHF + CHF = CHF,   but   CHF + cups is meaningless
The dimension check, in one line

Read the equation aloud in units first. P = 5.50q − (18 600 + 2.40q) is "CHF per cup times cups, minus CHF plus CHF per cup times cups", so CHF minus CHF, so CHF. If a term will not reduce to the unit on the left, the model is wrong.

The period mismatch

The commonest unit error here is a monthly figure next to an annual one. Pick one period at the start, convert everything to it, and write it next to the answer. "6000" is not an answer. "6000 cups per month" is.

The three relationships to know by heart

Almost every applied question in the autumn semester is one of three formulas, sometimes with a curve in place of a line. Learn them in words as well as in symbols, because the words let you recognise them inside a paragraph of English.

Cost, revenue, profit

q the quantity, p the price per unit, F the fixed cost, v the variable cost per unit:C(q) = F + v × q    R(q) = p × q    P(q) = R(q) − C(q)Fixed cost is what you pay whether you sell anything or not; variable cost is what each extra unit costs.

A fourth quantity hides in these, the one businesses talk about. Rearranging profit gives P(q) = (p − v)q − F. The bracket is the contribution per unit: what each cup puts towards the fixed costs once its ingredients are paid for.

Read it as a story. Every cup contributes (p − v) francs to a hole of size F, so profit starts at −F and climbs with each cup.

Break-even

Where revenue exactly covers cost, so profit is zero.p × q = F + v × q  ⇔  q = Fp − vThe fixed cost divided by the contribution per unit: how many must we sell before we stop losing money.

Break-even needs the price above the variable cost

If p ≤ v the denominator is zero or negative and there is no break-even quantity. That is the algebra telling you something true: if each cup loses money before rent is considered, selling more makes things worse. Read a negative break-even as "never", not as a sign to cross out.

A full pass: the Carouge cafe

Jane hands you this: "The Carouge cafe pays 18 600 francs a month in rent, wages and insurance. Each flat white costs 2.40 in ingredients and cup, and we sell them at 5.50. The manager says we are busy. Are we actually making anything?"

Stage 1: sharpen the question
  1. "Are we making anything" is not measurable. Replace it with two questions that are.
  2. How many flat whites a month before profit becomes positive?
  3. What is the profit at the volume we sell today?
Stage 2: build the model
  1. Let q = flat whites sold in one month
    Name the variable and its unit first. The period is a month, because that is how the rent was quoted.
  2. F = 18 600 CHF, v = 2.40 CHF per cup, p = 5.50 CHF per cup
    Three parameters, handed to us in the sentence.
  3. C(q) = 18 600 + 2.40q
    Fixed plus variable times quantity. Units: CHF plus CHF per cup times cups, so CHF.
  4. R(q) = 5.50q
    Price times quantity.
  5. P(q) = 5.50q − (18 600 + 2.40q) = 3.10q − 18 600
    The bracket matters: the minus applies to the whole cost. Contribution is 3.10 CHF a cup. Assumptions: every cup sells at full price, ingredients cost the same each time, rent does not move with volume.
Stages 3 and 4: the data and the answer
  1. 3.10q − 18 600 = 0
    Set profit to zero, which is the definition of break-even.
  2. q = 18 6003.10 = 6000
    Units: CHF per month divided by CHF per cup gives cups per month.
  3. R(6000) = 33 000 and C(6000) = 33 000
    Both sides agree, so the solution is right. Always worth ten seconds.
  4. P(7500) = 3.10(7500) − 18 600 = 4650
    The manager says about 7500 a month.
Stage 5: the decision, said properly

"The Carouge cafe breaks even at 6000 flat whites a month. At its current 7500 it makes roughly 4650 CHF a month. This assumes every cup sells at the full 5.50 and that rent does not rise with volume, so a month with discounting would come out lower."

A number, a unit, a period, and the assumption that would break it. The figure 6000 alone is only stage 4.

A second pass: should the subscription go up?

The first pass had no real decision in it. This one does, and it shows the hardest stage: a model needs an assumption before it can say anything about the future.

Jane hands you this: "The app subscription is 9 francs a month and we have 4200 subscribers. It costs 27 300 a month to run, plus about 1.20 per subscriber in fees and support. Marketing want 10 francs. Should we?"

Stages 1 and 2 together
  1. "Should we" becomes "would monthly profit be higher at 10 francs than at 9 francs".
  2. Variables: p the price in CHF per subscriber per month, n the number of subscribers.
  3. Parameters: F = 27 300 CHF a month, v = 1.20 CHF per subscriber.
  4. Assumption, and it is the whole question: going to 10 francs loses 8 per cent of subscribers. Nobody measured that. Marketing estimated it, and the answer depends on it.
Stage 4, part one: profit as things stand
  1. R = 9.00 × 4200 = 37 800
    Price times quantity, in CHF a month.
  2. C = 27 300 + 1.20 × 4200 = 32 340
    Fixed plus variable times quantity.
  3. P = 5460 CHF a month
    The number the new price must beat.
Stage 4, part two: profit at the new price
  1. n = 4200 × 0.92 = 3864
    Losing 8 per cent means multiplying by 0.92, from percentages.
  2. R = 10.00 × 3864 = 38 640
    Fewer subscribers, each paying more.
  3. C = 27 300 + 1.20 × 3864 = 31 936.80
    The variable cost falls too, with fewer subscribers to serve.
  4. P = 6703.20, a gain of 1243.20 CHF a month
    A rise of about 22.8 per cent on the old profit.

Before writing the decision, test the assumption: what loss of subscribers would wipe the gain out?

How bad would the loss have to be for the rise to be pointless?
  1. contribution at 10 CHF = 10.00 − 1.20 = 8.80
    Each subscriber now contributes 8.80 CHF towards the fixed 27 300.
  2. 8.80n − 27 300 ≥ 5460
    The new profit must be at least the old profit.
  3. n ≥ 32 7608.80 ≈ 3722.7, so n ≥ 3723
    Round up: 3722 would fall short, and there is no part of a subscriber.
  4. tolerable loss ≈ 11.4%
    1 − 37234200 is about 0.114. The rise pays while fewer than roughly 11.4 per cent leave. Marketing expect 8 per cent, so there is room, but not much.
Stage 5: the decision, with the caveat that matters

"Raising the subscription from 9 to 10 francs would lift monthly profit from 5460 CHF to about 6703 CHF, a gain of roughly 1243 CHF a month, if we lose 8 per cent of subscribers as marketing expect. It still pays while we lose less than about 11.4 per cent; above that we are worse off than today. The answer rests on the 8 per cent estimate, which I would want tested."

That last sentence names the assumption and tells the reader where the answer would break. It is the difference between a calculation and advice.

A model is a claim, not a fact

Both passes above are wrong in the strict sense: cups do not all sell at full price, and subscribers do not leave in a neat 8 per cent. A model is useful when it is wrong in ways that do not change the decision, so your job at stage 5 is to say which way it is wrong.

Why a number is not yet an answer

This stage costs the most marks, for a reason unconnected with mathematics. By the time you reach the number you have concentrated hard, it looks like the finish line, and you stop.

It is not. Somebody asked a question in English and is waiting for a reply in English. "6000" is not a reply. It is not even a sentence.

What a finished answer contains

a number   +   its unit   +   the question restated   +   the caveat"The cafe breaks even at 6000 flat whites a month, assuming rent does not rise with volume."

Not an answer

q = 6000. True, and it earns the computation marks only.

Better

"6000 cups." A unit, but no period and nothing about what it means.

An answer

"The cafe breaks even at 6000 flat whites a month, so at 7500 it is profitable, provided rent does not rise."

A sentence template that always works

"The [quantity] is [number] [unit] per [period], which means [what the business should notice], assuming [the thing you are least sure of]." Mechanical, and it earns the final mark every time.

Where marks are lost in this topic
  • No definition of the variable. Equations full of q without saying what it counts, or over what period.
  • Calling an assumption a fact. "Demand falls 8 per cent" was an estimate.
  • Mixing periods. Annual rent against monthly sales.
  • Dropping the bracket in profit. P = pq − (F + vq), not P = pq − F + vq.
  • Stopping at the number. The question was asked at stage 5.
What to remember
  • Question, model, data, answer, decision. The mathematics is stage four of five.
  • Name your variable, in words and with a unit, before any equation.
  • A variable changes inside the problem, a parameter is fixed for it, an assumption is something you chose to believe.
  • Carry units through every line. Units that do not reduce mean the model is wrong.
  • C(q) = F + vq, R(q) = pq, P(q) = R(q) − C(q), break-even at q = Fp − v.
  • Finish with a sentence: number, unit, period, and the assumption that would break it.
Part IIFunctions · Week 16 lessons

Part II  ·  Lesson 1 of 6

What a function is

Session 1. Every other idea this semester is a variation on this one, so it is worth going slowly. A function is how a business writes down the sentence “this depends on that” in a form you can compute with.

Before this lesson you need
  • How to substitute a number into an expression, from expanding and factoring
  • The order of operations, because evaluating a function is one long application of it
  • How to read a point off a pair of axes
  • What the modelling cycle is for
In this lesson you will learn
  • Why a business needs the idea of a function at all
  • The definition this course uses, and why it says at most one and not exactly one
  • The four representations, words, table, graph and formula, and what each one is good for
  • How to evaluate a function at a number, at a negative number and at an expression such as x + h
  • The vertical line test, and the reason it works
  • How to read a case-defined function, and which branch owns a boundary value
The same topic on Khan Academy
  • Algebra 1, unit 8: Functions

Free, no account needed to watch. Their exercises need one.

A question Jane cannot answer with a single number

XY Coffee Co roasts green beans in Geneva. The factory can handle up to 100 tons a day, and Jane, the Head of Insights, has been asked what it costs to run.

That question has no single answer. Cost is not a number the company has. It is a number that changes with how much you roast. On a quiet Monday the roaster costs one amount to run, on a busy Friday another. Every honest answer starts with the words “it depends”.

“It depends” is the beginning of a description, not a refusal. What Jane needs is a way of writing down what it depends on and how, precise enough that you can put a quantity in at one end and read a cost out at the other. That object is a function.

You put in

A quantity you choose or observe. Here, tons of beans to roast today. This is the input.

A rule acts

One fixed rule, the same one every time. It does not care who is asking or what day it is.

You read out

One cost in francs, and never two different ones. This is the output.

Everything a business models is shaped like that. Revenue depends on price, staff cost on headcount, subscription income on how many months have passed. Once one of these is written as a function you can draw it, compare it with another, find where it peaks, and in week 5 differentiate it.

Input

Also called the independent variable, or x. The thing you choose or observe. It is independent because nothing in the model tells it what to be.

Output

Also called the dependent variable, or y. The thing that results. It is dependent because the rule decides it entirely.

The definition this course uses

Definition

A function f : X → Y is a rule that assigns, to each element x in X, at most one element of Y. If something is assigned to x, it is writtenf(x)The set of x for which f(x) is defined is the domain. The set of values f(x) actually takes is the range.

Notice the three words in bold. Many textbooks say exactly one. This course says at most one, and the difference is deliberate.

Why at most one and not exactly one

Take the rule f(x) = xx − 2 and let X be all of ℝ. For every real number except 2 the rule produces one value. At x = 2 it produces nothing at all, because the denominator is zero.

Under a definition demanding exactly one output for every x in X, this rule would not be a function until you had shrunk X down to ℝ\{2} first.

Under this course’s definition you write the rule down, call it a function, and then ask separately which inputs it answers for. That set is the domain, and finding it is the whole of the next lesson.

What is forbidden, and it is only one thing

Two different outputs for the same input. That is the single prohibition. No output is allowed, and means the input is outside the domain. One output is the normal case. Two outputs break the rule, because then f(x) would not name a number.

The business version of the same sentence

Place the same order twice on the same terms and you must be quoted the same price twice. A price list that gave two prices for one order would not be a price list.

What f(x) means, and what it does not

The notation f(x) is read “f of x”. It names the output that the function f produces when you feed it the input x. The letter f is the name of the rule, and the bracket is a container for whatever you are feeding in.

f(x) is not f times x

This is the first notational trap of the course and it catches people all semester. In f(x) the bracket does not mean multiplication. It means application. So f(2 + 3) is f(5), one number fed into the rule. It is not f(2) + f(3), and there is no reason those two should agree. With f(x) = x2 you get f(5) = 25 while f(2) + f(3) = 4 + 9 = 13.

The letters are labels and nothing more. f(x) = 3x + 1, f(t) = 3t + 1 and f(☐) = 3☐ + 1 are the same function written three ways. What matters is the shape of the rule, not the letter you pour into it, and that is what makes f(x + h) ordinary in week 4 rather than alarming.

The four faces of one function

The same relationship can be presented in four ways, and a week 1 objective is to move between them in any direction. Each face makes one property obvious and hides the rest.

One function, four representations
FaceWhat it looks likeWhat it is good forWhat it hides
Words“Cost rises with quantity, gently at first and steeply at the end.”Meaning. It is the only face a manager will read.Every exact value.
TableA column of inputs beside a column of outputs.Exact values at the points you measured.Everything between those points.
GraphA curve drawn on a pair of axes.Shape. Peaks, troughs, and whether the curve is bending.Precision. You cannot read 32 476 off a graph.
FormulaC(q) = …Prediction at any input, and the input for differentiation.Intuition, until you draw it.

Here is XY Coffee Co’s cost as a table, measured on the factory floor.

Production cost as a function of quantity
Quantity q (tons)Total cost C (francs)
0500
2014 100
4021 300
6031 700
6132 476
7041 100
8054 900
100100 500

Written formally, C : A → B with q → C(q), where A = [0 ; 100] and B = [500 ; 100 500].

Three things are worth saying out loud. The cost at zero is not zero: 500 francs leave the bank before a single ton is roasted. That is a fixed cost, and it is why the graph misses the origin. The cost does not rise in a straight line: 0 to 20 tons adds 13 600 francs, or 680 a ton, while 80 to 100 tons adds 45 600 francs, or 2 280 a ton. The last tons cost more than three times the first ones, which is a fact about an overheating roaster. And the domain stops at 100 because the factory cannot do more, not because the arithmetic breaks.

Moving between the faces, in practice

Table to graph: plot the pairs and join them. Formula to table: substitute. Table to formula: the hard direction, and what regression does in your statistics course. Graph to words: describe the shape, then say what it means for the business. An exam gives you one face and asks for another, so practise the direction you like least.

How do we evaluate one?

Evaluating means replacing the variable by something and working the arithmetic out. The something can be a number, a negative number, or a whole expression. The method never changes, and the bracket is what keeps it safe.

Method: three steps, and the first one is a bracket
  1. Rewrite the rule with an empty bracket everywhere the variable appears: f( ) = 3( )2 − 5( ) + 2.
  2. Put the input inside every one of those brackets, including any that sit under a power or a root.
  3. Only now do the arithmetic, following the usual order of operations.
Evaluate f(4), with f(x) = 3x2 − 5x + 2
  1. f( ) = 3( )2 − 5( ) + 2
    Write the rule with holes. This costs you four seconds and saves the sign errors that follow.
  2. f(4) = 3(4)2 − 5(4) + 2
    Put 4 into both holes. Notice that the square applies to the 4, not to the 3.
  3. = 3(16) − 20 + 2 = 48 − 20 + 2
    Powers before multiplication, multiplication before addition.
  4. f(4) = 30
    One input, one output. That is the function doing its only job.

A negative input is the same method, and the bracket stops being optional. Almost every mark lost on this kind of question comes from squaring a minus sign that was never written down.

Evaluate f(−2), same f
  1. f(−2) = 3(−2)2 − 5(−2) + 2
    The whole of −2 goes in the bracket, minus sign included.
  2. (−2)2 = 4
    A negative squared is positive. Writing −22 without the bracket would have meant −4, which is a different number.
  3. −5(−2) = +10
    A negative times a negative is positive, so this term adds rather than subtracts.
  4. f(−2) = 12 + 10 + 2 = 24
    Both traps avoided, and the two of them are the whole difficulty of this question.
The bracket is not decoration

−22 and (−2)2 are different: the first is −4, the second is 4. The power binds tighter than the minus sign unless a bracket says otherwise. Write the bracket every time and the question never arises.

Evaluating at an expression, which is the one that matters later

Nothing changes when the input is an expression rather than a number. You still fill the holes. The only new work is expanding afterwards.

This looks like an odd thing to ask for until week 4, when the difference quotient evaluates a function at x + h and subtracts. Meeting that move for the first time on the day you also meet limits is hard. Do it now instead.

With f(x) = x2 + 4, find f(a + 1)
  1. f( ) = ( )2 + 4
    The hole is inside a square, so whatever goes in gets squared as a whole.
  2. f(a + 1) = (a + 1)2 + 4
    The entire expression a + 1 goes in, not only the a.
  3. = a2 + 2a + 1 + 4
    Expand with (p + q)2 = p2 + 2pq + q2. The middle term is the one people drop.
  4. f(a + 1) = a2 + 2a + 5
    Check it at a = 3: this gives 9 + 6 + 5 = 20, and f(4) = 16 + 4 = 20. They agree.
With the same f, find f(x + h) and then f(x + h) − f(x)h
  1. f(x + h) = (x + h)2 + 4
    Same move. The hole takes all of x + h.
  2. = x2 + 2xh + h2 + 4
    Expand. Here h is a second letter, treated exactly like a number.
  3. f(x + h) − f(x) = (x2 + 2xh + h2 + 4) − (x2 + 4)
    Subtract the original. Keep the second bracket until you have distributed the minus sign.
  4. = 2xh + h2
    The x2 and the 4 cancel. Everything left has an h in it, which is not an accident.
  5. f(x + h) − f(x)h = 2x + h
    Divide through by h. In week 4 you will let h shrink to nothing and read off 2x, the derivative. You have now done the algebra half of that a month early.

The vertical line test, and why it works

A graph is a picture of a set of pairs. Every point on it is (x, f(x)): first coordinate the input, second coordinate the output. The whole test falls out of that one sentence.

A vertical line at x = a collects every point whose first coordinate is a. So the number of times it meets the curve is the number of outputs the rule assigns to a. Compare that with the definition.

What each vertical line is telling you
The line at x = a meets the curveNumber of outputs for aVerdict
not at allnoneFine. a is outside the domain.
onceoneFine. The normal case.
twice or moretwo or moreNot a function. The rule is ambiguous at a.
The vertical line test

A curve is the graph of a function if no vertical line cuts it more than once. Note the wording: not exactly once. A line that misses the curve entirely is allowed, and pictures an input outside the domain. The test is the geometry of “at most one output per input”.

Two consequences. A circle is not the graph of a function, because a vertical line through its middle cuts it twice. And the vertical line x = 3 is itself not a function, which is why week 2 says it has no y-intercept and a slope that does not exist.

Case-defined functions, and who owns the boundary

One kind of function needs a word of its own: a rule made of several rules, each used on a different stretch of the domain. The course calls these case-defined, and anything with a threshold is one. A bulk discount, a tax band, free shipping above a certain order size, a commission rate that steps up after target.

Here is XY Coffee Co’s wholesale price per kilo of roasted beans.

p(q) = 24  if 0 ≤ q < 50
p(q) = 21  if 50 ≤ q < 200
p(q) = 18  if q ≥ 200
How to evaluate a case-defined function
  1. Read the conditions, not the formulas. Find the one line whose condition your input satisfies.
  2. Use that line only. You may cover the others with your hand.
  3. Watch the signs at the joins. ≤ and < decide which line owns a boundary value, and it belongs to one line only.
What does a customer pay for 50 kilos, and for 49?
  1. q = 50: check 0 ≤ 50 < 50
    False, because 50 < 50 is not true. The first line does not own 50.
  2. q = 50: check 50 ≤ 50 < 200
    True, because 50 ≤ 50 is true. The second line owns the boundary, so p(50) = 21.
  3. total for 50 kilos = 50 × 21 = 1 050 CHF
    Price per kilo times number of kilos.
  4. total for 49 kilos = 49 × 24 = 1 176 CHF
    Here 49 falls in the first line, so the price is still 24.
  5. 50 kilos cost 126 CHF less than 49 kilos
    Ordering more costs less. That is what a threshold discount does, and it is exactly the kind of thing a case-defined function is built to reveal.
The boundary is where the marks are

Consider G(x) = x − 1 for x ≥ 3, and G(x) = 3 − x2 for x < 3. Then G(3) = 3 − 1 = 2, because x ≥ 3 includes 3. It is not 3 − 9 = −6, and it is not both. If it were both, G would assign two outputs to one input and would not be a function. The inequality signs stop that happening, so read them first.

Where marks are lost in this topic
  • Reading f(x) as a product. It is application, not multiplication. f(2 + 3) is f(5).
  • Losing a bracket on a negative input. (−2)2 = 4 while −22 = −4.
  • Dropping the middle term. (a + 1)2 is a2 + 2a + 1, never a2 + 1.
  • Substituting into only one hole. If the variable appears three times, the input goes into all three.
  • Choosing the wrong branch. On a case-defined function, check the condition before you touch the formula.
  • Saying “exactly one” in a definition question. This course says at most one, and the wording is examined.
What to remember
  • A function assigns at most one output to each input. Two outputs for one input is the only thing forbidden.
  • The domain is the set of inputs that get an output. The range is the set of outputs actually produced.
  • f(x) is the output of the rule f at the input x. It is not f multiplied by x.
  • Words, table, graph, formula. Be able to move in every direction between them.
  • To evaluate anything, write the rule with empty brackets first, then fill every bracket.
  • Evaluating at x + h is ordinary substitution followed by expansion. Week 4 depends on it.
  • No vertical line may cut the graph more than once. Missing the graph entirely is allowed.
  • On a case-defined function, pick the branch from the conditions, then compute.

Part II  ·  Lesson 2 of 6

Domain and range

Finding a domain is a search for what is forbidden, not for what is allowed. It is four checks, done in order, and then one more question that only a business person thinks to ask.

Before this lesson you need
  • What a function is, and that an input may legitimately have no output
  • How to set a denominator to zero and solve, from equations with the unknown in a denominator
  • How to factor a quadratic, from quadratic equations
  • Interval notation and how to solve a simple inequality, from inequalities and absolute value
In this lesson you will learn
  • What the domain and the range actually are
  • The four things that can go wrong, and why there is no fifth
  • How to handle two conditions on one function without losing either
  • How to write a domain three ways, in words, as a set and as intervals
  • How to read a range off a graph or off the shape of a simple function
  • The business restriction that sits on top of the algebraic one
  • The single most common error in this topic, and how to make it impossible
The same topic on Khan Academy
  • Algebra 1, unit 8: Functions
  • Precalculus, unit 4: Rational functions

Free, no account needed to watch. Their exercises need one.

The day the calculator refuses

Jane asks you for XY Coffee Co’s average cost per ton. That is total cost shared over the tons produced, so A(q) = C(q)q. You build it in the spreadsheet, drag the formula down, and the first row comes back as an error.

The first row is q = 0. Sharing 500 francs of fixed cost over zero tons is not a hard calculation, it is a meaningless one. There is no such thing as the average cost per ton on a day you roast nothing.

The spreadsheet has told you something true about the model, in an unhelpful voice. The polite version is: 0 is not in the domain of A. Knowing that before you build the model is worth more than discovering it afterwards, and an exam will ask you for it directly.

What the domain and the range are

Definition

For a function f, the domain is the set of inputs x for which f(x) is defined. The range is the set of values that f(x) actually takes as x runs over the whole domain.

A useful picture: the domain is the shadow the graph casts on the horizontal axis, and the range is the shadow it casts on the vertical axis.

Domain

Every input the rule answers for. Found by ruling out what is forbidden, and then by asking what the business forbids on top of that.

Range

Every output the rule produces. Found from the shape of the function, or read off the vertical shadow of its graph.

Why we hunt for what is forbidden

You could try to find a domain by listing the inputs that work. That list is usually infinite, so you would never finish. The forbidden list is almost always finite, or at worst one inequality long.

That asymmetry is the whole method. Assume everything is allowed. Then go looking for the small number of places where the expression breaks, and remove those. What is left is the domain.

And the number of ways an expression can break at this level of the course is four. Not four that we happen to have listed, four in total. Learn them as a checklist and run the checklist every time.

Method: four things can go wrong, and only four

Scan the expression once for each of these, in this order.

  1. Division by zero. Set every denominator equal to zero and solve. Those values are excluded.
  2. An even root of a negative. Whatever sits under a square root must be ≥ 0.
  3. A logarithm of zero or a negative. Whatever sits inside a log or ln must be > 0.
  4. A root underneath a fraction bar. If a square root sits in a denominator, what is inside it must be strictly greater than zero, because the root now has to be non-zero as well as real. In 1q + 3 the condition is q > −3, not q ≥ −3.
If none of the four appears

A polynomial has no denominator, no root and no logarithm. So the domain of any polynomial, such as f(x) = 3x2 − 7x + 1, is all of ℝ. You should be able to say that in one second and move on to the part of the question that carries marks.

One thing wrong at a time

Start with the cases where the checklist fires once. The pattern is always the same: write down the condition, solve it, and state what is left.

Domain of f(x) = xx − 2
  1. a denominator is present, no roots, no logarithms
    Run the checklist. Only rule 1 fires, so there is exactly one condition to impose.
  2. x − 2 = 0 → x = 2
    Find where the denominator vanishes. That value, and only that value, is forbidden.
  3. domain = ℝ\{2}
    Every real number except 2. Note that the numerator is irrelevant here: a zero on top is allowed and gives an output of zero.
Domain of f(x) = xx2 − x − 2
  1. x2 − x − 2 = 0
    Same rule, but the denominator is now a quadratic, so it may vanish at more than one place.
  2. (x − 2)(x + 1) = 0
    Factor: two numbers with product −2 and sum −1, which are −2 and 1.
  3. x = 2 or x = −1
    A product is zero when one of its factors is zero, so each bracket gives a forbidden value.
  4. domain = ℝ\{2, −1}
    A quadratic denominator can exclude two values. A cubic one can exclude three.
Domain of g(x) = x − 4
  1. the root demands x − 4 ≥ 0
    Rule 2 fires. There is no denominator, so the inequality is not strict.
  2. x ≥ 4
    Add 4 to both sides. An inequality behaves like an equation here, because nothing was multiplied by a negative.
  3. domain = [4 ; +∞[
    The square bracket at 4 includes it, because 0 = 0 exists. The bracket at infinity always faces outwards, since infinity is never reached.
Domain of h(x) = ln(5 − x)
  1. the logarithm demands 5 − x > 0
    Rule 3 fires, and this one is strict: ln 0 does not exist either.
  2. 5 > x
    Add x to both sides. Doing it this way avoids multiplying by −1 and having to flip the sign.
  3. domain = ]−∞ ; 5[
    Everything below 5. If you had written x > 5 you reversed the inequality, which is the usual error here.

When two things can go wrong at once

A function can trip more than one rule. When it does, every condition must hold at the same time. The word to hold on to is and, never or: you are intersecting the conditions, not collecting them.

Write each condition on its own line, solve each one separately, and only then put them together. Trying to do both at once is how one of them gets lost.

Domain of f(x) = x + 5x − 2
  1. condition 1: x + 5 ≥ 0
    The root is in the numerator, so it is the ordinary non-strict condition.
  2. x ≥ −5
    Solve the first condition on its own.
  3. condition 2: x − 2 ≠ 0
    The denominator is separate from the root, so this is rule 1 acting independently.
  4. x ≠ 2
    Solve the second condition on its own.
  5. domain = [−5 ; 2[ ∪ ]2 ; +∞[
    Both at once: start at −5 and included, run upwards for ever, and punch out the single point 2. The union sign is joining the two surviving pieces of one interval.
Domain of f(x) = 1x − 7
  1. the root demands x − 7 ≥ 0
    Rule 2 gives the non-strict version first.
  2. the denominator demands x − 7 ≠ 0
    Rule 1 applies to the root itself, because the root is what sits under the fraction bar.
  3. so x − 7 > 0
    The two conditions collapse into one strict inequality. This is rule 4, and now you can see where it comes from rather than memorising it.
  4. domain = ]7 ; +∞[
    Strictly greater than 7. Compare with x − 7 on its own, whose domain was [7 ; +∞[. Moving the root into a denominator cost you the endpoint.
Domain of f(x) = ln(x − 1)x − 4
  1. condition 1: x − 1 > 0 → x > 1
    Rule 3, strict as always for a logarithm.
  2. condition 2: x − 4 ≠ 0 → x ≠ 4
    Rule 1, from the denominator.
  3. x > 1 and x ≠ 4
    Both must hold. Note that 4 is inside the region x > 1, so the second condition genuinely removes something.
  4. domain = ]1 ; 4[ ∪ ]4 ; +∞[
    Had the excluded value been x = 0 instead, it would already have been outside x > 1 and the second condition would have changed nothing. Always check whether the hole is inside the region.

Three ways to write the same domain

Lecturers move between three notations without announcing it, and an exam may ask for a particular one. They say the same thing. You should be able to translate in both directions on sight.

One domain, three notations
In wordsAs a setAs intervals
every real number except 2ℝ\{2}]−∞ ; 2[ ∪ ]2 ; +∞[
every real number except 2 and −1ℝ\{2, −1}]−∞ ; −1[ ∪ ]−1 ; 2[ ∪ ]2 ; +∞[
4 and everything above it{x ∈ ℝ : x ≥ 4}[4 ; +∞[
everything strictly below 5{x ∈ ℝ : x < 5}]−∞ ; 5[
Which bracket, and which way round

A square bracket turned towards the interval includes the endpoint: [4 means 4 is in. A bracket turned away excludes it: ]4 means 4 is out. At +∞ and −∞ the bracket always faces away, because infinity is a direction and not a number you can reach. The set notation with a backslash is quicker when you are removing isolated points; interval notation is quicker when you are keeping a stretch.

What about the range?

The range gets less attention than the domain and is examined less often, but it is half the definition and it answers a question a manager will actually ask: what values can this thing take?

From a graph, read it the way you read the domain, but vertically. Sweep your eye up the vertical axis and mark every height the curve reaches. That set of heights is the range.

Without a graph, use the shape of the function. Three facts get you most of the way.

Ranges you can write down without drawing anything
FunctionWhyRange
f(x) = x2a square is never negative, and every non-negative number is some square[0 ; +∞[
f(x) = x2 + 4the same shape lifted four units up[4 ; +∞[
f(x) = xthe root symbol means the non-negative root only[0 ; +∞[
f(x) = 1xa fraction with 1 on top is never zero, but takes every other valueℝ\{0}
f(x) = |x|a distance is never negative[0 ; +∞[
f(x) = 7the output never changes{7}
Range of f(x) = (x − 3)2 + 5
  1. (x − 3)2 ≥ 0
    A square is never negative, whatever is inside it.
  2. (x − 3)2 = 0 when x = 3
    And the smallest value a square can take is actually reached, at the point where the bracket is zero.
  3. f(3) = 0 + 5 = 5
    So the lowest output is 5, and it is attained rather than approached.
  4. range = [5 ; +∞[
    Everything from 5 upwards. The domain, by contrast, is all of ℝ: this function has nothing forbidden about it.
Domain and range are different questions

It is common to answer one when you were asked for the other. The domain is about what you are allowed to put in. The range is about what comes out. f(x) = (x − 3)2 + 5 has domain ℝ and range [5 ; +∞[. Neither one tells you the other.

The restriction the algebra cannot see

Everything so far was algebra. Now comes the step that an economics course cares about and a pure mathematics course does not: after the algebraic domain, ask what the situation forbids.

Quantities cannot be negative. Factories have a capacity. Prices below zero are not prices. Time, in most models, starts at zero. None of that is visible in the formula, and all of it is examinable.

Weekly demand for beans is q(p) = 400 − 8p kilos at a price of p CHF a kilo
  1. algebraic domain = ℝ
    It is a polynomial. Nothing is forbidden by the checklist.
  2. a price cannot be negative, so p ≥ 0
    The first restriction comes from the meaning of the letter, not from the formula.
  3. demand cannot be negative, so 400 − 8p ≥ 0
    The second comes from the meaning of the output. Nobody sells a negative number of kilos.
  4. 8p ≤ 400 → p ≤ 50
    Solve. Above 50 CHF a kilo the model predicts negative sales, which means the model has stopped describing anything.
  5. domain = [0 ; 50]
    A closed interval, with the algebra contributing nothing and the business contributing everything.
Say what the restriction means

The answer [0 ; 50] is worth more marks with a sentence after it. Something like: at a price of 50 CHF a kilo demand reaches zero, so 50 is the highest price at which XY Coffee Co sells anything at all. A domain in a business question is a fact about the business, and an examiner is checking that you noticed.

The average cost function from the start of the lesson works the same way. Algebraically A(q) = C(q)q needs q ≠ 0. In the business, q cannot be negative and the factory stops at 100 tons. Put the two together and the domain is ]0 ; 100]: open at zero because the algebra forbids it, closed at 100 because the factory can in fact run flat out.

The most common domain error in the course

Simplifying before finding the domain. In x2 − 4x − 2 the fraction reduces to x + 2, which looks defined everywhere. It is not. The original expression is undefined at x = 2, and the domain is ℝ\{2}.

The reason is that cancelling the factor (x − 2) is only legal when that factor is non-zero, so the cancellation itself assumed x ≠ 2. Simplifying quietly changed the function. Take the domain from the expression you were given, never from the one you produced.

Where marks are lost in this topic
  • Simplifying first. The tidy expression has a larger domain than the one you were asked about.
  • Finding one condition and stopping. Run the whole checklist every time, even when the first hit looks decisive.
  • Using ≥ where > was needed. A root in a denominator makes the condition strict. So does every logarithm.
  • Flipping an inequality. 5 − x > 0 gives x < 5, not x > 5.
  • Writing or instead of and. Two conditions on one function must both hold.
  • Stopping at the algebra. In a business question, ask what the context forbids as well.
  • Answering the range when the domain was asked for. Read the question twice.
What to remember
  • The domain is what you may put in. The range is what comes out. They are different questions.
  • Four things can go wrong: zero denominator, even root of a negative, logarithm of a non-positive, root in a denominator.
  • A root in a denominator makes the condition strict, because the root must be non-zero as well as real.
  • Two conditions on one function are joined by and. Solve each separately, then intersect.
  • ℝ\{2} and ]−∞ ; 2[ ∪ ]2 ; +∞[ are the same set. Write both fluently.
  • Always take the domain from the original expression, never from the simplified one.
  • Then ask what the business forbids on top of that, and say what your answer means.

Part II  ·  Lesson 3 of 6

The function library

Nine families. Recognising which one you are looking at tells you its shape, its domain, its likely business meaning and which tool to reach for, before you have computed anything.

Before this lesson you need
  • What a function is, and how to evaluate one
  • How to find a domain, since each family has its own hazards
  • How to factor and solve a quadratic
  • What a slope is, from the plane and straight lines
In this lesson you will learn
  • Why naming the family first makes every later question easier
  • The nine families, each with its form, its shape and the business quantity it models
  • How to tell a power function from an exponential one, which is the classic confusion
  • How to read a parabola: which way it opens, where its vertex sits and where its axis of symmetry is
  • How to find a revenue-maximising price with the vertex formula, two lessons before calculus does it
  • Why the x-intercepts of a parabola sit symmetrically about the vertex, and how to use that
  • Case-defined functions as a family in their own right
The same topic on Khan Academy
  • Algebra 1, unit 8: Functions
  • Algebra 1, unit 10: Absolute value and piecewise functions
  • Algebra 2, unit 5: Polynomial graphs

Free, no account needed to watch. Their exercises need one.

Four formulas in one email

Jane forwards you a message from the finance team with four formulas in it and one line of text: “can you sanity-check these before Thursday?” There is no explanation of what any of them does.

For the retail bagging line, in CHF a week for q kilos bagged: h(q) = 4 200, B(q) = 500 + 12q and A(q) = 500q + 12. And for the shop, R(p) = 400p − 8p2.

You do not need to compute anything to say useful things about all four. h never changes, so it is a fixed cost. B rises at a constant rate, so it is a fixed cost plus a variable one. A has a denominator, so something is forbidden, and what is forbidden is bagging nothing. R opens downwards, so it has a peak, and a peak in a revenue formula is a price worth knowing.

All four of those statements came from recognising a family. That is what this lesson is for.

Name the family

Look at the form. Where is the variable, and what is being done to it?

Read off the shape

Line, curve, peak, trough, V, cliff. You now know what the graph looks like.

Read off the hazards

Denominators and roots come with the family. So does the likely domain.

Then compute

And you now know whether the answer you get is plausible.

The families

Seven of these are introduced in week 1. Exponentials and logarithms get sections of their own, here and here, but they belong on this list and you should be able to name them on sight from today.

The function library
FamilyFormShapeWhat it models at XY Coffee Co
Constanth(x) = cA horizontal line.Rent, insurance, the roasting licence. Anything unchanged by volume. h(10) = h(−213) = c.
Linearf(x) = ax + bA straight line with slope a.Cost with a fixed part b and a variable part a per unit. The workhorse of week 2.
Powerf(x) = xmA curve through the origin, bending up if m > 1 and down if m < 1.Economies of scale when m < 1: doubling output costs less than twice as much.
Parabolicf(x) = ax2 + bx + cA parabola: one peak or one trough, never both.Revenue when the price you charge changes how much you sell. The family the exam loves.
Polynomialanxn + … + a1x + a0Up to n − 1 turning points.Flexible cost curves. The degree n is the highest power present.
Rationala polynomial over a polynomialBreaks at the excluded values, with asymptotes.Average cost, and demand curves such as 5 000 000p + 1.
Absolute valuef(x) = |x|A V, with a sharp corner at the bottom.Distance from a target. Deviation from forecast, counting a shortfall and an overshoot as equally bad.
Exponentialf(x) = axFlat then suddenly steep, and never touching the axis.Compound interest, subscriber growth, anything that grows by a fixed percentage each period.
Logarithmicf(x) = ln xSteep then flattening, undefined at zero and below.How long something takes to reach a target. The inverse question to the exponential one.

Power or exponential? The one everybody gets wrong

x2 and 2x are built from the same two symbols and behave in completely different ways. Confusing them is the single most common family error in week 1, so here is the test.

Where is the variable?

In a power function the variable is in the base and the constant is in the exponent: f(x) = xmIn an exponential function the constant is in the base and the variable is in the exponent:f(x) = axPoint at the variable and ask whether it is upstairs or downstairs. That is the entire test.

The difference is not cosmetic. Here are the two functions side by side at whole-number inputs.

x2 against 2x
xx22xWhich is bigger
1122x
244equal
398x2
41616equal
525322x
101001 0242x

The power function is ahead for a short stretch and then loses, permanently and by a growing margin. By x = 10 the exponential is already more than ten times larger, and the gap widens every step. That is what people mean when they say exponential growth beats polynomial growth eventually. The word eventually is doing work: between 2 and 4 it is the other way round.

A power function in the business

Roasting cost with economies of scale, K(b) = 200b0.8 CHF for b batches. One batch costs 200, two batches cost 348.22 rather than 400, four cost 606.29 rather than 800. The exponent below 1 is exactly what “it gets cheaper per unit as you scale” looks like in algebra.

An exponential function in the business

App subscribers growing 6 per cent a month, S(t) = S0 × 1.06t. The growth is in the exponent because each month multiplies what came before. It takes about 11.9 months to double, whatever the starting number is.

Two traps hiding in the same place

x2 is a power function; 2x is exponential. And f(x) = x½ is the same thing as x, still a power function, because the variable is still in the base. A fractional exponent does not make something exponential. Only a variable exponent does.

Reading a parabola properly

The parabolic family deserves more than a row in a table, because week 2 asks you to sketch one and week 8 asks you to optimise one, and because revenue in this course is almost always a parabola.

For f(x) = ax2 + bx + c, three numbers tell you everything about the picture.

Everything you need about a parabola

The sign of a decides the shape. a > 0 gives a U, a trough with a minimum. a < 0 gives an upside-down U, a peak with a maximum.

The turning point is the vertex, and it sits atx = −b2aSubstitute that value back into f to get the height of the vertex. The vertical line through the vertex is the axis of symmetry, and the curve is a mirror image on either side of it.

Mind the signs in the vertex formula

The formula is −b2a with b and a taken with their own signs. For f(x) = 400m − 10m2, read carefully: a = −10 and b = 400, not a = 10. Write the two coefficients down as a separate line before you use them, signs included. Half the errors on this formula are sign errors made before any arithmetic started.

Where does revenue peak? R(m) = 400m − 10m2, m staff on the roasting line
  1. a = −10, b = 400
    Read the coefficients with their signs. The squared term carries the a, wherever it is written.
  2. a < 0
    So the parabola opens downwards. The vertex is a peak, which is what you want it to be for a revenue question.
  3. m = −4002 × (−10) = −400−20
    The vertex formula, with the bracket keeping the minus sign safe.
  4. m = 20 staff
    The staffing level that maximises revenue. Past 20 the line is crowded and each extra person adds less than the one before.
  5. R(20) = 400(20) − 10(400) = 8 000 − 4 000 = 4 000
    The peak revenue itself. Week 8 recovers the same point with a derivative, and it will agree.

Now the version that appears on every paper: you are given demand, not revenue, and you have to build the parabola yourself before you can find its peak.

Which price maximises weekly revenue? Demand is q(p) = 400 − 8p kilos at p CHF a kilo
  1. R(p) = p × q(p)
    Revenue is price times quantity sold. This line is worth a mark on its own and is often missing.
  2. R(p) = p(400 − 8p) = 400p − 8p2
    Expand. Only now is it visible that revenue is a parabola, which is why you expand before you look for a vertex.
  3. a = −8, b = 400, and a < 0
    Coefficients with signs. Opening downwards, so the vertex is the maximum we want.
  4. p = −4002 × (−8) = 25
    The vertex formula gives the revenue-maximising price directly.
  5. q(25) = 400 − 200 = 200 kg, R(25) = 25 × 200 = 5 000 CHF
    At 25 CHF a kilo XY Coffee Co sells 200 kilos for 5 000 CHF a week. Charge more and the lost volume outweighs the higher price; charge less and the extra volume does not pay for the discount.
A minimum, for contrast. Weekly delivery cost is D(n) = 2n2 − 48n + 700 for n delivery runs
  1. a = 2, b = −48
    Coefficients with signs again. This time a is positive.
  2. a > 0
    So the parabola opens upwards and the vertex is a trough. A cost question wants a minimum, so this is the right shape.
  3. n = −−482 × 2 = 484 = 12
    Two minus signs cancel. This is where writing b = −48 on its own line earns its keep.
  4. D(12) = 2(144) − 48(12) + 700 = 288 − 576 + 700 = 412
    Twelve runs a week, costing 412 CHF. Fewer runs means bigger, slower loads; more runs means paying for half-empty vans.

The axis of symmetry, and the free information in it

The parabola is a mirror image about the vertical line through its vertex. That single fact hands you answers you would otherwise have to compute.

If the curve crosses the horizontal axis twice, the two crossings are the same distance from the axis of symmetry, one on each side. So the vertex sits exactly halfway between them, and you can find it by averaging the two intercepts without touching the quadratic formula.

The vertex from the two x-intercepts

If a parabola crosses the horizontal axis at x1 and x2, its axis of symmetry isx = x1 + x22and the vertex sits on that line. This agrees with −b2a, because the two roots add up to −ba, and halving that gives the same answer.

Profit is zero at 400 kilos and again at 900 kilos. Where is profit largest?
  1. P(q) = aq2 + bq + c with roots 400 and 900
    Profit is revenue minus cost, and with a parabolic revenue and a linear cost it is itself a parabola.
  2. the two roots are the break-even points
    Below 400 kilos you do not cover the fixed cost. Above 900 the rising marginal cost has eaten the margin.
  3. axis of symmetry: q = 400 + 9002
    Average the two roots. Nothing else about the parabola is needed.
  4. q = 650 kilos
    The output that maximises profit sits exactly halfway between the two break-even points, which is a fact worth carrying into an exam.
The vertex is not always inside your domain

The formula −b2a answers a question about a curve, not about a business. If the vertex of a revenue parabola lands at a price of −3 CHF, or at 4 000 kilos in a factory that makes 1 000, the maximum on the domain you are allowed is at the nearest endpoint instead. Compute the vertex, then check that it is somewhere you are permitted to be.

The families with something forbidden in them

Three families come with domain trouble attached, and recognising the family is how you remember to look for it.

Rational

A polynomial over a polynomial. Average cost is the standard example: the bagging line costs B(q) = 500 + 12q CHF a week, so the average cost per kilo is A(q) = 500q + 12. At 50 kilos that is 22 CHF, at 100 kilos 17 CHF, at 1 000 kilos 12.50 CHF. It falls towards 12 and never reaches it, because the fixed 500 is being spread thinner and thinner. That floor at 12 is an asymptote, and it is the variable cost per kilo.

Absolute value

|x| strips the sign and leaves the size. It draws a V with a corner at the bottom. Forecast error is the business case: a forecast of 500 kilos against actual sales of 470 gives an error of |470 − 500| = 30, and actual sales of 530 give the same 30. You use it whenever missing high and missing low are equally bad.

Polynomial

The general case, and the family that contains constant, linear and parabolic as its first three members. A polynomial of degree n has at most n − 1 turning points, so a cubic can bend twice. Polynomials never have a forbidden input, which is what makes them comfortable to work with.

Case-defined functions, a family in their own right

The last family is not defined by a shape but by a construction: several rules, each used on its own stretch of the domain. The course calls these case-defined, and once you start looking you find them everywhere in commerce, because every threshold in a contract is one.

Bulk discounts. Tax bands. Shipping that becomes free above an order size. A commission rate that steps up after target. Overtime pay. A mobile tariff with an included allowance.

f(x) = x      if 0 ≤ x < 3
f(x) = x − 1  if 3 ≤ x < 5
f(x) = 4      if 5 ≤ x < 7
What makes them their own family

A case-defined function is not one shape, it is several stuck together. The one above is linear, then linear again but shifted down, then constant. Its graph has a jump at x = 3, where the value falls from nearly 3 to 2, and another at x = 5.

That is the point. The whole reason a business uses a case-defined function is to describe a rule that changes at a threshold, and the jump or the kink at the threshold is the thing being modelled, not an accident. To evaluate one, find the line whose condition your input satisfies, then use only that line. Read the inequality signs, because ≤ and < decide which line owns a boundary value.

Where marks are lost in this topic
  • Calling 2x a power function. The variable is upstairs, so it is exponential.
  • Calling x exponential. It is x½, a power function. A fractional exponent is still a constant exponent.
  • Reading a without its sign. In 400m − 10m2, a = −10. Write the coefficients on their own line.
  • Dropping the minus in −b2a. When b is already negative, the two signs cancel and the answer is positive.
  • Giving the vertex height when the question asked for its position, or the reverse. Read which one is wanted.
  • Forgetting to build the revenue parabola. A demand function is not a revenue function. Multiply by the price first.
  • Reporting a vertex that lies outside the domain as though it were the answer.
What to remember
  • Name the family before you compute. It gives you the shape, the hazards and a way to check your answer.
  • Power has the variable in the base, xm. Exponential has it in the exponent, ax.
  • For ax2 + bx + c: a > 0 is a U with a minimum, a < 0 is a peak with a maximum.
  • The vertex is at x = −b2a, with the signs of a and b as written.
  • Revenue is price times quantity. Build the parabola before looking for its peak.
  • The two x-intercepts are symmetric about the vertex, so their average gives the axis of symmetry free.
  • Rational functions are the ones with excluded values. Polynomials never have any.
  • A case-defined function models a threshold. Pick the branch from the conditions, then compute.

Part II  ·  Lesson 4 of 6

Graphs

A graph is a claim about a relationship, drawn so that a reader can check it. This lesson teaches you to build one from a formula, to read one back, and to spot the axis trick that makes a small change look large.

Before this lesson you need
  • What a function is, and how to evaluate one at a number
  • How to read a domain, and what an excluded value is
  • The seven families in the function library, and the shape each one has
  • How to find intercepts by setting one variable to zero
In this lesson you will learn
  • What a graph is actually claiming, point by point
  • A four step method for sketching any function by hand
  • Three complete sketches: a parabola, a straight line from two data points, and a rational function that breaks
  • How to read intercepts, sign, direction and the extreme value straight off a curve
  • The presentation standard this course sets, and why it exists
  • How a truncated vertical axis exaggerates, with the numbers to prove it
The same topic on Khan Academy
  • Algebra 1, unit 4: Linear equations and graphs
  • Algebra 2, unit 9: Transformations of functions

Free, no account needed to watch. Their exercises need one.

Two pictures of the same month

Jane drops two charts on your desk. Both show XY Coffee Co’s subscription revenue for the first two quarters. Both are built from the same two numbers. One says the business is steady. The other says it has taken off.

Neither chart is lying about the data. They differ in one setting, and by the end of this lesson you will be able to name it, measure the distortion it creates, and choose on purpose which picture your reader sees.

What a graph is claiming

A function pairs each input with exactly one output. A graph is that pairing made visible: for every legal input x, you mark the single point (x, f(x)). The curve is the collection of all those marks and nothing else.

That gives you a test you can apply to any point, without drawing anything.

A point is on the curve

exactly when its coordinates satisfy the equation. (3 ; 5) lies on y = 2x − 1 because 2(3) − 1 = 5.

A point is off the curve

as soon as they do not. (3 ; 6) is not on that line, because 2(3) − 1 is 5 and not 6.

The curve makes a promise

that the pairing continues between the points you marked. The function family is what justifies that promise.

Definition

The graph of a function f is the set of points{ (x, f(x)) : x in the domain of f }drawn in the plane, with the input on the horizontal axis and the output on the vertical axis. Because a function gives one output per input, no vertical line can ever cross the graph twice. That is the vertical line test.

Joining the dots is a claim, not a decoration

Joining plotted points with a smooth curve asserts that the function behaves smoothly between them. You are entitled to that when you know the family the function belongs to, and not entitled to it when the points are raw measurements with nothing known in between. That is why a scatter of unconnected markers is sometimes the honest chart.

How do we sketch one by hand?

A sketch is not a plot. You are not trying to get every point right. You are getting the shape right, and a small number of exact points right, so that the shape is anchored to the page.

Four steps, in this order. The order matters, because each step narrows the work of the next one.

Method: sketching a function in four steps
  1. Find the domain. It tells you how far the curve may go, and warns you of any value where it must break.
  2. Find the intercepts. Set x = 0 for the vertical one. Set y = 0 and solve for the horizontal ones. These are the cheapest exact points you will get.
  3. Build a small table of values, five or six points chosen on purpose: one on each side of every intercept, and one on each side of every excluded value.
  4. Identify the family from the function library: line, parabola, cubic, root, exponential or rational. It tells you what curve may join your points.
Why the table is chosen and not random

A point on each side of an intercept shows the curve crossing rather than touching. A point on each side of an excluded value shows what happens as the curve approaches the gap from the left and from the right, which is usually the most interesting thing on the page. Five deliberate points beat twenty random ones.

Worked sketch 1: a parabola

Take y = 4x2 − 16. Work the four steps in order.

Sketch y = 4x2 − 16
  1. domain = ℝ
    It is a polynomial. There is no denominator and no root, so nothing is excluded. The curve is allowed to run the full width of the page.
  2. x = 0 → y = −16
    The vertical intercept. Substituting zero is the fastest exact point available, so take it first.
  3. y = 0 → 4x2 = 16 → x2 = 4 → x = ±2
    The horizontal intercepts. Remember both signs: (−2)2 is also 4, and dropping the negative root is the commonest slip here.
  4. x = −3, −1, 1, 3 → y = 20, −12, −12, 20
    One point on each side of each intercept. The values repeat in pairs, which is the symmetry of a parabola showing up in the arithmetic.
  5. a = 4 > 0
    The family step. The coefficient of x2 is positive, so this is a U, a trough with a minimum.
  6. lowest point (0 ; −16)
    The vertex sits at x = −b2a, and here b = 0, so it is on the vertical axis. Six marks and the curve draws itself.
The deliberate table of values
x4x2 − 16What this point is for
−320left of the intercept at −2
−20intercept
−1−12right of it, so we see the curve has crossed
0−16vertical intercept, and here also the minimum
1−12left of the intercept at 2
20intercept
320right of it

Worked sketch 2: a straight line from two data points

This one starts from the business rather than from a formula, which is how it usually arrives in practice. XY Coffee Co roasted 100 kg in a quiet week and the roastery cost 2 050 CHF to run. In a busy week it roasted 300 kg and cost 3 750 CHF. Jane believes cost is linear in volume. Two points are enough to draw the line.

Find and sketch the weekly cost line through (100 ; 2050) and (300 ; 3750)
  1. slope = 3750 − 2050300 − 100 = 1700200 = 8.5
    Change in cost divided by change in volume. The units come with it: 8.50 CHF of extra cost per extra kilogram.
  2. 2050 = 8.5(100) + b → b = 1200
    Put one known point back into y = ax + b. The 1 200 CHF is the fixed weekly cost, incurred before a single bean is roasted.
  3. C(q) = 8.5q + 1200
    Check with the second point: 8.5(300) + 1200 = 3750. It agrees, so no arithmetic slipped.
  4. intercepts: (0 ; 1200), and C(q) = 0 at q = −141.2
    The horizontal intercept is negative, so it lies outside any sensible domain. Cost is never zero here. Say so rather than plotting a point no one can use.
  5. plot (0 ; 1200) and (300 ; 3750), join with a ruler
    Two points fix a line, so the family step is free. Draw the domain the roastery can reach, about 0 ≤ q ≤ 400.
Say what the picture means

The line rises 8.50 CHF per extra kilogram and starts at 1 200 CHF. The only lever on this chart is volume, because the fixed 1 200 CHF is then spread thinner: at 100 kg the cost per kilogram is 20.50 CHF, at 300 kg it is 12.50 CHF. That falling average is a rational function, which is the next sketch.

Worked sketch 3: a rational function, where the curve breaks

Rational functions are the ones with an excluded value, and the excluded value is where the drawing gets interesting. Take f(x) = 2x − 6x − 1.

Follow the same four steps. The only difference is that step one now produces a warning instead of a reassurance.

Sketch f(x) = 2x − 6x − 1
  1. x − 1 ≠ 0 → x ≠ 1
    Domain: ]−∞ ; 1[ ∪ ]1 ; +∞[. The curve comes in two separate pieces. Draw a dashed vertical line at 1 before anything else.
  2. x = 0 → f(0) = −6−1 = 6
    The vertical intercept. Two negatives make a positive, so this point is above the axis even though both parts look negative.
  3. f(x) = 0 → 2x − 6 = 0 → x = 3
    A fraction is zero when its top is zero, and only then. A zero on the bottom does the opposite: it forbids the point entirely.
  4. left of the gap: f(−1) = 4, f(0) = 6, f(0.5) = 10
    Approaching 1 from below, the values climb away. The top stays near −4 and the bottom is a small negative number, so the quotient is large and positive.
  5. right of the gap: f(1.5) = −6, f(2) = −2, f(3) = 0
    From above, the curve dives the other way and then climbs back through the intercept at 3. The two sides of an excluded value usually go in opposite directions.
  6. far out: f(11) = 1.6, f(101) ≈ 1.96
    For very large x the top is close to twice the bottom, so the value settles towards 2. Draw a second dashed line at y = 2.
  7. two branches, dashed lines at x = 1 and y = 2
    On the far left the curve sits a little above y = 2, passes through (0 ; 6) and rises without limit as x nears 1. The right branch rises from far below, crosses at (3 ; 0) and flattens towards y = 2 from underneath.
The gap is a gap, not a steep bit

The commonest error in sketching a rational function is joining the two branches through the excluded value, so the curve appears to shoot up and come back down. There is no curve at x = 1 at all. Lift the pencil. If the branches touch, the drawing fails the vertical line test and is not a function.

Reading information back off a graph

Everything so far went from formula to picture. The exam also goes the other way, and so does every meeting you will sit in: a curve is put in front of you and you are asked what it says.

Work with XY Coffee Co’s monthly profit model P(q) = −0.5q2 + 30q − 250, where q is thousands of kilograms roasted and P is profit in thousands of CHF.

Five readings from one curve
The questionWhere to lookThe answer for P(q)
Where does it cut the vertical axis?the height at q = 0−250. With nothing roasted the fixed costs still run.
Where does it cut the horizontal axis?the points at height zeroq = 10 and q = 50, the two break-even volumes.
Where is it positive or negative?above or below the horizontal axispositive on ]10 ; 50[, negative outside it. Profit exists only between the break-even points.
Where is it increasing or decreasing?where the curve rises or falls, read left to rightincreasing on ]0 ; 30[, decreasing on ]30 ; +∞[. Volume stops helping after 30.
Where is the maximum or minimum?the turning pointa maximum of 200 at q = 30. That is the plan Jane should sign.
Confirm the readings of P(q) = −0.5q2 + 30q − 250
  1. P(0) = −250
    The vertical intercept. In business terms, the loss the month makes if the roastery stands still.
  2. −0.5q2 + 30q − 250 = 0 → q2 − 60q + 500 = 0
    Set the height to zero for the break-even points. Multiplying through by −2 clears the fraction and the leading minus at once.
  3. q = 60 ± 3600 − 20002 = 60 ± 402 = 10 and 50
    The quadratic formula, with 1600 = 40. Between the two roots a downward parabola is above the axis, so profit is positive there.
  4. vertex at q = −302(−0.5) = 30
    The turning point sits exactly halfway between 10 and 50, which is a free check on the roots.
  5. P(30) = −450 + 900 − 250 = 200
    Maximum profit of 200 thousand CHF at 30 thousand kilograms. Increasing to the left of it, decreasing to the right.
Increasing and decreasing are about direction, not sign

A function can be negative and increasing at the same time. Between q = 0 and q = 10 the curve is below the axis, so P is negative, and it is climbing, so P is increasing. The losses are shrinking. Read sign from the axis and direction from the slope.

The standard this course sets

A chart must stand alone

A graph has to be understandable without reading the text around it. Assume your reader sees it pasted into a slide with the paragraph left behind. That needs four things: an explicit title, both axes labelled with the quantity and its unit, deliberate minimum and maximum on each axis, and a chart type suited to the data.

Title

It states the claim, not the file name. "Weekly roastery cost against volume, 2025" tells the reader what they are seeing. "Chart 3" does not.

Axis labels with units

CHF, kilograms, months, percent. A number without a unit is not data. This is the item most often missing and the cheapest to add.

Deliberate limits

You should be able to say why each axis starts and ends where it does. If you cannot, you have accepted a default, and defaults mislead.

A suitable chart type

A smooth curve for a function known to be smooth. Straight segments for a series measured at intervals. Markers alone for observations with nothing known in between.

In a spreadsheet the two acceptable choices for drawing a function are a scatter of points joined by a smoothed curve, or a scatter joined by straight segments. A plain line chart is not the same thing: it spaces the inputs evenly whatever their real values are, which silently distorts the horizontal axis.

How a truncated vertical axis exaggerates

Back to Jane’s two charts. Subscription revenue was 96 000 CHF in the first quarter and 98 400 CHF in the second. The rise is 2 400 CHF, which is 2.5% of 96 000. Here is what the two charts do with it.

The same two numbers, two vertical axes
  1. rise = 98 400 − 96 000 = 2 400
    The real change, in CHF. As a percentage: 240096 000 = 0.025, so 2.5%.
  2. axis from 0 to 100 000: bars of height 96 000 and 98 400
    The second bar is 98 40096 000 = 1.025 times the first. It looks 2.5 per cent taller, which is what it is.
  3. axis from 95 000 to 99 000: visible heights 1 000 and 3 400
    Each bar is now measured from 95 000: 96 000 − 95 000 = 1 000 and 98 400 − 95 000 = 3 400.
  4. 34001000 = 3.4
    On the truncated axis the second bar is 3.4 times the height of the first. The reader sees a business that has more than tripled.
  5. exaggeration factor = 3.41.025 ≈ 3.32
    A 2.5% rise made to look about 3.3 times larger than it is, with no false number anywhere. Only the axis changed.
Truncation is not always dishonest, but it is always a decision

If every value sits between 96 and 99, a zero based axis wastes the chart and hides a change that genuinely matters, such as a service level or a margin. So the rule is not "never truncate". It is: truncate on purpose, say so in the axis label, and never truncate a bar chart, because the length of a bar is the quantity.

Where marks are lost in this topic
  • Only one root. Solving x2 = 4 and writing x = 2. There are two intercepts and the sketch needs both.
  • Joining across an excluded value. The curve has a gap there. Lift the pencil.
  • A random table of values. Points chosen without a reason miss the behaviour that matters, near an intercept or a gap.
  • No units on the axes. This costs marks here and credibility everywhere else.
  • Confusing negative with decreasing. A curve below the axis that is climbing is negative and increasing at once.
  • An accidental axis. Accepting whatever limits the software chose, and being unable to say why.
What to remember
  • The graph is the set of points (x, f(x)). A point is on it exactly when its coordinates satisfy the equation.
  • Domain, then intercepts, then a deliberate table, then the family. That order, every time.
  • One point on each side of every intercept and of every excluded value.
  • From a curve you can read: intercepts, where it is positive or negative, where it is increasing or decreasing, and the maximum or minimum.
  • Title, both axes labelled with units, deliberate limits, suitable chart type. The chart must stand alone.
  • A truncated axis turned a 2.5% rise into a bar 3.4 times as tall. Decide your limits on purpose.

Part II  ·  Lesson 5 of 6

Exponential functions and the number e

The model of anything that grows or shrinks by a percentage of itself. Compound interest, subscriber numbers, depreciation and half of the spring financial block all live here, and so does the constant e.

Before this lesson you need
  • How powers work, including negative and fractional exponents
  • How to turn a percentage into a multiplier
  • What a function is, and how to evaluate one
  • How to read a graph and what an asymptote looks like
In this lesson you will learn
  • What makes a function exponential, and why 2x and x2 are nothing alike
  • The two shapes: growth when the base is above 1, decline when it is between 0 and 1
  • Why an exponential is never zero and never negative, and what that forces on a model
  • How to build the multiplier from a described percentage change, which is the examinable skill
  • Why repeated percentage change is a power and not a multiplication
  • Where e comes from, and why week 5 will call ex the easiest function to differentiate
The same topic on Khan Academy
  • Algebra 1, unit 12: Exponential growth and decay
  • Algebra 2, unit 7: Exponential models

Free, no account needed to watch. Their exercises need one.

The subscriber number that will not behave

XY Coffee Co’s app subscription has 1 200 members and has been adding about 6 per cent a month since spring. Jane asks you two questions on her way past your desk. How many members in a year? And when do we reach 5 000?

Your first instinct is probably to multiply: 6 per cent a month, twelve months, 72 per cent, so about 2 064. That answer is wrong, and it is wrong by a lot. The true figure is 2 415.

The gap between 2 064 and 2 415 is the whole of this lesson. Percentage growth does not add up. It compounds, and compounding is an exponential.

A linear model adds

the same amount each period. Plus 72 members every month, whatever the size of the base.

An exponential model multiplies

by the same factor each period. Times 1.06 every month, so the amount added grows as the base grows.

Which one is right

depends on the business. Rent is linear. Interest, subscribers, infection, depreciation and inflation are exponential.

What makes a function exponential

Definition

For a base b > 0 with b ≠ 1, the exponential function with base b isf(x) = bxIts domain is all of ℝ and its outputs are strictly positive. The variable is in the exponent. That is the whole definition and the whole difference.

Compare it with a power function, where the variable sits in the base and the exponent is a fixed number: f(x) = x2, f(x) = x3. The two look similar written down and behave nothing alike.

x2 against 2x: the variable in the base against the variable in the exponent
xx22xWhich is ahead
112the exponential
244level
398the power
41616level again
52532the exponential, and from here for ever
101001 024the exponential, by a factor of about 10
204001 048 576the exponential, by a factor of about 2 600

The power function wins for a while and then loses permanently. That pattern is worth holding on to, because it is the reason an exponential model and a polynomial model can agree perfectly on your historical data and then diverge catastrophically on your forecast.

The two shapes

There are only two pictures to learn, and which one you get is decided by whether the base is above or below 1.

Base above 1: growth

2x at x = −3, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, 3 gives 0.125, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8. The curve hugs the horizontal axis on the left, passes through (0 ; 1), then rises ever more steeply.

Base between 0 and 1: decline

0.8x at x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 10 gives 1, 0.8, 0.64, 0.512, 0.328, 0.107. The curve falls steeply at first, passes through (0 ; 1), then flattens out towards the axis without ever touching it.

Both pass through the same point

b0 = 1 for every base, so every exponential graph goes through (0 ; 1). That is your free anchor point when sketching one.

Never zero, never negative

bx with b > 0 is strictly positive for every real x. A large negative exponent makes it very small, because b−n = 1bn, but a positive number divided by a positive number stays positive. The horizontal axis is a horizontal asymptote: the curve approaches y = 0 and never reaches it.

What that forces on a model

If you model XY Coffee Co’s cafe equipment value as 18 000 · 0.85t, that model can never reach zero. It says the espresso machine is worth 9 396 CHF after four years, 1 851 CHF after twenty, and something microscopic but positive after a century. A pure exponential decline is therefore the wrong model whenever the quantity genuinely hits zero, such as a stock that runs out. Equally, a pure exponential growth model can never predict a ceiling, so it will always eventually forecast more customers than there are people. Know the shape you have chosen and know where it stops being sensible.

Building the multiplier from a percentage

This is the step that turns a sentence in English into a formula, and it carries more marks than anything else in this topic.

A rise of r as a decimal leaves you with the original plus the rise, so you keep 1 + r of what you had. A fall of r leaves you with 1 − r. That single number is called the multiplier, and once you have it you raise it to the power of the number of periods.

Compound growth and decline

Starting from P, changing by a rate r each period, after n periods the amount isS = P · (1 + r)nwith r positive for growth and negative for decline. Writing a fall of 15 per cent as r = −0.15 gives the multiplier 0.85 automatically, so there is only one formula to remember, not two.

From a sentence to a multiplier
What the sentence saysThe rate rThe multiplierCheck
rises by 2 per cent a year0.021.02100 becomes 102
grows by 6 per cent a month0.061.06100 becomes 106
falls by 15 per cent a year−0.150.85100 becomes 85
drops by 7 per cent each winter−0.070.93100 becomes 93
increases by a half0.51.5100 becomes 150
loses a third of its value−1323 ≈ 0.666799 becomes 66
doubles each period12100 becomes 200
The multiplier is not the percentage

A growth of 6 per cent has multiplier 1.06, not 0.06. Using 0.06 does not grow the quantity, it destroys 94 per cent of it every month. And a fall of 15 per cent has multiplier 0.85, not −0.15, which would flip the sign of the quantity every period. Say the check out loud every time: "100 becomes what?"

10 000 CHF invested at 2 per cent a year, for three years
  1. multiplier = 1 + 0.02 = 1.02
    A rise of 2 per cent, so r = 0.02. Check: 100 becomes 102.
  2. S = 10 000 · (1.02)3
    P = 10 000, n = 3 years. The exponent counts the periods, not the years, and here they are the same thing.
  3. (1.02)3 = 1.061208
    Three multiplications: 1.02 · 1.02 = 1.0404, then · 1.02 again.
  4. S ≈ 10 612.08 CHF
    Simple interest would have given 10 000 + 3(200) = 10 600. The extra 12.08 CHF is interest earned on interest.
The subscriber question: 1 200 members growing 6 per cent a month, for a year
  1. multiplier = 1.06
    A rise of 6 per cent a month. The period is the month, so the exponent will count months.
  2. S = 1 200 · (1.06)12
    Twelve periods, because a year contains twelve months. Matching the period to the rate is where this goes wrong most often.
  3. (1.06)12 ≈ 2.0122
    The membership base has slightly more than doubled in twelve months.
  4. S ≈ 2 415 members
    Not 2 064. The naive answer treated 6 per cent a month as 72 per cent a year, and lost 351 members in the process.
Depreciation: an 18 000 CHF roaster losing 15 per cent of its value a year
  1. multiplier = 1 + (−0.15) = 0.85
    A fall, so r is negative and the multiplier is below 1. Check: 100 becomes 85.
  2. V(t) = 18 000 · (0.85)t
    The same single formula as for growth. Nothing about the method changes.
  3. V(1) = 15 300, V(2) = 13 005, V(3) = 11 054.25
    Notice the yearly loss shrinks: 2 700, then 2 295, then 1 950.75. It is 15 per cent of a smaller number each time.
  4. V(4) = 18 000 · 0.522006 ≈ 9 396.11 CHF
    After four years the roaster is worth a little over half of what it cost. Four falls of 15 per cent remove 47.8 per cent, not 60 per cent.

Why repeated percentage change is a power, not a multiplication

Applying a 6 per cent rise twelve times does not add up to 72 per cent, and it is worth seeing exactly why rather than taking it on trust.

Each month multiplies the base by 1.06. Doing that twelve times in a row means 1.06 · 1.06 · ... · 1.06, twelve factors, which is what (1.06)12 means. Multiplication repeated is a power, in the same way that addition repeated is a multiplication.

Twelve months of 6 per cent growth, month by month
MonthMembersAdded that month
01 200the starting base
11 27272
21 34876
31 42981
61 70296
122 415137

The column on the right is the point. A linear model would add 72 every month for ever. The exponential adds 72 in the first month and 137 in the twelfth, because 6 per cent of a larger base is a larger number. Over the year the total growth is 2.0122 − 1 = 1.0122, so 101.2 per cent, not 72 per cent.
