A number you can sanity check in your head

A 6 per cent monthly rise doubles a quantity in a little under twelve months. A 2 per cent annual rise doubles money in about 35 years. If a result you have computed sits far from a doubling time you recognise, look for a mistyped exponent before you look anywhere else.

Where the number e comes from

Everything above compounds in steps: once a year, once a month. A natural question is what happens if the steps get smaller and more frequent, and it has a clean answer that turns out to matter everywhere.

Put 1 CHF to work for one year at a rate of 100 per cent, and let n be the number of times the interest is added during that year. Each addition is 1n of the rate, applied n times, so you finish with (1 + 1n)n.

(1 + 1n)n as the compounding gets finer
nCompounded(1 + 1n)nWhat 1 CHF becomes
1once a year2.0000002.00 CHF
2every six months2.2500002.25 CHF
4quarterly2.4414062.44 CHF
12monthly2.6130352.61 CHF
52weekly2.6925972.69 CHF
365daily2.7145672.71 CHF
8 760hourly2.7181272.72 CHF
1 000 000almost continuously2.7182802.72 CHF

Read the fourth column downwards. The gain from compounding more often shrinks fast: moving from yearly to monthly is worth 61 centimes, moving from daily to hourly is worth less than a centime. The values are not running away. They are creeping up on a limit.

The definition of e

The sequence (1 + 1n)n increases towards a limit as n grows without bound. That limit is the numbere ≈ 2.718281828459So e is not an arbitrary constant someone chose. It is what 100 per cent growth becomes when it is applied continuously rather than in steps.

The natural exponential function is exp(x) = ex. Because e > 1, it has the growth shape, passes through (0 ; 1), is strictly positive everywhere and has the horizontal axis as an asymptote. Everything you learned about bx applies to it unchanged.

Continuous compounding uses it directly: capital P at a continuous rate r for t years becomes P · ert.

10 000 CHF for three years at 2 per cent: yearly against continuous
  1. yearly: 10 000 · (1.02)3 ≈ 10 612.08
    Interest added once at the end of each of the three years.
  2. continuous: 10 000 · e0.02 × 3
    The exponent is the rate multiplied by the time, so 0.06.
  3. e0.06 ≈ 1.0618365
    One key on the calculator. Note it is a little above 1.023 = 1.061208.
  4. continuous ≈ 10 618.37 CHF
    A difference of 6.29 CHF over three years. Continuous compounding is the ceiling, and on ordinary rates it sits very close to annual compounding.
Why week 5 will call it the easiest function to differentiate

Differentiating a function tells you its rate of change. For ex the answer is ex again: the function is its own rate of change. No other function does this, apart from multiples of it. That is the reason every growth model in the course is written with base e eventually, and the reason week 5 treats it as the one derivative you cannot get wrong.

Where marks are lost in this topic
  • Using the percentage as the multiplier. 0.06 instead of 1.06, or −0.15 instead of 0.85. Ask "100 becomes what?"
  • Adding the percentages. Twelve rises of 6 per cent are not 72 per cent, they are 101.2 per cent.
  • Mismatching the rate and the period. A monthly rate needs an exponent counting months. Mixing them is the error that survives every other check.
  • Confusing x2 with 2x. The variable in the base is a power function; the variable in the exponent is an exponential.
  • Letting an exponential model reach zero. It never does. If your answer says the value hit zero, the model was wrong, not the arithmetic.
  • Rounding the multiplier early. Rounding 1.0612 to 2.01 before multiplying costs francs. Round once, at the end.
What to remember
  • f(x) = bx with b > 0 and b ≠ 1. The variable is the exponent.
  • b > 1 grows, 0 < b < 1 declines, and every exponential passes through (0 ; 1).
  • The output is always strictly positive. y = 0 is a horizontal asymptote, never a value.
  • S = P(1 + r)n, with r negative for a decline. The multiplier is 1 + r, never r.
  • Repeated percentage change is a power, because repeated multiplication is a power.
  • An exponential eventually overtakes any power function, however large the power.
  • e ≈ 2.71828 is the limit of (1 + 1n)n, and it is continuous compounding.
  • exp(x) = ex is its own derivative, which is why week 5 likes it.

Part II  ·  Lesson 6 of 6

Logarithms

The question "what power do I need?", and the only tool that gets a variable out of an exponent. Every "how long until" question in the course is answered here.

Before this lesson you need
  • What an exponential function is, and how a multiplier is built from a percentage
  • How powers work, including negative and fractional exponents
  • How to read a domain and state a restriction
  • What a graph claims, and what an asymptote is
In this lesson you will learn
  • The question a logarithm answers, in one sentence
  • The definition as the exact mirror of an exponential, read in both directions
  • How to evaluate simple logarithms without a calculator
  • What log and ln mean, and which calculator key is which
  • Why the input of a logarithm must be strictly positive
  • How to answer a "how long until" question by taking logarithms of both sides
The same topic on Khan Academy
  • Algebra 2, unit 8: Logarithms

Free, no account needed to watch. Their exercises need one.

The question you could not answer last lesson

XY Coffee Co has 1 200 app subscribers growing 6 per cent a month. Last lesson you answered Jane’s first question: after twelve months there will be about 2 415 members, because 1 200 · 1.0612 ≈ 2 415.

Her second question was "when do we reach 5 000?". Written down it is 1 200 · (1.06)n = 5 000, and now you are stuck. You can divide both sides by 1 200 to get (1.06)n = 256, but n is in the exponent and none of the algebra you know reaches up there.

Guessing works, slowly. Twenty four months gives 4 859, twenty five gives 5 150, so the answer is in month 25. A logarithm gets you there directly, and it is the only tool that does.

The question a logarithm answers

An exponential takes a power and returns a value: give it 3 and base 2, and it returns 8. A logarithm runs the same machine backwards. Give it 8 and base 2, and it returns the power, 3.

The exponential asks

"I have the power. What value do I get?" Input 3, base 2, output 23 = 8.

The logarithm asks

"I have the value. What power did it take?" Input 8, base 2, output log2 8 = 3.

So a logarithm is an exponent

That one sentence is the whole topic. Every property of logarithms is a property of exponents, seen from the other side.

Definition

For a base b > 0 with b ≠ 1, and a strictly positive x,y = logb x   means exactly   by = xIn words: logb x is the power you must raise b to in order to get x. The two lines carry the same information. Which one you write depends only on which quantity you are hunting for.

Everything that follows comes from reading that sentence in both directions. log5 25 = 2 because 52 = 25. log64 8 = 12 because 6412 = 8. log2(116) = −4 because 2−4 = 116.

The same fact, written two ways
Exponential formLogarithmic formRead it as
52 = 25log5 25 = 2the power of 5 that gives 25 is 2
34 = 81log3 81 = 4the power of 3 that gives 81 is 4
100 = 1log10 1 = 0the power of 10 that gives 1 is 0
103 = 1000log10 1000 = 3the power of 10 that gives 1000 is 3
6412 = 8log64 8 = 12a square root is the power one half
2−4 = 116log2(116) = −4a value below 1 needs a negative power
e1 = eln e = 1the power of e that gives e is 1
Converting in either direction, mechanically

Going from logb x = y to by = x: the base stays the base, the answer becomes the exponent, and the thing inside the logarithm becomes the result. If you say "base to the answer gives the inside" while pointing at the three symbols, you will not get it backwards.

Evaluating one without a calculator

Most logarithms in an exam are built to come out whole, and the habit that finds them is a single question asked out loud: what power of the base gives this number?

Rewrite the inside as a power of the base, and the answer is then sitting there as the exponent. That is the whole method.

Method: evaluating a logarithm by inspection
  1. Look at the base. Write down its first few powers if that helps: for base 3, that is 3, 9, 27, 81, 243.
  2. Rewrite the number inside as one of those powers. Roots become fractional powers, reciprocals become negative powers.
  3. Read off the exponent. That exponent is the answer.
  4. Check by going back the other way: does the base raised to your answer give the inside?
Four evaluations by inspection
  1. log3 81: powers of 3 are 3, 9, 27, 81
    81 is the fourth one, so 81 = 34 and the answer is 4. Check: 34 = 81.
  2. log 100 = log10(102) = 2
    Written with no base, log means base 10. Rewrite 100 as a power of 10 and read off the exponent.
  3. log 0.001 = log(10−3) = −3
    A number below 1 is a negative power of 10, because 10−3 = 11000. Numbers below 1 always have negative logarithms.
  4. log9 3 = 12
    Ask what power of 9 gives 3. A square root is the power one half, and 912 = 3.
Two logarithms that are true in every base

logb 1 = 0, because b0 = 1 whatever the base is. And logb b = 1, because b1 = b. These two appear in almost every exam question as a term you are meant to recognise and collapse on sight.

log and ln: the two keys on your calculator

The two that get their own names

log10 x is the common logarithm, written log x with the base left off. loge x is the natural logarithm, written ln x. On your calculator these are two separate keys. Pressing the wrong one gives an answer that looks perfectly reasonable and is wrong, which is why this error is both frequent and invisible.

Base 10 is convenient for orders of magnitude, because multiplying a number by 10 adds exactly 1 to its logarithm: log 1 = 0, log 10 = 1, log 100 = 2, log 1 000 = 3. Base e is the one that makes calculus clean, so from week 5 onwards almost everything in this course is written with ln.

For the "how long until" questions later in this lesson, either key works and gives the same answer, as long as you use the same one on both sides.

Four evaluations mixing the two keys
  1. ln 1 = 0
    Because e0 = 1. The logarithm of 1 is 0 in every base, including this one.
  2. ln(e−1) = −1
    The natural logarithm reads the exponent off directly when the inside is already a power of e.
  3. log 0.1 = −1
    0.1 = 10−1, and the base of log is 10.
  4. ln e + log(110) = 1 + (−1) = 0
    Each term is evaluated in its own base and only then added. Mixing the bases inside one term is where this goes wrong.

Why the input must be strictly positive

Ask the defining question about log10(−5): what power of 10 gives −5? There is not one. Positive powers of 10 are large, negative powers are small positive fractions, and the power zero gives 1. A positive base raised to any real power is strictly positive, so it can never produce a negative number or zero.

The domain restriction, and where it costs marks

You cannot take the logarithm of zero or of a negative number. The domain of logb x is ]0 ; +∞[.

In a formula this becomes a condition on x. For f(x) = ln(x − 4) the argument must satisfy x − 4 > 0, so the domain is ]4 ; +∞[. The inequality is strict, because ln 0 does not exist either. Marks are lost here by writing x ≥ 4, which includes one illegal value.

The shape of the graph

Because a logarithm is an exponential read backwards, its graph is the exponential graph with the two coordinates swapped. Swapping the coordinates of every point is a reflection in the line y = x, so the two curves are mirror images in that line.

Every point of y = 2x becomes a point of y = log2 x
Point on y = 2xPoint on y = log2 xThe same fact
(−1 ; 0.5)(0.5 ; −1)2−1 = 0.5
(0 ; 1)(1 ; 0)20 = 1
(1 ; 2)(2 ; 1)21 = 2
(2 ; 4)(4 ; 2)22 = 4
(3 ; 8)(8 ; 3)23 = 8
A vertical asymptote at x = 0

The exponential had a horizontal asymptote at y = 0. Reflecting turns it into a vertical asymptote at x = 0. The curve plunges without limit as x approaches zero from the right, and never crosses to the left of the vertical axis.

It always passes through (1 ; 0)

Because logb 1 = 0 in every base. This is the mirror of the exponential always passing through (0 ; 1).

It increases, but ever more slowly

For log, moving from 10 to 100 raises the value by 1, and so does moving from 100 to 1 000. Each further unit of height costs ten times as much horizontal distance. A logarithm grows without bound, and it takes its time.

exp and ln undo each other

The two identities that make logarithms useful

For every legal input,logb(bx) = x      blogb x = xand with base e that reads ln(ex) = x and eln x = x. The logarithm undoes the exponential and the exponential undoes the logarithm. They are inverse functions, which is the subject of the next part of the course.

This is the entire reason logarithms appear in a business course. You are not asked to admire them. You are asked to use them to free a variable that is trapped in an exponent, and the identity on the left is the tool that does it.

How long until? The two worked questions

Every question of the form "how long until this reaches that" has the unknown in the exponent. The method is always the same: get the power on its own, take the logarithm of both sides, and bring the exponent down in front.

That last move needs one rule, and since the rules get their proper treatment later in the rules section, here it is with its reason.

The one rule you need today, with its reason

For a > 0,ln(an) = n · ln aWhy it is true: an means a multiplied by itself n times. A logarithm turns a product into a sum, so ln(a · a · ... · a) becomes ln a + ln a + ... + ln a, which is n copies of ln a added together, and that is n · ln a. Every growth multiplier is positive, so the condition a > 0 is always satisfied in these questions.

Method: solving for a time
  1. Write the situation as an equation, with the unknown time as the exponent.
  2. Divide by the starting amount so that the power stands alone on one side.
  3. Take ln of both sides. You may use log instead; the answer is identical as long as you are consistent.
  4. Use ln(an) = n · ln a to bring the exponent down in front.
  5. Divide to isolate n, then round upwards to a whole period, because a target is reached at the end of a period and not partway through.
How long until 10 000 CHF at 2 per cent a year doubles?
  1. 10 000 · (1.02)n = 20 000
    The question written as an equation. Doubling means the final amount is twice the starting amount.
  2. (1.02)n = 2
    Divide both sides by 10 000. Notice the starting capital has vanished, so a doubling time does not depend on how much you start with.
  3. ln((1.02)n) = ln 2
    Take the natural logarithm of both sides. Doing the same thing to both sides keeps the equation true, and this particular thing reaches into the exponent.
  4. n · ln(1.02) = ln 2
    The rule from the box above, with a = 1.02. The unknown is now an ordinary multiplier and the equation is linear in n.
  5. n = ln 2ln 1.02 ≈ 0.6931470.019803
    Two calculator keys. Both logarithms are natural logarithms, so the bases cancel out of the ratio and log would have given the same number.
  6. n ≈ 35.0 years, so 36 whole years
    Check it: after 35 years the balance is 19 998.90 CHF, a little short, and after 36 years it is 20 398.87 CHF. Interest is credited once a year, so the money has not doubled until the 36th payment lands.
When do the subscribers reach 5 000?
  1. 1 200 · (1.06)n = 5 000
    Jane’s question from the start of the lesson, with n counting months because the rate is monthly.
  2. (1.06)n = 5 0001 200 ≈ 4.1667
    Divide by the starting membership to leave the power alone. Keep the fraction exact for now and round at the very end.
  3. ln((1.06)n) = ln(4.1667)
    Take the natural logarithm of both sides, because the unknown is in the exponent and this is the move that reaches it.
  4. n · ln(1.06) = 1.42712
    Bring the exponent down in front. On the right, ln(4.1667) ≈ 1.42712.
  5. n = 1.427120.058269 ≈ 24.49
    Now ln(1.06) ≈ 0.058269. The answer is not a whole number of months, which is normal and expected.
  6. month 25
    Round upwards. Check: after 24 months there are 4 859 members, still short, and after 25 months 5 150. Jane can tell the board the 5 000 mark falls in month 25, a little over two years away.
Round up, and say which direction you rounded

A time to reach a target is almost always rounded up, because the target has not been reached until the period completes. Rounding 24.49 down to 24 gives an answer that is demonstrably false: at month 24 there are 4 859 members and the target is 5 000. Write the exact value, then the rounded one, then a sentence saying which period the event falls in.

Where marks are lost in this topic
  • Converting backwards. Writing logb x = y as yb = x. Say "base to the answer gives the inside".
  • Pressing the wrong key. log is base 10, ln is base e. The wrong one gives a plausible wrong number.
  • Forgetting the domain. ln(x − 4) needs x > 4, strictly, because ln 0 does not exist either.
  • Taking the logarithm of one side only. Whatever you do, do it to both sides.
  • Rounding a time down. 24.49 months means month 25, because the target is not reached at month 24.
  • Believing ln(a + b) = ln a + ln b. There is no rule for the logarithm of a sum. The rule that exists turns a product into a sum.
What to remember
  • logb x = y means by = x. A logarithm is an exponent. Read it both ways.
  • To evaluate one by hand, ask what power of the base gives the number inside.
  • log means base 10 and ln means base e. Two keys, two different answers.
  • The input of a logarithm must be strictly positive, which restricts the domain of any formula containing one.
  • The graph has a vertical asymptote at x = 0, passes through (1 ; 0) and is the mirror of the exponential in the line y = x.
  • ln(ex) = x and eln x = x. They undo each other, and that is what logarithms are for.
  • For a "how long until" question: isolate the power, take ln of both sides, use ln(an) = n · ln a, divide, round up.
Part IIIOperations on functions · Week 25 lessons

Part III  ·  Lesson 1 of 5

Combining functions

Adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing whole functions. Total cost is a sum of cost functions and profit is a difference, so almost every business formula you will meet this year is built this way.

Before this lesson you need
  • What a function is, and how to evaluate one at a number
  • How to read a domain, and the three things that can go wrong inside one
  • How to expand and collect terms, from expanding and factoring
  • How to find where a quadratic is zero, from quadratic equations
In this lesson you will learn
  • Why a business adds functions at all, rather than adding numbers
  • The five operations, each defined and each worked through
  • The difference between evaluating a combination and building its formula
  • Why the domain of a combination is the intersection of two domains
  • The one extra condition a quotient carries, and why it can exclude a brand new value
  • The sign discipline that subtraction demands, which is where the marks go
The same topic on Khan Academy
  • Precalculus, unit 1: Composite and inverse functions

Free, no account needed to watch. Their exercises need one.

The cost nobody has written down

XY Coffee Co roasts beans in Geneva and sells them in sacks. The finance team keeps three separate records of what a month costs, because three different people are responsible for them.

Rent, insurance and the lease on the roaster come to the same amount whatever happens: f(q) = 10 000 CHF. Green coffee is bought per sack: g(q) = 200q. Wages include overtime, and overtime climbs faster than volume does, so the payroll model is h(q) = 5q2. In all three, q is the number of sacks roasted in the month.

Jane wants one number: the total cost of a month at any volume. No one has written that function down, because it is not a fourth fact about the business. It is the three facts already on the table, added together.

Three records

f for fixed costs, g for materials, h for wages. Each is a function of the same q.

One operation

Add them, function to function, and call the result C.

One answer

C(q) = 5q2 + 200q + 10 000, the cost of any month, from one formula.

Writing C = f + g + h is a statement about functions, not about numbers. It means that at every quantity q, the value of C is the sum of the three values. Nothing more clever than that is happening, and the whole of this section is the consequences of that one sentence.

The five operations

There are five ways to combine functions with ordinary arithmetic. Each is defined the same way: do the arithmetic to the outputs, one input at a time. The technical word for that is pointwise.

Definition

For two functions f and g, and a constant k:

(f + g)(x) = f(x) + g(x)
(f − g)(x) = f(x) − g(x)
(f · g)(x) = f(x) · g(x)
(fg)(x) = f(x)g(x),  provided g(x) ≠ 0
(k · f)(x) = k · f(x)

Read the first line slowly. On the left, the plus sign sits between two functions, and it is a new kind of plus that has to be defined. On the right, the plus sign sits between two numbers, and it is the plus you have used since primary school. The equation is the definition of the new one in terms of the old one.

Pointwise, seen as a table of months at XY Coffee Co
qf(q) fixedg(q) materialsh(q) wagesC(q) total
010 0000010 000
2010 0004 0002 00016 000
4010 0008 0008 00026 000
6010 00012 00018 00040 000
10010 00020 00050 00080 000

Every row is added on its own. The last column is not a new measurement; it is the other three columns, added across. Notice how the shape of the total changes as q grows: at 20 sacks the fixed cost is most of the bill, at 100 sacks the wage term alone is 50 000. That shift is a business fact, and it fell out of the addition without anyone modelling it separately.

Sum and difference

We will use the same pair for all five operations, so that you can compare them: f(x) = 3x − 1 and g(x) = x2 + 3x. Both are polynomials, so both are defined for every real number, and no domain question can arise yet. That comes later in the section, on purpose.

Build (f + g)(x), with f(x) = 3x − 1 and g(x) = x2 + 3x
  1. (f + g)(x) = f(x) + g(x)
    Write the definition first. This line costs nothing and it keeps the two functions in the right order.
  2. = (3x − 1) + (x2 + 3x)
    Substitute each formula, each inside its own bracket. The brackets are not needed for a sum, but writing them now builds the habit that a difference will demand.
  3. = x2 + 3x + 3x − 1
    Drop the brackets, since everything is being added, and gather the terms by degree.
  4. (f + g)(x) = x2 + 6x − 1
    Two like terms of 3x make 6x. Check at x = 3: the formula gives 9 + 18 − 1 = 26, and adding the outputs gives 8 + 18 = 26.

Subtraction is where the marks are lost, so it gets its own warning before the worked example rather than after it.

The minus applies to every term, not to the first one

(f − g)(x) means f(x) − [ g(x) ], with the whole of g inside that bracket. If g has three terms, all three change sign. This is the most frequent error in the whole of week 2, and it is not a conceptual error: it is a sign error made in a hurry. The defence is mechanical. Write the bracket, then remove it as a separate step.

Build (f − g)(x), same f and g
  1. (f − g)(x) = f(x) − g(x)
    The definition again, with a minus this time.
  2. = (3x − 1) − (x2 + 3x)
    Now the bracket around g is doing real work. Do not remove it yet.
  3. = 3x − 1 − x2 − 3x
    Remove it, changing the sign of both terms inside. The +3x became −3x.
  4. (f − g)(x) = −x2 − 1
    The 3x and the −3x cancel exactly. Check at x = 2: the formula gives −4 − 1 = −5, and subtracting the outputs gives 5 − 10 = −5.
A second example, with more terms to lose

With F(x) = 2x2 − 5x + 1 and G(x) = x2 − 7x + 4, the difference is (F − G)(x) = x2 + 2x − 3. Every sign inside G flipped: −5x − (−7x) = +2x and 1 − 4 = −3. The answer you get by flipping only the first sign is x2 − 12x + 5, which is wrong in two places at once.

Product, quotient, and multiplying by a constant

A product of functions is an ordinary expansion once the two formulas are in place. A quotient is written down rather than computed, and the work goes into saying where it is legal. Multiplying by a constant is the easiest of the five, and it still catches people who multiply only one term.

Build (f · g)(x), with f(x) = 3x − 1 and g(x) = x2 + 3x
  1. (f · g)(x) = (3x − 1)(x2 + 3x)
    Both formulas, each bracketed, side by side.
  2. = 3x(x2 + 3x) − 1(x2 + 3x)
    Distribute one bracket over the other, one term at a time.
  3. = 3x3 + 9x2 − x2 − 3x
    Four products. The second line of two is where the minus sign must travel across both terms again.
  4. (f · g)(x) = 3x3 + 8x2 − 3x
    Collect the two x2 terms. Check at x = 2: the formula gives 24 + 32 − 6 = 50, and multiplying the outputs gives 5 · 10 = 50.
Build the quotient and say where it lives
  1. (fg)(x) = 3x − 1x2 + 3x
    The quotient is a single fraction of the two formulas. There is nothing to expand.
  2. x2 + 3x = 0
    The real work is the condition. Set the bottom function to zero and solve, because those are the forbidden inputs.
  3. x(x + 3) = 0
    Factor out the common x. A product is zero only when one of its factors is zero.
  4. x = 0 or x = −3
    Two forbidden values.
  5. domain = ℝ \ {−3 ; 0}
    Every real number except those two. Neither f nor g had any restriction on its own, and the quotient has two.
Multiplying by a constant

(k · f)(x) = k · f(x). The constant multiplies every term of f. With f(x) = 3x − 1, half of it is 12 f(x) = 32x − 12, not 32x − 1. Check at x = 4: f(4) = 11, so half is 112, and 32(4) − 12 = 6 − 12 = 112. It agrees.

Do you need a number, or a formula?

These are two different questions and they take very different amounts of work. If the question asks for a value at one input, you never have to build the combined formula at all. Evaluate each function separately, then do the arithmetic on the two numbers.

If the question asks what the combination is, or asks you to graph it, or to find where it is zero, then you do need the formula. Read the question first and decide which one it wants. Building a formula you were not asked for costs time in an exam and introduces chances to slip.

Find (f · g)(2) in the least work possible
  1. (f · g)(2) = f(2) · g(2)
    The definition, read at a single input. No algebra is required anywhere in this calculation.
  2. f(2) = 3(2) − 1 = 5
    One substitution.
  3. g(2) = 22 + 3(2) = 10
    A second substitution.
  4. (f · g)(2) = 50
    Two substitutions and a multiplication. Building 3x3 + 8x2 − 3x first and then substituting gives 50 as well, after about four times as much writing.
The shortcut has a limit

Evaluating pointwise works for a single input. It does not tell you the domain, it does not let you graph the combination, and it will not find the quantity at which profit is zero. Those all need the formula. The skill is knowing which of the two the question is asking for, and that is usually visible in the first three words of it.

Where is the combination defined?

For a combination to have a value at some x, both original functions must have a value there. That is the whole idea, and the set of inputs where both are defined has a name: the intersection of the two domains.

The symbol is ∩, and in plain words it means the part they have in common. Not the part either one has. The part both have.

The domain of a combination

For f + g, f − g and f · g, the domain is D(f) ∩ D(g)For the quotient (fg), the domain is that same intersection, with every x satisfying g(x) = 0 removed as well.

An intersection can only be smaller than, or the same size as, the sets it came from. So combining functions can shrink a domain. It can never enlarge one.

Domain of (u + v)(x), with u(x) = x + 1 and v(x) = 5 − x
  1. x + 1 ≥ 0 → x ≥ −1
    A square root needs a non-negative inside, so D(u) = [−1 ; +∞[.
  2. 5 − x ≥ 0 → x ≤ 5
    The same reasoning on v, giving D(v) = ]−∞ ; 5].
  3. D(u) ∩ D(v)
    Now take the part both have. Sketch the two intervals one above the other if it helps; the answer is where they overlap.
  4. domain of u + v = [−1 ; 5]
    The intersection has shrunk the domain from both ends. Each function alone stretched to infinity in one direction; the sum lives on an interval six units long.

The quotient carries its own extra condition, and that condition can exclude a value that neither original function had any objection to. This is worth seeing once with your own eyes, because it is easy to assume that a combination inherits its problems rather than inventing new ones.

Domain of (FG)(x), with F(x) = x2 + 4 and G(x) = x − 3
  1. D(F) = ℝ
    A polynomial. There is no denominator, no root and no logarithm, so nothing is forbidden.
  2. D(G) = ℝ
    Also a polynomial. Also defined everywhere.
  3. D(F) ∩ D(G) = ℝ
    The intersection of everything with everything is everything. So far the quotient looks safe.
  4. G(x) = 0 → x = 3
    Now the extra condition. The bottom function is zero at 3, so 3 has to go.
  5. domain = ℝ \ {3}
    A value neither F nor G excluded is excluded by their quotient. Division created the problem.
Do not read the domain off the simplified fraction

Take F(x) = x2 − 9 and G(x) = x − 3. The quotient simplifies to x + 3, which looks defined for every real number. It is not. The original denominator was zero at 3, so 3 was never a legal input, and cancelling a factor does not give it back. The domain is decided by the functions you started with, never by the tidy expression you finished with. The same rule governs composition.

Profit is a difference of functions

Now the operation that the rest of the course leans on. XY Coffee Co sells a sack for 800 CHF, so revenue is R(q) = 800q. Cost is the C we built at the start. Profit is what is left, and it is a difference of two functions, not of two numbers.

Build the profit function for XY Coffee Co
  1. P(q) = (R − C)(q) = R(q) − C(q)
    Profit is revenue minus cost, at every quantity. That is a definition, not a calculation.
  2. = 800q − (5q2 + 200q + 10 000)
    The whole of C goes inside the bracket. Three terms are about to change sign.
  3. = 800q − 5q2 − 200q − 10 000
    Remove the bracket as a separate step, flipping all three signs.
  4. P(q) = −5q2 + 600q − 10 000
    Collect: 800q − 200q = 600q. Check at q = 40: revenue 32 000, cost 26 000, profit 6 000, and the formula gives −8 000 + 24 000 − 10 000 = 6 000.
Read the answer, do not only write it

The leading coefficient is negative, so P is a downward parabola. Profit therefore rises, peaks and falls again. At q = 0 it is −10 000, which is the fixed cost being paid for a month of roasting nothing. Somewhere it crosses zero, and that quantity is the break-even point. Finding it is exactly the work of the next section, intercepts.

Where marks are lost in this topic
  • The minus on only the first term. (f − g)(x) flips every sign in g. Write the bracket, then remove it in a separate line.
  • A constant multiplying only the first term. 12 of 3x − 1 is 32x − 12.
  • Forgetting the quotient condition. Setting the bottom function to zero is a separate piece of work from finding the two domains.
  • Giving the union instead of the intersection. The combination needs both functions to work, so you want the overlap, not the total.
  • Reading the domain off a simplified expression. A cancelled factor still forbids its value.
  • Building a formula when a number was asked for. (f · g)(2) is two substitutions and a multiplication.
What to remember
  • All five operations are pointwise: do the arithmetic to the outputs, one input at a time.
  • (f − g)(x) = f(x) − [ g(x) ]. The bracket is the whole difficulty.
  • Sum, difference and product live on D(f) ∩ D(g), the intersection.
  • A quotient lives on that intersection minus every solution of g(x) = 0.
  • Combining can shrink a domain and can invent a new exclusion. It can never enlarge a domain.
  • Total cost is a sum of cost functions; profit is R − C, a difference.

Part III  ·  Lesson 2 of 5

Intercepts

The two places a curve meets the axes. In business they are the two numbers a manager asks for first: where does this start, and where does it turn positive?

Before this lesson you need
  • How to read a point (x, y) on the plane
  • How to solve a quadratic equation, including the discriminant
  • How to handle an equation with the unknown in a denominator
  • What combining functions does, since profit is a difference
In this lesson you will learn
  • What an intercept means for a business, not only for a graph
  • The method, which is two substitutions and then honest equation solving
  • Why y = f(x) has at most one y-intercept, and why an ellipse can have two
  • How to report an intercept as a point, so that it earns the mark
  • x-intercepts of a quadratic, of a factored expression and of a rational function
  • How to say that there is no x-intercept, and how break-even is one
The same topic on Khan Academy
  • Algebra 1, unit 4: Linear equations and graphs
  • Algebra 1, unit 14: Quadratic functions and equations

Free, no account needed to watch. Their exercises need one.

Two numbers Jane asks for by name

In the previous section we built XY Coffee Co’s profit function: P(q) = −5q2 + 600q − 10 000, where q is sacks of coffee roasted in a month.

Jane does not want to look at a parabola. She wants two figures for the board pack. How much do we lose if we roast nothing at all? And at what volume do we stop losing money?

Both of those are intercepts. The first is where the curve meets the vertical axis, the second is where it meets the horizontal one. The whole topic is two substitutions, and then whatever equation solving those substitutions leave behind.

The y-intercept

Set x = 0. This is the value before anything happens: the starting height. For a cost line it is the fixed cost. For a profit curve it is the loss you make on a month of doing nothing.

The x-intercept

Set y = 0. This is where the quantity turns from negative to positive, or the other way. For a profit curve it is break-even. For a debt it is the month it is cleared.

Definition

An intercept is a point where a graph meets an axis. The y-intercept has x = 0; the x-intercept has y = 0. An x-intercept is also called a root or a zero of the function, and those three words mean the same thing.

The method

Two substitutions, then solve
  1. For the y-intercept: put x = 0 into the equation and solve for y.
  2. For the x-intercept: put y = 0 into the equation and solve for x. There may be none, one, or several.
  3. Report each as a point, such as (0, 3), with both coordinates, unless the question asks only for the value.

The substitutions are the easy half. The marks live in the second half of each step, where an equation has to be solved properly, and every technique from Part 0 can turn up there.

Intercepts of y = x3 + x
  1. x = 0 → y = 03 + 0 = 0
    Substitute zero for x. Nothing survives, so the curve passes through the origin.
  2. y-intercept = (0, 0)
    Written as a point, with both coordinates.
  3. y = 0 → x3 + x = 0
    Now the other substitution. This one leaves an equation to solve.
  4. x(x2 + 1) = 0
    Factor out the common x. Never divide by x here: that would throw away the solution x = 0.
  5. x = 0 or x2 + 1 = 0
    A product is zero only when one factor is zero, so take the two cases separately.
  6. x-intercept = (0, 0) only
    x2 + 1 = 0 would need x2 = −1, and a square is never negative. So the second case gives nothing.

Why there is usually at most one y-intercept

If the equation is written as y = f(x), then putting x = 0 in leaves you a single expression, f(0), and an expression has one value. So there can be at most one y-intercept. If 0 is not in the domain, there is none at all.

That is not a rule about graphs. It is the definition of a function: one input, one output. A curve with two points above x = 0 would be assigning two outputs to the same input, and would not be a function.

An equation that is not of the form y = f(x) carries no such promise. Then putting x = 0 in leaves an equation in y, and that equation can have several solutions.

Intercepts of the ellipse 9x2 + 4y2 = 25
  1. x = 0 → 4y2 = 25
    Substitute zero. Notice what is left: an equation in y, not a value of y.
  2. y2 = 254
    Divide both sides by 4.
  3. y = ±52
    Take the square root of both sides, and keep both signs. This is the step where a mark is lost.
  4. y-intercepts = (0, 52) and (0, −52)
    Two of them. The curve meets the vertical axis twice, which no graph of a function ever does.
  5. y = 0 → 9x2 = 25 → x = ±53
    The same work on the other axis, and again both signs.
  6. x-intercepts = (53, 0) and (−53, 0)
    Check one: 9(53)2 = 9 · 259 = 25. It sits on the curve.
Report the point, not the number

An answer of “3” does not say which axis it is on. (3, 0) and (0, 3) are different places on the plane and usually different answers to different questions. Write both coordinates every time, and the reader knows what you found. This costs one second and is worth a mark in most marking schemes.

x-intercepts of a quadratic

Setting y = 0 on a quadratic leaves ax2 + bx + c = 0, and you already have two ways to solve it: factor it if the numbers are friendly, or use the quadratic formula if they are not. Factoring is faster when it works, so try it for a few seconds before reaching for the formula.

Intercepts of y = x2 − 7x + 10
  1. x = 0 → y = 10
    The y-intercept is (0, 10). For any polynomial it is the constant term, which is worth knowing as a check.
  2. y = 0 → x2 − 7x + 10 = 0
    The other substitution leaves a quadratic.
  3. (x − 2)(x − 5) = 0
    Two numbers multiplying to +10 and adding to −7: they are −2 and −5.
  4. x = 2 or x = 5
    Each factor set to zero in turn.
  5. x-intercepts = (2, 0) and (5, 0)
    Check the first: 4 − 14 + 10 = 0. It is on the curve.

x-intercepts of a factored expression

When the expression arrives already factored, do not expand it. Expanding destroys exactly the information you want. Set each factor to zero in turn, and discard the factors that have no real solution.

x-intercepts of y = (2x − 6)(x + 4)(x2 + 1)
  1. 2x − 6 = 0 → x = 3
    First factor.
  2. x + 4 = 0 → x = −4
    Second factor.
  3. x2 + 1 = 0
    Third factor. Set it to zero like the others and see what happens.
  4. x2 = −1, no real solution
    A square is never negative, so this factor contributes nothing. Say so in writing; it is part of the answer.
  5. x-intercepts = (3, 0) and (−4, 0)
    Two intercepts from a degree four expression. Expanding it first would have given 2x4 + 2x3 − 22x2 + 2x − 24, which is much harder to solve and no more informative.

x-intercepts of a rational function

A fraction equals zero when its numerator is zero. The denominator has no say in making the fraction zero, but it does have a veto: wherever the denominator is zero, the function has no value at all, so that input cannot be an intercept even if the numerator happens to vanish there too.

So the procedure has two parts. Solve the numerator for the candidates. Then check each candidate against the denominator, and strike out any that the denominator forbids.

Intercepts of y = x2 − 9x2 − 5x + 6
  1. x = 0 → y = −96 = −32
    The y-intercept is (0, −32). Substituting zero into a fraction is no different from substituting it anywhere else.
  2. x2 − 5x + 6 = 0 → x = 2 or x = 3
    Find the forbidden values first, before you commit to any candidate. These two inputs have no output.
  3. x2 − 9 = 0 → x = 3 or x = −3
    Now the numerator. Two candidates.
  4. x = 3 is forbidden
    It makes the denominator zero as well, so the function has no value there at all. It cannot be an intercept.
  5. x-intercept = (−3, 0) only
    Check it: the numerator is 9 − 9 = 0 and the denominator is 9 + 15 + 6 = 30, so the value is 030 = 0. One intercept, from two candidates.
A cancelled factor is still forbidden

The fraction above simplifies to x + 3x − 2, because x − 3 divides out of top and bottom. That simplified form looks as though x = 3 is perfectly fine, and it is not. Cancelling a factor never restores a forbidden input; it only hides it. Find the forbidden values from the original denominator, before simplifying anything.

When there is no x-intercept at all

Some functions never reach zero. A parabola that sits entirely above the horizontal axis is the standard case, and “there is no x-intercept” is a complete and correct answer. It is not a sign that you have made a mistake, but you do have to prove it rather than assert it.

For a quadratic the proof is the discriminant, Δ = b2 − 4ac. If it is negative, the square root in the quadratic formula has nothing to work with, and there are no real roots.

Intercepts of y = x2 − 4x + 7
  1. x = 0 → y = 7
    The y-intercept is (0, 7), the constant term as always.
  2. Δ = (−4)2 − 4(1)(7)
    Before solving, test whether there is anything to find.
  3. Δ = 16 − 28 = −12
    Negative.
  4. no x-intercept
    The curve never touches the horizontal axis. To see why, complete the square: x2 − 4x + 7 = (x − 2)2 + 3, which is at least 3 for every x.
What the sign of the discriminant tells you

Δ > 0: two x-intercepts, the curve cuts the axis twice. Δ = 0: one x-intercept, the curve touches the axis and turns back. Δ < 0: none, the curve stays entirely on one side. You can answer “how many x-intercepts?” without solving anything at all, which is worth remembering under time pressure.

A vertical line has no y-intercept

x = 3 never meets the vertical axis, because x is never 0 anywhere on it. It is also not a function, so the “at most one y-intercept” promise does not cover it. Read the sentence carefully: the promise applies to equations written as y = f(x), and x = 3 cannot be written that way.

Break-even is an x-intercept

Now Jane’s two figures. Profit is P(q) = −5q2 + 600q − 10 000, and both of her questions are intercept questions in different clothes.

Both intercepts of the XY Coffee Co profit function
  1. q = 0 → P(0) = −10 000
    Substitute zero. Nothing is roasted, nothing is sold, and the fixed costs are still paid.
  2. y-intercept = (0, −10 000)
    A loss of 10 000 CHF in a month of doing nothing. That is Jane’s first figure, and it is simply the fixed cost.
  3. P(q) = 0 → −5q2 + 600q − 10 000 = 0
    Break-even means profit exactly zero, which is the second substitution.
  4. q2 − 120q + 2 000 = 0
    Divide every term by −5. Dividing by a negative here is a convenience, and every sign changes.
  5. Δ = (−120)2 − 4(1)(2 000) = 14 400 − 8 000 = 6 400
    The discriminant is positive, and 6 400 = 80 exactly, so the roots will be whole numbers.
  6. q = 120 ± 802
    The quadratic formula, with the tidy numbers the previous line promised.
  7. q = 20 or q = 100
    Check the first: −5(400) + 600(20) − 10 000 = −2 000 + 12 000 − 10 000 = 0.

Two x-intercepts, so two break-even points, and the interpretation matters more than the arithmetic. The parabola opens downwards, so profit is positive between them and negative outside them. XY Coffee Co makes money only when it roasts between 20 and 100 sacks a month.

Below 20 sacks the 10 000 CHF of fixed cost has not been recovered. Above 100 sacks the wage term 5q2 has overtaken the revenue line, because a square grows faster than a straight line eventually does. That upper limit is a real operational constraint, and it came out of an intercept calculation, not out of anyone’s intuition.

Say what the number means

“q = 20 and q = 100” is half an answer. The full answer is: the firm breaks even at 20 sacks and again at 100 sacks, and is profitable only in between. In an exam the sentence carries its own marks. In a meeting it is the only part anyone hears.

Where marks are lost in this topic
  • Giving a bare number. Report (0, 10) or (2, 0), so that the reader knows which axis.
  • Losing a sign when taking a square root. y2 = 254 gives two values of y, not one.
  • Dividing by x instead of factoring it out. That discards the intercept at the origin.
  • Expanding a factored expression. It is already in the most useful form there is.
  • Taking a rational intercept from a cancelled factor. Check every candidate against the original denominator.
  • Reporting one break-even point when the discriminant gives two. A curve against a line can cross twice.
  • Stopping at the number. Interpret it: below 20 sacks the fixed cost is not covered.
What to remember
  • y-intercept: set x = 0. x-intercept: set y = 0. Then solve honestly.
  • An equation written y = f(x) has at most one y-intercept. An equation not of that form can have several.
  • Report every intercept as a point with both coordinates.
  • For a rational function the x-intercepts come from the numerator, and the denominator vetoes.
  • Δ < 0 means no x-intercept, and that is a complete answer.
  • Break-even is the x-intercept of P = R − C, and it can happen twice.

Part III  ·  Lesson 3 of 5

Composition of functions

Feeding one machine’s output straight into the next. Six steps. Watch the Khan lesson at the top of each, then read the short version and practise.

1Step 1 of 6Not startedWhat a composite is, and which one goes firstOne function’s output becomes the next one’s input.
Learn it on KhanRead: Intro to composing functionsWatch: Composing functions

XY Coffee Co knows that advertising brings customers, N(x) = 100x, and that customers bring revenue, R(n) = 70n + n220. Jane wants revenue as a function of advertising. That is not a third fact about the business. It is the two she has, joined end to end.

The notation is (g ∘ f)(x) = g(f(x)) said g after f. Point at the x: whichever letter is touching it acts first. That is the opposite of reading order, and it is the single thing people get wrong.

It is not a product

(g ∘ f)(x) is not g(x) · f(x). With f(x) = x + 1 and g(x) = x2 at x = 3: the composite gives g(4) = 16, the product gives 9 · 4 = 36.

2Step 2 of 6Not startedEvaluating at a numberWork inside out, and write the middle value down.
Learn it on KhanWatch: Evaluating composite functions

When you only need one number, never build the formula. Take it one machine at a time.

(g ∘ f)(4), with f(x) = 2x + 1 and g(x) = x2 − 3
  1. (g ∘ f)(4) = g(f(4))
    The definition with 4 in place of x. This line fixes the order.
  2. f(4) = 2(4) + 1 = 9
    Inside first. f is touching the 4.
  3. g(9) = 92 − 3 = 78
    Feed 9 into g.

The same pair the other way round gives g(4) = 13, then f(13) = 27. Seventy-eight against twenty-seven, from the same two functions and the same input.

More practice on Khan: Evaluate composite functions

3Step 3 of 6Not startedBuilding the formulaSubstitute the whole inner function, not just its name.
Learn it on KhanWatch: Finding composite functions

When you need the whole relationship rather than one value, the method is fixed: write the outer function with an empty bracket, then fill every bracket with the entire inner function. The word entire is the work, and the bracket is how you honour it.

(g ∘ f)(x), with f(x) = 2x + 1 and g(x) = x2 − 3
  1. g( ) = ( )2 − 3
    The outer function with a hole where its variable was.
  2. (2x + 1)2 − 3
    Drop the whole of f in. The square applies to all of 2x + 1.
  3. 4x2 + 4x − 2
    Expand, then check against step 2: at x = 4 this gives 78.

The other order gives 2(x2 − 3) + 1 = 2x2 − 5. Drawn together, they are plainly not the same function.

The bracket is the whole step

(F ∘ G)(p) with F(p) = p2 and G(p) = 2p + 1 is (2p + 1)2, not 2p2 + 1. Bracket first, expand second.

More practice on Khan: Find composite functions

4Step 4 of 6Not startedModelling a chainThe business question Jane actually asked.
Learn it on KhanWatch: Modelling with composite functions

Revenue depends on customers, and customers depend on spend. So revenue is the outer function and customers the inner one. From there it is step 3 again.

Revenue as a function of advertising spend
  1. R( ) = 70( ) + ( )220
    Two holes, and one of them is inside a square.
  2. 70(100x) + (100x)220
    Every n becomes 100x, including the one being squared.
  3. 7000x + 500x
    Because (100x)2 = 10 000x, and 10 000x20 = 500x.

Then read it. The 7000x grows fast and flattens; the 500x keeps a steady rate for ever. Early advertising francs buy more than late ones, which is the business fact sitting inside the algebra.

More practice on Khan: Model with composite functions

5Step 5 of 6Not startedThe domain of a compositeTwo conditions, and this is where the marks are.
Learn it on KhanRead: Composing functions, including domains

For x to be legal in (g ∘ f)(x), two separate things must hold: x must be legal for f, and what f produces must be legal for g Both are checked on the original functions, never on the tidied-up composite.

f(x) = x − 4 and g(u) = u
  1. f is defined for every x
    A straight line rules nothing out, so condition one is free.
  2. u needs u ≥ 0
    Condition two is the live one: what f produces must be non-negative.
  3. x − 4 ≥ 0 → x ≥ 4
    Translate it back into x, which is what the question asked about.
Do not read the domain off the tidy formula

(f ∘ g)(x) with f(x) = x2 and g(u) = u simplifies to x, which looks defined everywhere. It is not: the inner x still demands x ≥ 0.

6Step 6 of 6Not startedTaking a composite apartThe reverse question, and the one week 5 cannot do the chain rule without.
Khan Academyno Khan lesson matches this one, so the explanation below is the full one

Here is a function; find two simpler ones that build it. Ask what you would compute last on a calculator That last operation is the outer function, and everything it acts on is the inner one.

What you would do last
The compositeLast thing you doOuter g(u)Inner f(x)
3x + 5take the rootu3x + 5
(x2 + 1)5raise to the fifthu5x2 + 1
e2x + 1raise e to a powereu2x + 1
ln(5x)take the logarithmln u5x

More than one split is correct. 3x + 5 also comes from outer u + 5 with inner 3x. Prefer the one whose inner function is the whole of what sits inside the operation, because that is the one the chain rule wants.

Part III  ·  Lesson 4 of 5

Inverse functions

Running the machine backwards. A demand curve tells you how much you will sell at a price; its inverse tells you what price to set to sell a given amount, which is the question management actually asks.

Before this lesson you need
  • What a function is, and how to read a domain and a range
  • How to compose two functions, since the check is a composition
  • How to solve linear and fractional equations for a chosen letter
  • What a logarithm is, for the last worked example
In this lesson you will learn
  • Why a business inverts a function at all, and the two identities that define an inverse
  • Why f−1 is not 1f, which is the single most common misreading
  • Why an inverse exists only for a one-to-one function, and how restricting the domain repairs a failure
  • The four-step method, and the idea of peeling operations off in reverse order
  • Four worked inverses of rising difficulty, including a root and an exponential
  • Why the graph is a mirror image, and why the domain of the inverse is the range of the original
The same topic on Khan Academy
  • Precalculus, unit 1: Composite and inverse functions

Free, no account needed to watch. Their exercises need one.

The question management actually asks

XY Coffee Co has estimated how much coffee it sells at any retail price. Daily demand is Q(p) = 5 000 000p + 1 − 500 000 grams, for a price p between 0 and 9 CHF, and zero above 9.

That function answers a question nobody in the room asked. Marketing has not proposed a price and asked how much will sell. Marketing has committed to a volume, and wants to know what price achieves it.

Both questions concern the same relationship between price and quantity. They differ only in which end you hold on to and which end you are solving for. Turning one round into the other is what an inverse function is.

The function you have

Q takes a price and returns a quantity. Price in, quantity out.

The question you are asked

A quantity is given. What price produces it?

The function you need

P takes a quantity and returns a price. It is Q run backwards.

Definition

The inverse of f, written f−1, is the function that undoes it. It is defined by the two identitiesf−1(f(x)) = x    and    f(f−1(x)) = xIn composition language, f ∘ f−1 = f−1 ∘ f = Id, where Id(x) = x is the identity function that leaves everything alone.

Read the first identity in words: put x through f, then put the result through f−1, and you are back where you started. The second says the same thing in the other order. Both are needed, because a function can undo another in one direction and not the other.

The superscript does not mean a reciprocal

f−1 means the inverse function. It does not mean 1f, and it does not mean 1f(x). The same symbol means two different things depending on whether it sits on a number or on a function name, and there is no way round that: it is standard notation and the course relies on you keeping the two apart. With f(x) = 4x − 7, the inverse is f−1(x) = x + 74, while 1f(x) is 14x − 7. Those are not remotely the same function. If you are ever unsure which is meant, check whether the thing being inverted is a function or a value.

When does an inverse exist?

Not every function can be undone, and the reason is easy to see. To run a function backwards you need each output to identify the input it came from. If two different inputs produce the same output, then when you meet that output going backwards you cannot tell which input to return to, and there is no function to build.

A function that never sends two different inputs to the same output is called one-to-one, or injective. Being one-to-one is exactly the condition for an inverse to exist.

The horizontal line test

Draw the graph. If every horizontal line meets the curve at most once, f is one-to-one and has an inverse. If any horizontal line meets it twice, it does not.

Compare this with the vertical line test from graphs, which decides whether a curve is a function at all. Vertical for “is it a function”, horizontal for “can it be inverted”. One test each way.

Why f(x) = x2 has no inverse on all of ℝ
  1. f(−3) = 9
    One input that produces 9.
  2. f(3) = 9
    A second, different input that produces the same 9.
  3. f−1(9) = ?
    Going backwards from 9 there are two candidates and no reason to prefer either. The line y = 9 cuts the parabola twice.
  4. no inverse on ℝ
    A function must give one output per input, and this backwards rule would give two. So it is not a function, and f has no inverse here.

The repair is to throw away half the parabola. On the domain x ≥ 0 the function f(x) = x2 is increasing throughout, so it never repeats an output, and now it does have an inverse: f−1(x) = x. Restricting the domain has not changed the formula at all. It has changed which inputs are allowed, and that was enough.

Every function you are asked to invert in this course is either always increasing or always decreasing on its stated domain. That is precisely what makes it one-to-one, and it is why the stated domain is part of the question and not decoration.

Undoing a knot: reverse the operations and their order

Before any algebra, here is the idea that makes every inverse in this section feel obvious. A function is a sequence of operations applied in a fixed order. To undo it you apply the opposite operations in the opposite order.

Putting on socks then shoes is undone by taking off shoes then socks. Not socks then shoes. The order reverses, and if it did not, you would be pulling a sock through a shoe.

Peeling the operations off a function
f(x) = 4x − 7 doesso the inverse must
multiply by 4, firstadd 7, last
subtract 7, lastdivide by 4, first

Reading the right-hand column downwards: add 7, then divide by 4. That is f−1(x) = x + 74, and you have written the inverse down without solving anything. Use this to predict the answer, then use the method below to confirm it.

Method: four steps
  1. Write y = f(x).
  2. Solve for x in terms of y. This is the real work, and it is ordinary equation solving.
  3. The expression you obtain is f−1(y). Rename the variable to x if the question wants it that way, and state its domain.
  4. Check by composing: f(f−1(x)) must collapse to x.
A linear inverse: f(x) = 4x − 7
  1. y = 4x − 7
    Step one, unchanged from the given formula.
  2. y + 7 = 4x
    Solve for x. Undo the subtraction first, because it was done last.
  3. x = y + 74
    Undo the multiplication. The x is now alone, which was the goal.
  4. f−1(x) = x + 74
    Rename y to x. The domain is all of ℝ, because a straight line reaches every height exactly once.
  5. check: f(x + 74) = 4 · x + 74 − 7 = x
    The 4 cancels, leaving x + 7 − 7 = x. Confirmed. At x = 3: f(3) = 5 and f−1(5) = 124 = 3.

A fractional one, where the unknown appears twice

When x appears on both the top and the bottom of a fraction, you cannot peel operations off one at a time. The move is to clear the denominator, gather every term containing x on one side, and factor x out. That last factoring step is the one that is easy to forget.

f(x) = 2x + 1x − 3, for x ≠ 3
  1. y = 2x + 1x − 3
    Step one.
  2. y(x − 3) = 2x + 1
    Multiply both sides by the denominator. This is legal because we have excluded the value that makes it zero.
  3. yx − 3y = 2x + 1
    Expand the left side, so that every term is visible.
  4. yx − 2x = 3y + 1
    Move every term containing x to the left and everything else to the right.
  5. x(y − 2) = 3y + 1
    Factor x out. This is the step the method exists for.
  6. f−1(x) = 3x + 1x − 2, x ≠ 2
    Divide by y − 2 and rename. Check at a value: f(4) = 91 = 9, and f−1(9) = 287 = 4.
Where the excluded value of the inverse comes from

The inverse forbids x = 2, and 2 did not appear anywhere in the original formula. It is the horizontal asymptote of f: as x grows, 2x + 1x − 3 approaches 2 without ever reaching it. So 2 is not in the range of f, and therefore not in the domain of f−1. Notice the pattern: f forbids 3 and its inverse forbids 2, and the two numbers have swapped roles along with everything else.

One with a square root, where the inverse needs a restricted domain

Here is the case that carries the most marks and gets the least attention. When you solve for x you sometimes obtain a formula that is defined for more inputs than it should be. The formula alone is not the inverse. The formula together with the right domain is.

f(x) = x − 1 + 2, on x ≥ 1
  1. y = x − 1 + 2
    Step one. The domain is stated, and the root is defined from 1 upwards.
  2. y − 2 = x − 1
    Isolate the root before doing anything to it.
  3. (y − 2)2 = x − 1
    Square both sides. Squaring is safe here because the left side y − 2 is a square root and so is never negative.
  4. x = (y − 2)2 + 1
    Solve for x.
  5. f−1(x) = (x − 2)2 + 1,  x ≥ 2
    The formula would happily accept x = 0 and return 5. But f(5) = 4, not 0, so that would be wrong. The domain must be x ≥ 2.
The domain of the inverse is the range of the original

f(x) = x − 1 + 2 has smallest value f(1) = 2 and climbs from there, so its range is [2 ; +∞[. An inverse can only accept what the original produced, so that range becomes the domain of f−1.

This is not bookkeeping. Written without its domain, (x − 2)2 + 1 is not one-to-one and is not the inverse of anything. The restriction is part of the answer, and in most marking schemes it is a separate mark.

Everything swaps
For fbecomes, for f−1
the domainthe range
the rangethe domain
the point (a, b)the point (b, a)
f(5) = 4f−1(4) = 5

One with an exponential

An exponential traps its variable in the exponent, and the only tool that frees it is a logarithm. The two are inverses of each other, which is the whole reason logarithms were invented. The rules you will need are collected in the next section.

f(x) = 3e2x + 1
  1. y = 3e2x + 1
    Step one.
  2. y − 1 = 3e2x
    Peel off the outermost operation, the addition of 1.
  3. y − 13 = e2x
    Then the multiplication by 3. The exponential now stands alone, which is what the logarithm needs.
  4. 2x = ln(y − 13)
    Take the natural logarithm of both sides. ln and eu undo each other, so the left side is left with the exponent.
  5. f−1(x) = 12 ln(x − 13),  x > 1
    Divide by 2 and rename. The domain is x > 1, because 3e2x is always strictly positive, so f never produces 1 or anything below it.
  6. check: f(0) = 3 + 1 = 4, f−1(4) = 12 ln(1) = 0
    A pair of values that agree. The strict inequality matters: at x = 1 the logarithm would be ln 0, which does not exist.
The business reading

If 10 000 CHF grows at 5% a year, its value is V(t) = 10 000(1.05)t, which answers “how much after t years”. The inverse answers “how long until it is worth V”, and it is a logarithm: t = ln(V ÷ 10 000)ln 1.05. To reach 25 000 CHF that gives t ≈ 18.8 years. Every compound growth question in this course is one of these two, and which one you are being asked decides whether you need the function or its inverse.

The graph is a mirror in the line y = x

If (a, b) is on the graph of f, then (b, a) is on the graph of f−1, because the inverse sends outputs back to inputs. Swapping the two coordinates of every point is exactly what reflecting in the line y = x does.

So you can draw an inverse without any algebra: sketch f, draw the line y = x, and reflect. It also gives a fast sanity check. If your computed inverse does not look like the mirror image, one of the two is wrong.

A consequence worth noticing

Any point where f meets the line y = x is a point where f and f−1 meet too, because reflecting it leaves it where it is.

And a warning

The mirror picture is a picture. It does not excuse you from stating the domain of the inverse, which is where the marks are.

The demand curve, inverted

Back to Jane. We have a function from price to quantity, and we want one from quantity to price.

Invert Q(p) = 5 000 000p + 1 − 500 000 on [0 ; 9]
  1. q = 5 000 000p + 1 − 500 000
    Step one, with q in place of y because it names a real quantity.
  2. q + 500 000 = 5 000 000p + 1
    Move the constant across, isolating the fraction.
  3. p + 1 = 5 000 000q + 500 000
    The two outer quantities exchange places, which is legal because both are strictly positive on this domain.
  4. P(q) = 5 000 000q + 500 000 − 1
    Subtract 1. This is the price needed to sell q grams a day.
  5. domain of P = [0 ; 4 500 000]
    Q(0) = 4 500 000 and Q(9) = 0, so the range of Q is [0 ; 4 500 000], and that becomes the domain of P.
  6. check: P(4 500 000) = 5 000 0005 000 000 − 1 = 0
    Selling the maximum requires a price of 0, as it should. And P(0) = 10 − 1 = 9, the price at which demand dies.

Read it back for Jane. To sell 1 500 000 grams a day, P(1 500 000) = 5 000 0002 000 000 − 1 = 1.5 CHF. That is a price, which is a thing the business can actually set. The original function could never have produced it.

Where marks are lost in this topic
  • Reading f−1 as 1f. They are different objects and usually different answers.
  • Not checking that the function is one-to-one. If it is not, the honest answer is that there is no inverse on that domain.
  • Giving the formula without the domain. The domain of the inverse is the range of the original, and it is its own mark.
  • Forgetting to factor x out when it appears twice in a fractional function.
  • Reversing the operations but not their order. Shoes before socks, both ways round.
  • Losing a sign when squaring. Ask first whether the side you are squaring can be negative.
  • Skipping the check. One composition, or even one numerical pair, catches most slips in seconds.
What to remember
  • f−1(f(x)) = x and f(f−1(x)) = x. An inverse undoes.
  • f−1 is not 1f.
  • An inverse exists only for a one-to-one function. Horizontal line test, and restrict the domain to repair a failure.
  • Method: write y = f(x), solve for x, rename, state the domain, check by composing.
  • Reverse the operations and reverse their order.
  • The graph of f−1 is the mirror image of f in the line y = x.
  • The domain of the inverse is the range of the original. Every question of this type tests it.

Part III  ·  Lesson 5 of 5

The rules for exponentials and logarithms

The toolkit for every equation where the unknown sits in an exponent. Growth, interest and doubling times all land here, and so does a short list of rules that do not exist but look as though they should.

Before this lesson you need
  • What an exponential function is, and what the number e is
  • What a logarithm is, as the inverse of an exponential
  • How to handle powers and roots, including fractional exponents
  • How to solve a quadratic equation, for the substitution example
In this lesson you will learn
  • The exponential rules, each with the reason it is true
  • The logarithm rules, why each is an exponential rule in disguise, and why log of 1 and of the base are what they are
  • The change of base formula, and the practical reason it exists
  • The four false rules that look plausible and are not
  • How to expand a logarithm into pieces, and how to condense pieces back into one
  • How to solve an equation that is quadratic in an exponential, and when to reject a candidate solution
The same topic on Khan Academy
  • Algebra 2, unit 8: Logarithms
  • Algebra 2, unit 6: Rational exponents and radicals

Free, no account needed to watch. Their exercises need one.

How long until the money doubles?

XY Coffee Co has 10 000 CHF sitting in a deposit account paying 2% a year. Jane asks a question that sounds simple and is not: in how many years will it be worth 20 000?

Written as an equation it is 10 000(1.02)n = 20 000. Every technique from Part 0 fails on it, because the unknown is in the exponent, and nothing you do to both sides will bring it down.

Logarithms bring it down. This section is the rules that make them work, and the short list of rules that do not.

The exponential rules, and why each is true

Every one of these is a counting argument. b3 means three copies of b multiplied together, and once you see that, the rules are bookkeeping rather than something to memorise.

The rules for a base b > 0
RuleWhy it is true
bx · by = bx+yThree copies next to four copies is seven copies. The exponents count the copies, so multiplying adds them.
bxby = bx−yDividing cancels copies from top and bottom, so it takes the counts away from each other.
(bx)y = bxyy groups of x copies each is xy copies in total.
(bc)x = bxcx and (bc)x = bxcxMultiplication can be reordered, so the copies of each factor gather separately.
b0 = 1Set x = y in the division rule: anything non-zero divided by itself is 1.
b−x = 1bxSet x = 0 in the division rule: 1by = b−y. A negative exponent is a reciprocal, not a negative number.
b12 = bBecause (b12)2 = b1 = b, and that is what a square root is.
A negative exponent does not make a negative number

2−3 is 18, positive and small. It is not −8. An exponential with a positive base is positive for every exponent, and that fact will reject a solution for you later in this section.

A logarithm is an exponent

logb m is the answer to one question: to what power must I raise b to obtain m? So a logarithm is not a new kind of number. It is an exponent, seen from the other side.

That single sentence generates every logarithm rule. Each one is an exponential rule, translated.

The defining relationship

logb m = y  ⇔  by = mvalid for b > 0, b ≠ 1 and m > 0. That last restriction is not a technicality: a positive base raised to any power is positive, so the logarithm of a negative number does not exist.

Where the product rule comes from
  1. let M = logb m and N = logb n
    Name the two logarithms, so that they can be handled as ordinary quantities.
  2. bM = m and bN = n
    Rewrite each in exponential form, using the defining relationship in the other direction.
  3. mn = bM · bN
    Multiply the two, which is what a product rule ought to be about.
  4. mn = bM+N
    Apply the exponential rule: multiplying powers of the same base adds the exponents.
  5. logb (mn) = M + N = logb m + logb n
    Translate back. The logarithm of a product is the sum of the logarithms, and it is the addition rule for exponents wearing a different hat.
The logarithm rules, and the exponential rule behind each
RuleIt is this exponential rule, translated
logb (mn) = logb m + logb nbx · by = bx+y
logb (mn) = logb m − logb nbxby = bx−y
logb (mr) = r · logb m(bx)y = bxy
logb (1m) = −logb mb−x = 1bx
logb 1 = 0b0 = 1
logb b = 1b1 = b

The third rule is the one that does the work in this course. It moves an exponent to the front as an ordinary multiplier, where you can divide by it. That is how the unknown escapes the exponent in Jane’s question.

The two you will stop having to think about

logb 1 = 0, because no power is needed to reach 1. logb b = 1, because one power of b is b. So ln 1 = 0, ln e = 1, log 1 = 0 and log 10 = 1, where log with no base written means base 10 and ln means base e.

Change of base, and the very practical reason it exists

Jane’s question needs log1.02 2. Your calculator has an ln key and a log key and nothing else. No calculator has a log base 1.02 key, and none ever will, because there are infinitely many possible bases. The change of base formula converts any logarithm into a ratio of logarithms in a base you do have.

Change of base

logb m = loga mloga bfor any convenient base a, in practice e or 10. The result is the same either way.

Why the formula is true, and a worked value of log5 90
  1. let y = log5 90
    Name the thing you want.
  2. 5y = 90
    The defining relationship, used to get rid of the logarithm.
  3. ln(5y) = ln 90
    Take a logarithm the calculator understands, of both sides.
  4. y · ln 5 = ln 90
    The power rule brings the exponent down in front. This is the whole trick.
  5. y = ln 90ln 5 ≈ 4.49981.6094
    Divide. Both logarithms are ordinary numbers from the calculator.
  6. log5 90 ≈ 2.796
    Sanity check it: 52 = 25 and 53 = 125, so the answer had to be between 2 and 3.
How long until 10 000 CHF at 2% becomes 20 000?
  1. 10 000(1.02)n = 20 000
    The question, written as an equation.
  2. (1.02)n = 2
    Divide by the starting capital. Notice that the starting amount has vanished: the doubling time does not depend on it.
  3. ln((1.02)n) = ln 2
    Take the natural logarithm of both sides. Both sides are positive, so this is legal.
  4. n · ln(1.02) = ln 2
    The power rule brings n down in front, where it is an ordinary factor.
  5. n = ln 2ln 1.02 ≈ 0.69310.019803 ≈ 35.0
    And notice the shape: this is log1.02 2 computed by change of base.
  6. n = 36 years
    Read it back. At n = 35 the balance is 19 999 CHF, a shade under. Interest is credited once a year, so the money first exceeds 20 000 during the 36th year.

The rules that do not exist

Every true rule above turns a multiplication into an addition. There is no rule for the logarithm of a sum, because addition inside a logarithm corresponds to nothing on the exponential side. The four statements below look like the true rules and are false. Test each once, so that you have seen it fail.

Four false rules, each tested with numbers
The false ruleA counter-example
ln(a + b) = ln a + ln ba = 3, b = 5: left ln 8 ≈ 2.079, right ≈ 2.708, which is really ln 15.
ln a · ln b = ln(ab)Same numbers: ln 3 · ln 5 ≈ 1.768, against ln 15 ≈ 2.708.
ln aln b = ln(a − b)a = 8, b = 2: left exactly 3, right ln 6 ≈ 1.792. That quotient is a change of base.
ln(x2) = 2 ln x for every xx = −4: left ln 16 ≈ 2.773, right needs ln(−4), which does not exist.
The power rule needs a strictly positive argument

logb (mr) = r · logb m holds only when m > 0. For x < 0 the quantity x2 is positive and its logarithm exists, but ln x does not, so the two sides are not equal. The correct statement for all non-zero x isln(x2) = 2 ln|x|Before pulling any exponent out in front, ask whether what is inside can be negative. When you meet a sum inside a logarithm, the only legal move is to factor it first: ln(3x + 12) = ln(3(x + 4)) = ln 3 + ln(x + 4).

Expanding a logarithm into pieces

Expanding means using the rules from left to right, until every logarithm contains a single letter. Work outwards in: the outermost quotient first, then the products inside it, then the powers. Convert every root into a fractional power before you start, because a root is invisible to the power rule until you do.

Expand ln(x3 yz5)
  1. ln(x3 yz5) = ln(x3y) − ln(z5)
    The outermost structure is a quotient, so it becomes a difference. One rule, one line.
  2. = ln(x3) + ln(y) − ln(z5)
    The first term is a product, so it becomes a sum. The minus sign in front of the last term has not moved.
  3. = ln(x3) + ln(y12) − ln(z5)
    Rewrite the root as a fractional power, so that the power rule can reach it.
  4. = 3 ln x + 12 ln y − 5 ln z
    Three applications of the power rule. Check with x = 2, y = 9, z = 3: both sides give ≈ −2.315.
Expand log(100x2y), in base 10
  1. = log(100x2) − log y
    A quotient becomes a difference.
  2. = log 100 + log(x2) − log y
    A product becomes a sum.
  3. = 2 + 2 log x − log y
    log 100 = 2 because 100 = 102, and the power rule handles the x2. Check with x = 5, y = 4: both sides give ≈ 2.7959.

Condensing pieces back into one logarithm

Condensing is the same rules read from right to left. It is what you do before solving an equation, because an equation with one logarithm on each side can have both removed at once.

The order is fixed: turn every multiplier in front into a power first, because coefficients cannot be joined. Only then combine the terms.

Condense 2 ln x + 3 ln y − ln z into one logarithm
  1. = ln(x2) + ln(y3) − ln z
    Every coefficient goes up as a power first. Nothing can be joined while the numbers sit in front.
  2. = ln(x2y3) − ln z
    A sum of logarithms becomes the logarithm of a product.
  3. = ln(x2y3z)
    A difference becomes a quotient. Check with x = 3, y = 2, z = 5: both sides give ≈ 2.6672.
Condense 12 log x − 2 log y
  1. = log(x12) − log(y2)
    Coefficients become powers. A half power is a square root.
  2. = log(x) − log(y2)
    Write the half power as a root, since that is how the answer is usually wanted.
  3. = log(xy2)
    A difference becomes a quotient. Check with x = 16, y = 3: both sides give ≈ −0.3522.

Solving equations with the rules

Two shapes come up again and again. The first is a quadratic in disguise, and a substitution reveals it. The second has logarithms on both sides, where the danger is a solution the algebra produces and the logarithm forbids.

Solve e2x − ex − 6 = 0
  1. e2x = (ex)2
    Rewrite the first term using (bx)y = bxy. Now the same quantity appears twice.
  2. let u = ex, with u > 0
    Substitute. The condition u > 0 is not optional: an exponential is always strictly positive, and this condition will do real work in two lines.
  3. u2 − u − 6 = 0
    An ordinary quadratic, which you can already solve.
  4. (u − 3)(u + 2) = 0
    Two numbers multiplying to −6 and adding to −1.
  5. u = 3 or u = −2
    Two roots of the quadratic, but not yet two answers to the question.
  6. u = −2 is rejected
    ex is strictly positive for every real x, so it can never equal −2. This candidate is discarded.
  7. ex = 3 → x = ln 3 ≈ 1.0986
    Undo the exponential with a logarithm. Check: e2 ln 3 = 9 and eln 3 = 3, so 9 − 3 − 6 = 0.
Substitution is the general move

Any equation a(b2x) + c(bx) + d = 0 becomes a quadratic under u = bx. 32x − 12(3x) + 27 = 0 becomes u2 − 12u + 27 = 0, so u = 3 or u = 9, giving x = 1 and x = 2. Both are positive, so both survive, and both check: at x = 2, 81 − 108 + 27 = 0.

Solve ln x + ln(x − 3) = ln 10
  1. x > 0 and x − 3 > 0
    Write the conditions down before solving, while you can still see what is inside each logarithm.
  2. so x > 3
    The two conditions together. Any answer at or below 3 will have to be rejected.
  3. ln(x(x − 3)) = ln 10
    Condense the left side: a sum of logarithms is the logarithm of a product.
  4. x(x − 3) = 10
    The logarithm is one-to-one, so equal logarithms mean equal arguments. Both sides lose their ln together.
  5. x2 − 3x − 10 = 0 → (x − 5)(x + 2) = 0
    An ordinary quadratic again.
  6. x = 5 or x = −2
    Two candidates from the algebra.
  7. x = 5
    x = −2 fails the condition x > 3, and concretely it would require ln(−2), which does not exist. Check the survivor: ln 5 + ln 2 = ln 10. Correct.
Condensing can invent a solution

Condensing widens what the expression accepts: ln x + ln(x − 3) needs x > 3, but ln(x2 − 3x) is happy at x = −2. The extra candidate was created by the step, not by the problem. So write the conditions down first, and check every candidate against them at the end.

Where marks are lost in this topic
  • Inventing a rule for a sum. ln(a + b) does not break up. Factor first or leave it alone.
  • Confusing ln aln b with ln a − ln b. The first is a change of base.
  • Using the power rule on a possibly negative argument. ln(x2) = 2 ln|x|, with the absolute value.
  • Keeping a rejected candidate, or rejecting it without saying why. The reason is where the mark is.
  • Forgetting to convert a root to a power. The power rule cannot see a root sign.
  • Combining logarithms while coefficients are still in front. Move them up as powers first.
What to remember
  • A logarithm is an exponent: logb m = y means by = m.
  • Product becomes sum, quotient becomes difference, power becomes a multiplier in front. logb 1 = 0 and logb b = 1.
  • Change of base: logb m = ln mln b, which exists because calculators have only two logarithm keys.
  • There is no rule for the logarithm of a sum, and a product or quotient of logarithms simplifies to nothing.
  • The power rule needs a strictly positive argument, so ln(x2) = 2 ln|x|.
  • An equation with b2x and bx is a quadratic under u = bx, and u must stay positive.
Part IVHomework and quizzes4 lessons

Part IV  ·  Lesson 1 of 4

Week 1 homework

Ten questions. Method and checkpoint for each; the official answer sheet and the solving video are the authority.

Before you read any of this. Attempt the question on paper. Then compare with the checkpoint. Only if they disagree, open the official answers PDF and the "Solving homework" video for week 1 on Cyberlearn. Those show the full working in the lecturers' own notation, which is the notation the exam will mark.
Three things to know about the week 1 answer sheet

Working through it against the question sheet turns up three places where the printed answer does not match the printed question. None changes what you need to learn, but all three will confuse you if you meet them cold.

  • 1.5: the question defines g(x) = |x − 2|; the answer sheet solves g(x) = |x − 3|. The two give different numbers. Ask which one is intended.
  • 1.7: the answer writes the multiplier as (0.085)t. It should be (0.985)t; the final figure of 334 485 is computed from 0.985 and is right.
  • 1.10: the supply equation should be read as p = log(10 + q2). With q = 1980 that gives log(1000) = 3, which is the printed answer.
1.1 · zero profit

Revenue 100q, variable cost 2 per unit, fixed cost 1200

Find the values of q for which total revenue equals total cost.

Method
  1. Write both sides: revenue 100q, cost 2q + 1200. Set them equal.
