  2. Divide through by 2 to make the numbers smaller before squaring. This is optional but halves the arithmetic.
  3. Square both sides to remove the root. Squaring can introduce false solutions, so check at the end.
  4. You now have a quadratic. Move everything to one side and factor. With b = −1300 and c = +360 000 the two numbers are both negative: −400 and −900.

Checkpoint. q = 400 or q = 900. Two break-even points. Interpret them: revenue exceeds cost only between 400 and 900 units. Below 400 the fixed cost of 1 200 has not been recovered. Above 900 the linear cost has overtaken the flattening revenue curve, because 100q grows more and more slowly while 2q does not. A curve against a line can cross twice, once, or not at all, so always solve rather than assume.

1.2 · two pay scales

9.00 per hour, or 320 plus 3 for each hour under 40

For a job taking t hours with t ≤ 40, when is the hourly rate better?

Method
  1. Write each scheme as a function of t. Hourly: 9t. Per job: 320 + 3(40 − t), where 40 − t is the number of hours saved.
  2. "Better" means greater, so write an inequality, not an equation.
  3. Expand, collect, and divide. Watch whether you divide by a positive or a negative number.

Checkpoint. t > 36.7 hours, approximately. Interpret it: below about 36.7 hours the per-job deal pays more, because finishing early earns the bonus.

1.3 · value of a business

Capital 50 000, weekly income 7 200, weekly expenses 4 900

Express the value V after t weeks.

Method

Find the weekly surplus first, then recognise the shape: a starting amount plus a constant amount per period is a linear function. Multiplied by t, not raised to a power, because retained profit here does not itself earn a return.

Checkpoint. V(t) = 50 000 + 2 300t.

1.4 · a supply function

p = q48

How many pounds are supplied at 8.39 per pound, and at 19.49? What happens as the price rises?

Method

The relation gives price in terms of quantity, and the question asks for quantity, so invert it first: q = 48p. Then substitute each price. Answer the third part in words, referring to the sign of the slope.

Checkpoint. 402.72 and 935.52 pounds. Supply rises with price, which is what an upward-sloping supply curve means.

1.5 · evaluating two functions

An absolute value, and a case-defined function

For g(x) = |x − 2| find g(10), g(3), g(−3). For G(x) = x − 1 if x ≥ 3 and 3 − x2 if x < 3, find G(8), G(3), G(−1), G(1).

Method

For the absolute value: compute the inside, then drop the sign. For the case-defined function: check which condition the input satisfies before computing, and pay attention to G(3), where ≥ means the first branch owns the boundary.

Checkpoint. With the question sheet's |x − 2|: 8, 1, 5. The answer sheet, using |x − 3|, prints 7, 0, 6. For G: 7, 2, 2, 2, on which both agree.

1.6 · group ticket pricing

9.50 each below 12 people, 8.75 each from 12

Write a case-defined function for the cost of n tickets.

Method

Two branches, split at 12. Decide which branch owns n = 12: the words "12 or more" put it in the cheaper branch. Write the condition with the correct inequality sign, and remember the cost is the price times n, not the price alone.

Checkpoint. c(n) = 9.5n for 0 ≤ n < 12, and 8.75n for n ≥ 12. Notice that a group of 12 pays 105 while a group of 11 pays 104.50, so buying a twelfth ticket you do not need is almost free.

1.7 · a declining population

350 000 falling 1.5% a year

What is the population after three years, to the nearest person?

Method

A constant percentage change per period is exponential, not linear. Build the multiplier 1 − 0.015 = 0.985 and raise it to the power 3. Do not subtract 1.5% three times.

Checkpoint. P(3) ≈ 334 485. If your answer is near 334 250 you subtracted 4.5% once; if it is tiny, you used 0.085 as the answer sheet mistakenly prints.

1.8 · two logarithms

log6 36 and log16 4

Method

Ask the definition's question: what power of the base gives this number? Write the inside as a power of the base and read off the exponent. No calculator is needed or wanted.

Checkpoint. 2 and 12.

1.9 · a cost equation with a logarithm

c = 5q ln q + 15, at q = 12

Method

Pure substitution and careful key-pressing. Use the ln key, not log. Compute ln 12 first, multiply by 5 and by 12, then add 15. Round at the very end, to two decimals as asked.

Checkpoint. ≈ 164.09. If you get about 79.7 you used log instead of ln, which is the single most common slip in this question.

1.10 · a supply equation with a logarithm

p = log(10 + q2), at q = 1980

Method

Work inside the bracket first, then take the base-10 logarithm. The numbers are chosen so that the bracket lands on a clean power of ten, which is a hint that you have read the formula correctly.

Checkpoint. Inside: 10 + 990 = 1000, so p = 3. If the bracket gives 995 you have read the formula as 10 + q2, and the logarithm will not come out whole, which is the signal to re-read it.

Part IV  ·  Lesson 2 of 4

Week 1 review quiz

Seven multiple-choice questions. The same format as the week 9 midterm, so treat it as a timed rehearsal.

Where the answers are. The quiz on Cyberlearn marks itself and shows the correct option as soon as you submit, so it is its own answer key. When an option still does not make sense, the "Solving homework" and week video for week 1 cover the same techniques in the lecturers' notation. The table below gives the technique and a checkpoint, not a worked solution.
How to work an MCQ in this course
  1. Solve it properly first, without looking at the options. The wrong options, called distractors, are built from the usual errors, so a wrong method often lands exactly on a printed option and feels like confirmation.
  2. Only then match your answer to the list.
  3. If your answer is not there, do not force the nearest one. Check whether "none of the above" is the honest answer, because in this course it sometimes is.
  4. Watch the clock: 60 minutes for the midterm means roughly two minutes a question, so a question that has taken five needs to be abandoned and revisited.
The seven questions, the technique each tests, and where it is explained here
QQuestionTechniqueCheckpoint
1x + 4x = 15Fractional equation: state x ≠ 0, cross-multiplyx = −5
2(x + 1)2 + 4x = x2 + 3Expand the square; the x2 cancels, leaving a linear equationx = 13
3x3 − x = 0Factor completely: x(x − 1)(x + 1)x = 0, 1, −1
4f(x) = 2xx + 3Domain: set the denominator to zeroℝ\{−3}
5f(x) = 2xx2 − 9x + 14Domain: factor the quadratic denominatorℝ\{2, 7}
6ln(e4) + log(0.001)Each logarithm in its own base; 0.001 = 10−31
7exp(⅓ ln(log(10…)))Work outward from the innermost logarithm read the exponent from the slidesee below
Question 3: why the answer is all three values

The temptation is to divide both sides by x, giving x2 = 1 and the answer ±1. That is wrong, and it is wrong in a way worth naming: dividing by x silently assumes x ≠ 0, and throws away the solution x = 0.

The safe move is always to factor instead of dividing: x(x2 − 1) = x(x − 1)(x + 1) = 0, so a product is zero when any factor is, giving 0, 1 and −1. The option offering only ±1 exists precisely to catch the division.

Question 7: the method, and an honest caveat

Method. Nested functions unwind from the inside. First log(10k) = k. Then take ln of that. Then multiply by one third. Then apply exp, which undoes the ln.

The reason the question works at all is that the exponent is a perfect cube. If the inner value is n3, then ln(n3) = 3 ln n, the one third cancels the 3, and exp(ln n) = n. So the answer is simply n, the number being cubed.

Caveat The exponent on the slide did not extract cleanly into these notes, so read it from the original quiz. If the inner exponent is 23 = 8, the answer is 2; if it is 27, the answer is 3; if 64, then 4. The method is identical in every case, and that method is the examinable part.

Part IV  ·  Lesson 3 of 4

Week 2 homework

Twelve questions, including three review problems. The official answers appear on Cyberlearn one week after the homework is set.

These checkpoints are not official

For week 1 there is a published answer sheet, so the checkpoints above can be compared against it. For week 2 the official answers were not yet available when these notes were written. Everything below is worked from the course's own methods and is internally checked, but the answer sheet and the solving video are the version that counts. Where they differ from a checkpoint here, they are right and this is wrong.

Check Cyberlearn first. The week 2 official answers PDF and the "Solving homework" video are published one week after the homework is set. Open them once you have attempted each question, and let them overrule anything here. The methods below are there to get you moving, not to replace the lecturers' working.
2.1 · nine combinations

f(x) = x2 − 1 and g(x) = x2 + x

Method
  1. Parts a to f are the four arithmetic operations. Do them symbolically first, then substitute the number only where asked.
  2. For the quotient, factor before you simplify: x2 − 1 = (x − 1)(x + 1) and x2 + x = x(x + 1), so the (x + 1) cancels, but only for x ≠ −1.
  3. Parts g and h are compositions. Substitute the entire inner function in brackets.
  4. Part i asks for a value: evaluate inside first, then outside.

Checkpoints. (f+g)(x) = 2x2 + x − 1; (f−g)(x) = −x − 1; (f−g)(−12) = −12; (fg)(x) = x4 + x3 − x2 − x; (fg)(x) = x − 1x for x ≠ 0, −1; (fg)(−12) = 3; (f∘g)(x) = (x2 + x)2 − 1; (g∘f)(x) = (x2 − 1)2 + (x2 − 1); (g∘f)(−3) = 72.

2.2 · both orders

f(x) = 3x2 + 5, g(x) = 4 − 2x

Method

Evaluate the inner function at the number, then feed that single number into the outer one. Two short steps beat one long substitution.

Checkpoints. f(g(2)) = 5 and g(f(2)) = −30. The gap between them is the point of the exercise.

2.3 · a function composed with itself

f(x) = x2 + 2x − 1, find (f ∘ f)(x)

Method

Replace every x in the formula with the whole formula, in brackets. You may leave the answer unexpanded unless asked; if you do expand, expect a quartic.

Checkpoint. (x2 + 2x − 1)2 + 2(x2 + 2x − 1) − 1.

2.4 · output, employees and revenue

q = f(m) = 40m − m24 and r = g(q) = 40q

Find (g ∘ f)(m) and say what it describes.

Method

Substitute f into g, then simplify by cancelling the 4 into the 40. The second half of the question is worth as much as the first: name the composite in business language, with its units.

Checkpoint. 400m − 10m2, the total daily revenue in francs as a function of the number of employees. Note that it is a downward parabola, so revenue peaks at some staffing level and falls after it. Week 8 will find that peak with a derivative.

2.5 · a supply function and its inverse

p = q48 for q > 0

Method

Solve for q, then demonstrate the relationship by composing in both directions and obtaining the identity.

Checkpoint. q = 48p, and both p(q(p)) = p and q(p(q)) = q. This is the same pair as week 1 homework 1.4, now named as an inverse.

2.6 and 2.7 · reading a graph

Estimate values, domain, range and an x-intercept

Method
  1. f(0) means: go to x = 0, move vertically to the curve, read the height.
  2. The domain is the shadow of the curve on the horizontal axis; the range is its shadow on the vertical axis. Watch for filled and hollow endpoints, which decide whether a bound is included.
  3. An x-intercept is where the curve meets the horizontal axis.
  4. These say "estimate", so a reasonable read from the picture is the expected answer.

No checkpoint. These two questions depend on figures that are part of the homework PDF and cannot be reproduced here. Read them from the original, and check against the answer sheet.

2.8 · intercepts and sketches

y = x3 + x  and  y = 4x2 − 16

Method

Set x = 0, then set y = 0 and solve. Factor before solving. For the sketch, plot the intercepts, then use the family to decide the shape: a cubic rises from lower left to upper right, a positive parabola is a U.

Checkpoints. (a) only (0, 0), because x2 + 1 has no real root. (b) (0, −16) and (±2, 0).

2.9 · intercepts of implicit equations

Three equations that are not written as y = f(x)

Method

The technique does not change just because y is not alone: substitute x = 0 and solve for y, then substitute y = 0 and solve for x. Some of these have two x-intercepts, some have one point only.

Checkpoints. For x2 + xy + y2 = 0: both substitutions give (0, 0) and nothing else. For 9x2 + 4y2 = 25: y = ±52 and x = ±53, four intercepts, because the curve is an ellipse. check the original The first equation of the three did not extract legibly into these notes; read it from the homework PDF and apply the same two substitutions.

2.10 · price, quantity and work hours

p = 1q2 + 2 + 1 and q = w + 1

Method
  1. For part a, compose. The useful observation is that q appears only as q2, and squaring the root removes it cleanly: q2 = w + 1.
  2. For part b, invert the composite: subtract the 1, take the reciprocal, then subtract the 3.

Checkpoints. (a) p(w) = 1w + 3 + 1. (b) w(p) = 1p − 1 − 3. If part a gives you something with a w still in it, you have read the second relation as w + 1 rather than w + 1; the clean cancellation is the sign that the second reading is intended.

2.11 · a demand function

P(q) = 2q + 1 + 3 for q > 0

Method
  1. Peel the layers in reverse: subtract 3, divide by 2, square, subtract 1.
  2. For part b, substitute Q(p) into P and simplify until only p remains. The square root and the square must annihilate each other.

Checkpoints. (a) Q(p) = (p − 3)24 − 1. (b) substituting gives 2(p − 3)24 + 3 = 2 · |p − 3|2 + 3, and since P(q) ≥ 3 for every q > 0 we know p ≥ 3, so |p − 3| = p − 3 and the whole thing collapses to p, the identity. Writing the absolute value is not pedantry: A2 = |A| in general, and the exam expects the justification of the sign.

2.12 · MIC-ADO

Meals = 1000restaurants + 1 + 100, Revenue = Meals2 − 500

Express the number of nearby restaurants as a function of revenue, then find it when revenue is 89 500.

Method
  1. This is a composition you must run backwards, through two functions. Undo the outer one first: from revenue, recover meals by adding 500 and taking the square root.
  2. Then undo the inner one: subtract 100, and invert the fraction to free the number of restaurants.
  3. For part b, substitute and keep an eye out for the clean numbers, which confirm the algebra.

Checkpoints. (a) R = 1000Revenue + 500 − 100 − 1. (b) 90 000 = 300, then 1000200 = 5, so 4 restaurants. Verify forwards: 4 restaurants give 300 meals, and 3002 − 500 = 89 500. That round trip is the check to run on every inverse question.

Four multiple-choice questions on combining, composing and inverting.

Where the answers are. Submit the quiz on Cyberlearn and it shows you the correct option straight away. For the working behind it, use the week 2 "Solving homework" video and the video of the week. The checkpoints in the table are for confirming your own arithmetic, nothing more.

Question 2 deserves care

Working it properly gives −5(x2 + x) + 3 = −5x2 − 5x + 3. Several printed options differ from that only by one sign, and one of them squares the outer function instead of substituting into it, which is the error the question is hunting for. Part V  ·  Lesson 2 of 8

Your two sheets

Four sides of notes, allowed in every exam of the module. They are worth building deliberately.

What the rules actually permit

A personal summary of at most two sheets, recto verso, handwritten or typed, in the midterm and both final exams. That is four sides. They are checked, so stay within two physical sheets.

How to build them, starting in week 1
  1. Add to them weekly, never at the end. A sheet assembled in week 15 is a transcription exercise. A sheet built weekly is a revision exercise that happens to produce a sheet.
  2. Put on it what you get wrong, not what you find easy. If you always remember that log 1 = 0, it is wasting space. If you keep dropping the minus in −4ac, that belongs in capitals.
  3. Prefer one worked example to three formulas. A single fully worked inverse function tells you the method; the bare definition does not, under time pressure.
  4. Write the traps as instructions to yourself. "Bracket the whole numerator." "Check Δ sign." "Read the exponent twice."
  5. Leave white space. A dense wall of text cannot be searched in a 60-minute MCQ. Use headings, and keep the same layout all year so you know where to look.
Side 1 · Algebra

Quadratic formula with a worked example. Factoring patterns. Powers and roots. The sign-flip rule for inequalities. Domain checklist.

Side 2 · Functions

The four operations. Composition with an order reminder. The four-step inverse method with one full example. Intercepts.

Side 3 · Exp and log

The definition both ways. The product, quotient and power rules. The four exp-ln links. The three false rules, crossed out.

Side 4 · Later material

Left empty for now. Derivative rules arrive in week 5 and will fill it faster than you expect.

One thing not to put on them. Anything you have never used. A formula copied from the slides that you have not applied in an exercise will not become usable during the exam; it will only cost you the seconds you spend reading it.

Part V  ·  Lesson 3 of 8

How marks are earned in an open-question exam

The two fall and spring exams are 120 minutes of open questions. A correct number with no working is worth less than correct working with an arithmetic slip.

The midterm is multiple choice, so only the final letter counts there. The two 120-minute exams are different. A marker reads what you wrote and awards marks for the steps, not only for the answer. That changes how you should write, and most of the marks students leave on the table are lost to presentation rather than to mathematics.

The shape of a full-mark answer
  1. Name what you are about to do. One short line. "Set revenue equal to cost." "Take the natural logarithm of both sides." The marker now knows your plan and can follow a slip without losing you the method marks.
  2. Define every symbol you introduce. If you write q, say what q counts and in what unit. An undefined symbol is an unreadable answer.
  3. One operation per line. The same rule the derivations in this document follow. Two steps in one line is where a marker stops being able to give partial credit.
  4. State the conditions you are relying on. "The denominator is not zero here." "This root is positive because a quantity cannot be negative." "The function is one-to-one on this domain, so the inverse exists." These sentences carry marks of their own.
  5. Check the candidate solutions. Anything that came from squaring or from clearing a denominator must be tested against the original equation, in writing.
  6. Answer the question that was asked, in a sentence, with units. If the question says "advise the manager", the last line is advice, not a number.
The five presentation habits that cost the most
  • No working. A bare number earns the answer mark and nothing else. If it is wrong you get zero for a question you nearly solved.
  • Crossing out a whole page. If you change approach, draw one line through the old attempt and start again below. Heavily crossed work cannot be given credit, and sometimes the abandoned attempt was the correct one.
  • Losing the units. 4 050 is not an answer. 4 050 CHF a month is.
  • Rounding too early. Carry the exact value, ln 2ln 1.02 or 1103, through the algebra and round only on the final line. Rounding at an intermediate step changes the last digits and can turn a correct method into a wrong answer.
  • Not reading the verb. "Find" wants a number. "Show that" wants you to arrive at a given result, so you must not start from it. "Interpret" wants a sentence about the business. "Justify" wants a reason, and the reason is the mark.
How to spend 120 minutes

Five minutes reading the whole paper and marking the questions you can do immediately. Then those questions first, in any order, because early marks are the cheapest marks. Watch the mark allocation: a part worth 4 marks should not take fifteen minutes, and if it is taking that long you have misread it. Leave ten minutes at the end to go back to anything unfinished and to write the interpretation sentences you skipped. An unfinished question with a clear method statement still scores.

What to remember
  • Method marks are most of the paper. Write the method even when you cannot finish.
  • Define your symbols, state your conditions, check your candidates.
  • Keep exact values until the final line, then round and give units.
  • Read the verb in the question and answer that verb.

Part V  ·  Lesson 4 of 8

Where marks are lost

Each one paired with the habit that prevents it.

1 · Distributing over a sum

(a + b)2 ≠ a2 + b2, and the same for roots and logarithms.

Habit: whenever a sum sits inside a power, root or logarithm, stop and expand or factor properly.

2 · The sign of c in the discriminant

With c = −18, −4ac is +216.

Habit: write a =, b =, c = in a column with signs before touching the formula.

3 · Dividing by x

It destroys the solution x = 0.

Habit: factor instead of dividing, always.

4 · Forgetting the domain

Simplifying hides an excluded value that was there in the original.

Habit: write the exclusions from the given expression, before simplifying anything.

5 · Composition in the wrong order

g ∘ f is not f ∘ g.

Habit: say "g after f" aloud, and substitute the right-hand function first.

6 · Substituting without brackets

(2p + 1)2, never 2p2 + 1.

Habit: write the bracket before you write anything inside it.

7 · Reading f−1 as 1f

They are different objects.

Habit: check your inverse by composing; if it does not collapse to x, it is wrong.

8 · The minus in a subtraction of functions

It applies to every term of the second function.

Habit: write f(x) − [g(x)] with the bracket, then distribute.

9 · log instead of ln

Two different keys, two different answers, no warning.

Habit: circle which one the question uses before reaching for the calculator.

10 · Percentages added rather than compounded

Up 20% then down 20% is a 4% loss.

Habit: convert every percentage to a multiplier and multiply them.

11 · Calculator precedence

10 ÷ 2 + 3 is 8, not 2.

Habit: bracket every numerator and every denominator, even when it looks unnecessary.

12 · Answering with a bare number

A quantity without units or a sentence is an incomplete answer in an open-question exam.

Habit: finish every applied question with one sentence naming the quantity and its unit.

When you are stuck in the exam

Write down what you are looking for and what you have been given, in words, with units. Most blocked questions in this course are blocked at the modelling step, not the algebra step, and naming the variable usually unblocks them. If it does not, move on and come back: in a 60-minute MCQ, five minutes on one question costs you two others.

Show the answers and the reasoning

Mark it honestly. Below 12 out of 20, go back to the sections the failed questions came from before doing anything else. Between 12 and 16, you know the material and are losing marks to speed and to signs. Above 16, move on to the open-question paper, which is a different skill.

1. C. Factor the denominator: x2 − 4x + 3 = (x − 1)(x − 3), which vanishes at 1 and 3. D comes from a sign error when factoring. The numerator plays no part in a domain.

2. A. Require 5 − 2x ≥ 0, so 5 ≥ 2x and x ≤ 52. B is the answer you get if you divide by −2 without reversing the inequality.

3. D. A logarithm needs a strictly positive argument, so 2x − 6 > 0 and x > 3. A fails because ln 0 does not exist.

4. B. At x = 2 the condition x ≥ 2 holds, so use the second line: 3(2) − 1 = 5. At x = −1 use the first: (−1)2 = 1. The sum is 6. C is what you get by taking the wrong branch at the boundary, which is the whole point of the question.

5. A. Inside first: f(2) = 5. Then g(5) = 2(5) − 3 = 7. B is (f ∘ g)(2), the other order, which is a different function.

6. D. Write y = 3x − 52, multiply by 2 to get 2y = 3x − 5, add 5, divide by 3: x = 2y + 53. Then swap the letters. B is the reciprocal, not the inverse.

7. B. f(−3) and f(3) are both 5, so the function is not one-to-one and cannot be run backwards: from an output of 5 you cannot tell which input produced it. The other three are strictly increasing on ℝ. Restricting the domain to x ≥ 0 would repair A.

8. C. Ask what power of 3 gives 81. Since 34 = 81, the answer is 4. A is 81 written as 33 confused with 34.

9. D. ln(e5) = 5 because ln and exp undo each other, and log(100) = 2 because log is base 10. So 5 − 2 = 3. A adds instead of subtracting.

10. B. A sum of logarithms is the logarithm of the product, and a difference is the logarithm of the quotient. C is the false rule the document warns about: there is no rule for the logarithm of a sum.

11. A. Take the natural logarithm of both sides: x ln 5 = ln 20, so x = ln 20ln 5 = 2.99571.6094 ≈ 1.861. C is the same fraction upside down. Check it: 51.861 ≈ 20.

12. C. Multipliers compose, they do not cancel: 1.2 × 0.8 = 0.96, a fall of 4%. The 20% fall is taken on the larger figure, which is why the round trip loses money. D is the intuitive wrong answer.

13. B. 4000 × 1.035 = 4000 × 1.159274 ≈ 4637.10. D is simple interest, 4000 × (1 + 0.15), which ignores that each year earns interest on the previous years.

14. D. 3x2 = 12, so x2 = 4 and x = ±2. B forgets to divide by 3 first. C forgets that a square root of a positive number has two signs.

15. C. Δ = (−4)2 − 4(2)(5) = 16 − 40 = −24, which is negative, so there is no solution in ℝ. Do not force a square root of a negative number.

16. A. Note first that x ≠ 1. Cross-multiply: x + 2 = 3(x − 1) = 3x − 3, so 5 = 2x and x = 2.5. That is allowed, since it is not 1. B is the excluded value itself.

17. C. Add the two equations to eliminate y: 3x = 9, so x = 3, and then y = 1. D is the pair written in the wrong order, which the exam will mark wrong.

18. B. −3x > 9. Dividing by −3 reverses the direction: x < −3. C is the answer if you forget to flip, and it is the most common error in the topic.

19. A. A distance of 4 from zero means 2x − 6 = 4 or 2x − 6 = −4, giving x = 5 or x = 1. B keeps only the positive case.

20. D. a = −2 < 0, so the parabola opens downwards and the turning point is a maximum. It sits at x = −122(−2) = 3, and f(3) = −18 + 36 − 7 = 11. A has the right point but the wrong shape; C forgets the −7.

What to remember
  • Solve first, look at the options second. The distractors are designed to catch the common error.
  • Three minutes a question. A question that has taken five needs to be abandoned and revisited.
  • No negative marking, so every box gets an answer even if it is a guess.
  • When your answer is not on the list, suspect a sign or a domain condition before you suspect the paper.

Functions, domains and inverses

(c) A roasting machine bought for 80 000 CHF loses 12% of its value every year. Write its value V(t) after t years, and find the first whole year in which it is worth less than 30 000 CHF. (8)

Spending x thousand CHF on advertising produces N(x) = 200x + 1500 app users. Revenue from n users is R(n) = 12n − 400 CHF.

(a) Express revenue directly as a function of advertising spend. (6)

(b) How much must be spent to reach 50 000 CHF of revenue? (6)

Question 5  · 20 marks

A demand curve and the revenue it produces

The demand for XY Coffee Co's espresso blend is p = 90 − 0.5q CHF, for 0 ≤ q ≤ 180 kilograms a week.

(a) Interpret the number 90 and the number −0.5 in business terms, with units. (4)

(b) Write weekly revenue R(q) and find the quantity that maximises it, and the revenue there. (7)

(c) At which quantities is weekly revenue exactly 4 000 CHF? (6)

(d) Explain why there are two such quantities, and which one the firm should prefer. (3)

Show the full solutions and the mark scheme

Question 1

(a) Two conditions. The root needs x − 2 ≥ 0, so x ≥ 2. The denominator needs x − 5 ≠ 0, so x ≠ 5. Both must hold at once, so the domain is [2 ; 5[ ∪ ]5 ; +∞[, which is the same set as {x ∈ ℝ : x ≥ 2 and x ≠ 5}.

(b) (g ∘ h)(x) = g(x2 + 2) = 3(x2 + 2) − 1 = 3x2 + 5. And (h ∘ g)(x) = h(3x − 1) = (3x − 1)2 + 2 = 9x2 − 6x + 3. At x = 1: (g ∘ h)(1) = 8 and (h ∘ g)(1) = 6. Two different numbers from the same pair of functions and the same input, so composition is not commutative.

(c) y = 3x − 1 gives x = y + 13, so g−1(x) = x + 13. g is a straight line with a non-zero slope, so it is strictly increasing and therefore one-to-one. h is not: h(−1) = h(1) = 3, so from an output of 3 you cannot recover the input.

(d) x = 0 gives the y-intercept (0, −1). y = 0 gives 3x = 1, so the x-intercept is (13, 0).

Mark scheme, question 1
PartWhat earns the marksMarks
(a)Root condition 1, denominator condition 1, combining them 1, set form 1, interval form 15
(b)Each composite 2, both evaluations 1, the conclusion that they differ 16
(c)Correct inverse 3, one-to-one justification for g 2, counterexample for h 16
(d)Each intercept 1, written as a point 13

Question 2

(a) Divide by 3 first: 2x = 32. Since 32 = 25, x = 5. Taking logarithms also works and earns the same marks: x = ln 32ln 2 = 5.

(b) The domain comes first: x > 0 and x − 3 > 0, so x > 3. Combine the left side with the product rule: ln(x(x − 3)) = ln 10. Both sides are logarithms in the same base, so x(x − 3) = 10, that is x2 − 3x − 10 = 0, which factors as (x − 5)(x + 2) = 0. The candidates are 5 and −2. Only x = 5 survives, because −2 is not greater than 3 and would ask for the logarithm of a negative number. Saying why you reject it is worth a mark.

(c) Losing 12% means multiplying by 0.88 each year, so V(t) = 80 000 × 0.88t. Set 80 000 × 0.88t < 30 000, so 0.88t < 0.375. Take natural logarithms: t ln 0.88 < ln 0.375. Now ln 0.88 is negative, so dividing reverses the inequality: t > ln 0.375ln 0.88 = −0.9808−0.1278 ≈ 7.67. The first whole year is t = 8. Check it: V(8) ≈ 28 771 and V(7) ≈ 32 694.

Mark scheme, question 2
PartWhat earns the marksMarks

(b)Domain stated 2, product rule 1, quadratic formed 1, factored 1, correct root 1, rejection justified 17
(c)Multiplier 0.88 identified 2, model written 1, inequality set up 1, logarithms taken 1, direction reversed 2, answer as a whole year 18

Question 3

(a) Let q be the number of boxes sold in a month. C(q) = 14q + 9 000, R(q) = 32q, and P(q) = 32q − (14q + 9 000) = 18q − 9 000, all in CHF a month. The 18 is the contribution margin, what each box adds once its own variable cost is paid.

(b) Break-even is P(q) = 0, so 18q = 9 000 and q = 500 boxes. Revenue there is 32 × 500, that is 16 000 CHF. The shortcut is worth knowing: break-even quantity is fixed costcontribution margin.

(c) P(900) = 18(900) − 9 000 = 16 200 − 9 000, so 7 200 CHF a month.

(d) The new contribution margin is 35 − 14 = 21 CHF, so profit becomes 21 × 780 − 9 000 = 16 380 − 9 000, that is 7 380 CHF. That is 180 CHF a month better, so on these figures the rise is worth making. Say the condition out loud, because it carries a mark: the conclusion depends entirely on the estimate of 780 boxes, and the proposal breaks even against the old profit at 7 200 + 9 00021, that is 772 boxes. Below roughly 772 boxes the price rise loses money.

PartWhat earns the marksMarks

(b)Setting profit or revenue equal to cost 2, quantity 2, revenue 26
(c)Substitution 2, arithmetic 1, units 14

Question 4

(a) Substitute the whole of N into R: R(N(x)) = 12(200x + 1500) − 400 = 2400x + 18 000 − 400, so R(N(x)) = 2400x + 17 600 CHF, with x in thousands of CHF.

(b) 2400x + 17 600 = 50 000 gives 2400x = 32 400 and x = 13.5, that is 13 500 CHF of advertising. Watch the unit: the answer is 13.5 in the model's own unit, and the sentence must convert it.

(c) Solve for x: x = R − 17 6002400. A manager uses it backwards, to turn a revenue target into the advertising budget that reaches it, which is exactly what part (b) did once.

(d) x ≥ 0, because you cannot spend a negative amount on advertising. A second acceptable answer is an upper bound from the marketing budget, since the linear model cannot keep adding 200 users per thousand CHF for ever.

PartWhat earns the marksMarks

Question 5

(a) The 90 is the price in CHF per kilogram at which demand falls to zero, the highest price anyone would pay. The −0.5 is the slope: every extra kilogram the firm wants to sell requires the price to drop by 0.50 CHF per kilogram. Units are the mark here.

(b) R(q) = pq = q(90 − 0.5q), so R(q) = 90q − 0.5q2. That is a parabola with a = −0.5 < 0, so it opens downwards and its vertex is a maximum, at q = −902(−0.5) = 90. Then R(90) = 8 100 − 0.5(8 100) = 8 100 − 4 050, so the maximum is 4 050 CHF at q = 90 kg. That quantity is inside the stated range, which you should say.

(c) 90q − 0.5q2 = 4 000. Multiply by 2 and rearrange: q2 − 180q + 8 000 = 0. Then Δ = 32 400 − 32 000 = 400 and Δ = 20, so q = 180 ± 202, giving q = 80 kg or q = 100 kg.

(d) Revenue rises to its peak at 90 kg and falls afterwards, so every revenue level below the maximum is reached twice, once on the way up and once on the way down. The firm should prefer 80 kg: the same revenue for fewer kilograms produced, so lower cost and higher profit. This is the standard follow-up and it is worth all three marks on its own.

After you mark it
  • Count separately the marks you lost to mathematics and the marks you lost to presentation: a missing unit, an unstated domain, an unjustified rejection, a missing interpretation sentence. The second pile is the easiest twenty marks you will ever recover.
  • Anywhere you wrote the right number with no working, rewrite that part properly. On the day it is worth double.
  • Any part you could not start is a section to reread, not a question to remember.

Part V  ·  Lesson 8 of 8

The road ahead

Exactly how much of the examined course is in this document, when the rest arrives, and what to do with each week as it lands.

How much of the exam this document currently covers

Be clear about this before you rely on it. This document teaches Part 0 and weeks 1 and 2 in full, which is everything the course has released. The rest of the semester is locked on Cyberlearn and opens one week at a time.

So it will carry you through the first weeks completely, and it will not, on its own, get you through the midterm on 9 November 2026, which also examines weeks 3 to 8. Nothing here is invented from the syllabus to fill that gap, because guessing at the lecturers' notation and their choice of method would do more harm than leaving it out. Each week's deck, homework and quiz can be added to the same depth as soon as it is published.

What to do with each new week, the day it opens
  1. The material appears on Cyberlearn at 20:00 the evening before the class. Week 3 opens on 27 September at 20:00, week 4 on 4 October, and so on through the semester.
  2. Read the slides once before the lecture, without trying to understand everything. You are looking for the vocabulary, not the content.
  3. Attempt the homework before the official answers are published one week later. This is the part that cannot be skipped.
  4. Watch the "Solving homework" video afterwards and compare it with what you wrote, especially the notation.
  5. Take the review quiz against a clock, because the midterm is a timed MCQ and speed is a separate skill.
  6. Add one line to your two sheets. One line a week is eleven lines by the midterm, and they will be the right eleven.

The two things that carry the whole year

First, the idea of a function: a rule from input to output, with a domain. Derivatives measure how it changes, integrals accumulate it, a regression estimates it from data, and a matrix holds many of them at once. Second, the modelling cycle: question, model, data, answer, decision. Every exam question is a small trip around that loop, and the marks are mostly at the two ends, where words become mathematics and mathematics becomes advice.

A study plan that fits the calendar
  • Now: finish Part 0 until none of it is slow. It is the cheapest work you will ever do in this module.
  • Each week: attempt the homework before the answers appear, watch the solving video afterwards, take the quiz timed, and add one line to your two sheets.
  • Before week 9: redo every quiz under 60-minute conditions. The midterm is MCQ, and speed is a skill you can only practise against a clock.
  • Week 6: do the self-study case properly. It is examinable, and there is no lecture to fall back on.
